# Goal

This roadmap continues #14199, initiated by @ClawSeven, and builds on the community's work toward robust, efficient block-diffusion serving and Jev-style decisions on diffusion LLMs.

Carry forward unfinished serving goals alongside newer work. Fixes for crashes and wrong results on main come before new features. Full-sequence models get baseline compatibility. Checked items record merged work. Unchecked items track remaining work or evaluation. Phases can overlap. Jev-style decisions on causal models are tracked separately, starting with #40826.

# Roadmap

### Phase 1: Shared runtime and request lifecycle

- [ ] Complete shared scheduling support.

  - [x] Dynamic batching. #14883

  - [ ] FDFO + LowConfidence overlap scheduling. @Betelgeu #40756
  - [ ] Extend overlap to other algorithms after state-lifetime qualification.
  - [ ] Derive the default running-request count and graph capture sizes from available memory instead of serving one request at a time.

- [ ] Fail early on unsupported configurations.

  - [ ] Refuse or support attention data parallelism, which crashes today.

  - [ ] Reject sampling and grammar fields that the selected algorithm does not apply.

- [ ] Harden request lifecycle and caching.

  - [ ] Qualify committed streaming, EOS/stops, cancellation, and final assembly. @zxr-creator

### Phase 2: Prefill and CUDA graphs

### Phase 3: Models, decoding, and backends

  - [x] SDAR dense and MoE models. #19044
  - [x] DiffusionGemma text and image-input serving. #34061
  - [x] DiffusionGemma FA4 and CUDA graphs on Blackwell. #42239
  - [ ] Route `sglang serve` dLLM launches to the LLM runtime. #40942
  - [ ] Quantized DiffusionGemma checkpoints, FP8 first.
  - [ ] Radix cache and chunked prefill for DiffusionGemma.
  - [x] LLaDA2.2 block routing. #31768
  - [x] LLaDA2.2 insertion/deletion decoding. #31773
  - [ ] LLaDA2.2 routing and editing on Ascend. #32280
  - [ ] Qualify LLaDA2.2 mini and 128K context with a documented launch command.
  - [ ] Nemotron Labs Diffusion with its autoregressive, block-diffusion, and LinearSpec modes. #25803

items.title: num_matched_prefix_tokens stays 0 for cache-agnostic policies (fcfs, lof, random, routing-key)
items.author: phphlio1
items.body_excerpt:
# Issue: `num_matched_prefix_tokens` stays 0 for cache-agnostic policies - load snapshots and cache-hit reporting read zero reuse

## Summary

With `--schedule-policy fcfs` (and the other cache-agnostic policies: `lof`, `random`, `routing-key`), `Req.num_matched_prefix_tokens` stays at 0 for the request's whole lifetime, even though the request does reuse cached prefixes. Every consumer of the field then reads zero reuse.

## Root cause

2 facts combine:

1. `SchedulePolicy.calc_priority` only populates `num_matched_prefix_tokens` at sort time for cache-agnostic policies when `tree_cache.supports_fast_match_prefix()` is true - which is  false for the current radix implementations - so the field is never set there (`python/sglang/srt/managers/schedule_policy.py`).
2. `Req.init_next_round_input` runs the real admission-time re-match (`tree_cache.match_prefix(...)`) and unpacks `prefix_indices` /   `host_hit_length`, but never records the match length into `num_matched_prefix_tokens` - the field keeps its init value 0 (and its retraction reset value 0).

So the scheduler reuses cached prefixes correctly at admission (behavior is fine), but the bookkeeping field stays 0.

## Impact

- `SchedulerLoadInquirer.get_num_waiting_uncached_tokens` computes `req.seqlen - req.num_matched_prefix_tokens` whenever `waiting_queue_prefix_matched()` is true => The uncached waiting-token estimate counts full input lengths, i.e. load snapshots overestimate pending prefill work for cache-agnostic policies.
- Any observability or reporting that reads per-request matched tokens for these policies reads 0.

## Evidence

A 30-minute agentic-replay benchmark run with `--schedule-policy fcfs` (~217 finished requests, 12.9M total input tokens):

- `sum(num_matched_prefix_tokens) == 0` across every request, while an identical-ordering run of the same workload with the sort-time match forced on measured a **91.6% token-weighted prefix hit rate**.
- The fcfs run's own latency/throughput was consistent with real prefix reuse (same ballpark as the matched arm), confirming the runtime reuse happens and only the reported number is wrong.

## Suggested fix

Record the admission re-match length in `init_next_round_input` (read-only, the match already ran and inserts nothing);

```python
self.num_matched_prefix_tokens = min(
    len(self.prefix_indices) + self.host_hit_length,
    self._compute_max_prefix_len(input_len),
)
```

Retraction resets the field to 0, the next admission re-match re-records it. Happy to send a PR with unit tests.

items.title: [Bug] bench_serving: --dataset-name openai counts every prompt as 2 input tokens (transformers 5)
items.author: mkschulz9
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

With `--dataset-name openai`, `bench_serving` records every request's prompt length as **2 tokens**, however long the prompt is. So `Total input tokens`, `Input token throughput` and `Total token throughput` are wrong, in both the console report and the JSON output.

**Cause.** The `openai` loader measures each prompt like this ([`benchmark/datasets/openai_dataset.py#L86-L90`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/benchmark/datasets/openai_dataset.py#L86-L90)):

```python
        prompt_len = len(
            tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
                messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True
            )
        )
```

In transformers 5, `apply_chat_template(..., tokenize=True)` returns a `BatchEncoding` (a dict holding `input_ids` and `attention_mask`) unless `return_dict=False` is passed. `len()` of that dict is its number of keys: 2.

When the loader was added (#17219, first released in v0.5.9), SGLang pinned transformers 4.57.1, where the call returns a plain list, so the count was right. It became 2 when SGLang moved to transformers 5.3.0 (#17784, v0.5.10). The other loaders that apply a chat template (ShareGPT, custom, Mooncake) and the server's chat endpoint already pass `return_dict=False` (#13229).

**Impact.**
- **Wrong:** `Total input tokens`, input token throughput and total token throughput. The totals add up the loader's value ([`benchmark/serving.py#L1162`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/benchmark/serving.py#L1162)), so the per-request correction from the server's `usage` (#39889) doesn't reach them.
- **Not affected:** the requests sent, all latency metrics, request throughput and output tokens.
- **Why tests pass:** `test_openai_sampler` checks the row count and pass-through fields, but not `prompt_len`.

**Suggested fix.** Pass `return_dict=False`, as the other loaders do, and add a `prompt_len` assertion to `test_openai_sampler`:

```diff
         prompt_len = len(
             tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
-                messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True
+                messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=False
             )
         )
```

Possibly related (not verified): [`benchmark/datasets/speed_bench.py#L72-L81`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/benchmark/datasets/speed_bench.py#L72-L81) calls `apply_chat_template(..., tokenize=True)` the same way, then `decode()`s the result inside a bare `except` that falls back to the raw prompt without the chat template.


### Reproduction

Model: `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct` (any chat model behaves the same). No server or GPU needed; this calls the loader directly:

```python
import json, tempfile
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from sglang.benchmark.datasets.openai_dataset import sample_openai_requests

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct")  # any chat model
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the plot of Hamlet in three sentences."},
]
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("w", suffix=".jsonl", delete=False) as f:
    f.write(json.dumps({"messages": messages, "max_tokens": 64}) + "\n")

row = sample_openai_requests(dataset_path=f.name, num_requests=1, tokenizer=tokenizer)[0]
ids = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=False
)
print("prompt_len from the openai loader:", row.prompt_len)
print("tokens the chat template produces:", len(ids))
```

Output:

```
Loaded 1 OpenAI-format requests
#Input tokens: 2
#Output tokens: 64
prompt_len from the openai loader: 2
tokens the chat template produces: 31
```

The first three lines are printed by the loader itself.

End to end, every `bench_serving` run with this dataset reports 2 input tokens per request. We first saw it in `bench_serving` runs using our own (private) model's tokenizer, with `--backend sglang-oai-chat --dataset-name openai`:
- A run of 40 requests reported `total_input_tokens: 80`.
- For 450 of our requests, the loader counted 900 tokens. Counting the chat template's tokens directly gave 156,171, matching the server's `prompt_tokens` counter for the same requests.

### Environment

Client only, since the bug is client-side: the `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21-cu130-runtime` image, in a Linux pod without a GPU. Without a GPU, `check_env` itself stops with `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'nvidia-smi'`. This output was produced with a stand-in `nvidia-smi` on `PATH` that exits 1, so only the GPU topology section is missing.

```

items.title: [RFC] Monokernel framework for SGLang
items.author: kevin-mii
items.body_excerpt:
This RFC adds one framework for monokernels in SGLang. Each model supplies a spec and its kernels. The framework supplies the switch, the checks, the routing, the safety rules, and the CI gate. ## Motivation A monokernel is a persistent kernel that runs most of a decoder layer, including the tensor-parallel all-reduce, in one or two launches. At small batch sizes, it removes most launch gaps, synchronization, and repeated weight reads. In the open PRs, it lowers the time per output token by up to 44% at one to four users on gfx950. The gain decreases at higher concurrency and with speculative decoding. The first comment has the results for each PR. Four open PRs add approximately 22k lines for these kernels. Each PR has its own runtime, env vars (12 in total), and failure behavior, and no PR puts a time limit on its cross-GPU waits. This RFC defines one shape before these PRs merge. Goals: - One switch, `--enable-monokernel`. It is off by default, and when it is off, nothing changes. - A new model adds only its kernels and a few hundred lines of glue code. - No tokens from a failed step, and no hangs. - One CI kit for all models, and a contract that is not specific to one vendor. Non-goals: prefill, extend, and mixed steps; op-level fused kernels such as MegaMoE; launches across layers; draft-model layers; recovery after a failed step; on by default. ## Design The framework uses existing SGLang hooks: | Stage | Hook | Framework action | | --- | --- | --- | | Config | `handle_monokernel` in `arg_groups/pipeline.py`, after the CUDA graph, memory, model, and attention-backend hooks | Find the spec. Refuse an unsupported setup. Set the decode capture sizes. | | After weight load, before KV sizing | `mono.attach()` in `precompile_kernels_after_loading()` | Check the weights and backends. All ranks agree before the peer handshake. Allocate all memory, and build all widths. | | Before graph capture | `mono.prepare_capture()` in `prepare_before_cuda_graph_capture()` | Bind the caches. Compare the routing plans of all ranks. | Each stage lists all refusal reasons, and any refusal stops startup. Each decode step then runs as follows: ```mermaid flowchart TD R["mono.route()
One plan from the graph key"] --> C["Covered span
Launch, then copy error words to host"] R --> O["Everything else
Normal SGLang code"] C --> S["Tokens reach the host
mono.check_errors() reads the copy"] O --> S S --> E["Error word set
Raise and stop all ranks"] S --> N["No error
Send tokens to the client"] ``` ### Changes to existing code | SGLang part | Change | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | `arg_groups/` | One `ExecKernel` field, `enable_monokernel`, and the `handle_monokernel` hook | The switch, and the refusal before processes start | | `Resources` in `runtime_context.py` | One slot for the `MonoRuntime` | The error check finds the runtime without a module global | | `batch_result_processor` | One `mono.check_errors()` call after the tokens reach the host | No tokens from a failed step | | `kernels/ops/__init__.py` | `mono` added to `_GROUPS` | Registers the new kernel group | | Each covered model | `mono.*` calls in its load and capture hooks, and at each span start | The only seams in a model file | Nothing else changes, including `ModelRunner`, `Scheduler`, `TokenizerManager`, the model workers, and the weight updater. A model PR can still add a cache feature that its kernel needs, for example a new state dtype. ### Spec and spans Each model has one `MonoSpec` for each vendor. The spec declares what the kernels can do, and the framework enforces it. A registry maps each HF architecture to the import path of its spec, so the config hook imports only the spec module, not the model. ```python @dataclass(frozen=True) class MonoSpec: name: str architectures: tuple[str, ...] # HF architectures devices: Mapping[str, DeviceLimits] # per ISA: widths, TP sizes, resident blocks features: frozenset[Feature] # features that the spec accepts requires: Requirements # dtypes, caches, attention and MoE backends spans: Callable[[PretrainedConfig], Mapping[int, tuple[Span, ...]]] # spans per layer numerics: Numerics # BITWISE, or TOLERANCE with bounds config_disable_reasons: Callable[..., list[str]] # before load model_disable_reasons: Callable[..., list[str]] # after load eligible: Callable[[ShapeKey], str | None] # per graph key: None, or why it can't run build: Callable[..., "MonoModel"] # views, copies, and kernels for all widths bind: Callable[..., list[str]] # caches, before capture repack: Callable[..., None] | None = None # None: weight updates are refused ``` A span covers part of a layer between two of these points: `layer_in` → `attn_in` → `core_in` → `core_out` → `attn_partial` → `mlp_in` → `mlp_partial` → `layer_out` `attn_in` and `mlp_in` come after the norms. `core_in` and `core_out` are around the attention backend call. The two partial points come before each all-reduce. A multi-step attention core, for example sparse attention with an indexer, can declare more points. - The default span is the whole layer. Each other span needs a reason: backend state in the attention, a hardware limit, a measured slowdown, or no waits on other GPUs. - A span that ends at a partial point leaves the all-reduce to SGLang. A span that starts at a partial point does the all-reduce in the kernel. - A kernel takes and returns the same tensors as the code that it replaces, and it writes KV and state exactly as that code does. Covered and normal code can then alternate, in one step and across steps. Parameter names do not change. items.title: [RFC]: Limit the use of envvars in vLLM
items.author: zhuohan123
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

vLLM's envvars are on the edge of getting out of control. There are many envvars should instead be configs. Like the attention backend, all2all kernel backend, and even there is a flag to control KV cache layout. envvars are evil because:

1. It is equivalent of using global variables everywhere in the code, which is a bad programming practice.
2. envvars have no advanced structure like, hierarchy, typechecks, etc. 

In summary, I think envvars are the kind of thing that is very easy to add so people tend to add envvars as the shortest path to implement their feature, but this can quickly becomes unmanageable and makes the project very hard to use. 

### Proposed Change.

I think we should:

1. Spend some effort on reviewing the current envvars and move many of them to configs.
2. Have very strict bar on what can be an envvar and question every new envvars in vllm.

items.title: [Docs] Document NIXL KV connector metrics aggregation semantics
items.author: NickLucche
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The NIXL KV connector logs transfer metrics periodically:

```
KV Transfer metrics: Num successful transfers=4, Avg xfer time (ms)=1.381, P90 xfer time (ms)=2.601, Avg post time (ms)=0.672, P90 post time (ms)=0.801, Avg MB per transfer=2.25, Throughput (MB/s)=1629.549, Avg number of descriptors=72.0
```

Currently there is no documentation explaining what these metrics represent, especially in the context of **multi-rank (TP > 1) deployments**. This has already caused confusion among users.

## Current behavior

All metrics are **aggregated across all TP ranks** before summary stats are computed:

1. Each TP rank independently records per-transfer telemetry (`transfer_duration`, `post_duration`, `bytes_transferred`, `num_descriptors`) via `NixlKVConnectorStats.record_transfer()` in [`stats.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py).
2. Stats from all ranks are concatenated via `aggregate()` (`list.extend()`).
3. `reduce()` computes averages, percentiles, and throughput over the **combined** pool of observations from all ranks.

This means:
- **"Num successful transfers"** is the total count across all ranks, not per-rank.
- **"Avg MB per transfer"** is the average over all individual rank-level transfers, not the total bytes moved for a single KV cache transfer operation.
- **"Throughput (MB/s)"** is `total_MB_all_ranks / total_time_all_ranks` — effectively an average per-rank throughput, not the aggregate system throughput.
- **Percentiles (P90)** are computed over the combined distribution of all ranks' transfer times.

This is unintuitive because users may expect metrics to reflect per-engine totals or aggregate system throughput.

## What needs to be documented

1. **Docstrings in `stats.py`**: Add clear documentation to `NixlKVConnectorStats` explaining that stats are aggregated across all TP ranks and what each metric represents in that context.
2. **Inline comments in `reduce()`**: Clarify the semantics of throughput and averages — that they are per-rank averages over the combined observation pool.
3. **Docstrings in `metrics.py`**: Document the `observe()` → `aggregate()` → `reduce()` → `log()` pipeline and the fact that stats arrive pre-aggregated across workers.
4. **(Optional) Docs page**: Add a section to the disaggregated serving documentation explaining how to interpret the KV Transfer metrics log line.

## Relevant files

- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py` — `NixlKVConnectorStats` (recording, aggregation, reduction)
- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/metrics.py` — `KVConnectorLogging` (observe/log pipeline), `KVConnectorStats` (base class)

## Context

See related discussion: metrics are aggregated across ranks rather than reported per-rank or per-engine. This is a deliberate design choice (fire-and-forget from workers), but it needs to be clearly documented so users can correctly interpret the numbers.

items.title: [RFC]: DeepSeek-V4 Performance Optimization on ROCm (Phase Two)
items.author: shen-shanshan
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

> Continue working on phase one: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/41820.

DeepSeek-V4 introduces CSA (Compressed Sparse Attention, `compress_ratio=4`), HCA layers, and a large MoE backbone. A side-by-side trace comparison of the vLLM decode path against vLLM-ATOM on ROCm shows that vLLM still leaves measurable performance on the table. The gaps cluster into three areas:

1. **Unfused mHC kernels.** vLLM runs `mhc_post` and `mhc_pre` as separate kernels, and `mhc_pre_big_fuse` + `add_rmsnorm_quant` as two kernels, while ATOM fuses each pair into a single kernel (`mhc_fused_post_pre` and `mhc_pre_big_fuse_rmsnorm`). Every extra kernel launch on the decode critical path costs launch latency and cache/register thrash.
2. **Serial execution where overlap is possible.** ATOM forks auxiliary HIP streams to run compressor GEMMs (CSA pre-attention), SWA KV insertion (HCA), and the MoE router/shared experts concurrently with the main stream. vLLM executes all of these serially.
3. **Slower attention support kernels.** ATOM replaces the vLLM CSA top-k selection kernels and the post-attention batched GEMMs (`torch.mm` + `manual_unroll`) with dedicated optimized kernels (e.g., `batched_gemm_bf16_kernel`).

An earlier attempt at closing gap #2 — PR #51794, which enables three-stream overlap for CSA pre-attention — is currently a draft: the overlapped region itself is faster when there is no bubble, but some ranks see a much slower tail all-reduce due to inter-rank latency jitter. The un-optimized kernels running in the parallel streams contend for hardware resources and desynchronize ranks. This suggests the correct order of work is: **replace the kernels with ATOM's optimized versions first, then enable stream overlap on top of them.**

## Proposed Change

Port the ATOM-optimized decode path into vLLM's ROCm DeepSeek-V4 implementation, using the ATOM trace as the reference for each change. The work is organized per module:

### CSA:

- [x] **Fuse mHC kernels:** merge `mhc_post` + `mhc_pre` into `mhc_fused_post_pre`, and `mhc_pre_big_fuse` + `add_rmsnorm_quant` into `mhc_pre_big_fuse_rmsnorm`. #52737 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Fuse SWA q/kv RMSNorm and q FP8 group quant:** #53540 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Fuse main-compressor and indexer-compressor projection:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53838 @Fangzhou-Ai 
- [x] **Pre-attention three-stream overlap:** Before the input GEMMs, fork three HIP streams: (1) **default stream**: fused wqa+wkv GEMM → q/kv RMSNorm → wq_b → qnorm/RoPE → SWA KV insert; (2) **aux stream 0**: main-compressor wkv_gate GEMM → compress kernels (compressed KV cache write); (3) **aux stream 1**: indexer-compressor wkv_gate GEMM → K-cache write. After the join, the indexer weights GEMM, the indexer q-side (wq_b + fused q RoPE+quant), the sparse indexer op (top-k selection), and the MLA attention run serially on the main stream. Each aux stream is a self-contained chain starting from `hidden_states`, so no fine-grained cross-stream dependencies are required. **This item stays disabled (draft) until the kernels in the parallel streams are replaced with ATOM's**.
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50866 @shen-shanshan 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51794 @shen-shanshan
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54571 @shen-shanshan  
- [ ] **Support FP4 indexer:**
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56834 @LiuYinfeng01
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60834 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Remove MQA temporary fix:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55808 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Replace top-k kernels:** between `gluon_deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_preshuffle` and the core `sparse_attention`, replace the vLLM top-k implementation with ATOM's fused sparse-indexer kernels. #52882 @Fangzhou-Ai 
- [x] **Support FP8 attention output projection:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54894 @LiuYinfeng01 

### HCA:

- [x] **Pre-attention two-stream overlap:** for `c128a` layers (which have no indexer), run the main KV compression concurrently with SWA token insertion on an auxiliary stream. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56853 @shen-shanshan 

### MoE:

- [x] **Router and shared-experts dual-stream overlap:** run the router computation concurrently with the shared experts on a second stream, then join before the routed experts. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56098 @mawong-amd 
- [x] Enable AITER heterogeneous fused MoE:
  - [x] TP: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53161 @Fangzhou-Ai 
  - [ ] DP: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54134 (not needed now, prefer to use dual-stream MoE for DP) @LiuYinfeng01
- [x] Enable mega MoE: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59685 @micah-wil 

### Others:

- [ ] Prefill optimization:
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54855 @jiacao-amd 
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57773 @shen-shanshan 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58405 @ZhengGong-amd

items.title: [RFC]: Hardening /v1/messages (Anthropic API) for Claude Code across model families
items.author: robertgshaw2-redhat
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

Claude Code can run against vLLM through the Anthropic Messages endpoint (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` → `/v1/messages`). Claude Code's agentic loop is a demanding client of that endpoint:

- It sends every request with ~25 tools, many with large nested JSON schemas.
- It uses interleaved thinking with parallel tool calls.
- It sends inline `role: "system"` messages that change every turn.
- It sends side queries (title generation, the auto-mode permission classifier) with `stop_sequences` and small `max_tokens` budgets.
- It recovers from context overflow based on the error it gets back.

This issue audits the current converter (`vllm/entrypoints/anthropic/`) and the HF chat templates of the major open model families against real Claude Code traffic. We found:

- several gaps that affect every model family;
- a set of model-specific breakages, some of which return **400 on Claude Code's default requests**.

Many of the small fixes already have open PRs, often more than one per problem. This issue gathers them so they can be deduplicated and prioritized, and it proposes the pieces that have no owner yet.

**How we checked**

- We captured `/v1/messages` traffic from Claude Code 2.1.281 through a logging proxy (~50 requests covering main-loop turns, title generation and the auto-mode classifier).
- We replayed synthetic Claude Code-shaped conversations through `AnthropicServingMessages.to_chat_completion_request` → `chat_utils` post-processing.
- We rendered the result with the current HF templates, and with `mistral_common` / the DeepSeek Python encoders / Harmony where applicable.

Items marked *(unverified)* were not reproduced at runtime.

**Observed request shape (from captures)**

| Field | Values seen |
|---|---|
| `system` | List of text blocks with `cache_control`. The first is the `x-anthropic-billing-header` line. |
| `messages` | Contains inline `role: "system"` messages at non-leading positions (e.g. a `<total_tokens>` update each turn). |
| `thinking` | `{"type":"adaptive"}`, `{"type":"adaptive","display":"omitted"}`, `{"type":"enabled"}`, `{"type":"disabled"}`, or absent |
| `output_config` | `{"effort":"high"}`; title generation adds `format: json_schema` |
| `context_management` | `{"edits":[{"type":"clear_thinking_20251015","keep":"all"}]}` |
| `max_tokens` | `32000` (main loop), `2112` (classifier, `stop_sequences: ["</block>"]`), `64` (stage-1 classifier, `stop_sequences: ["</severity>"]`) |
| `tool_result` | `is_error` is set on most results. Content is a string or a list of text/image blocks. User turns often carry extra text blocks (system reminders) after the tool results. |

---

### Part 1: Converter / API gaps (all models)

| # | Gap | Location | Impact | Existing work |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Inline system messages are always hoisted into the leading system prompt.** `_detect_merge_inline_system` is called with the CLI `--chat-template` value, which is `None` by default, so it returns `True` for every deployment that uses the model's own template. Claude Code sends a changing inline system message every turn, so the leading system text changes every request. | `serving.py:142,152,248-257` | **Prefix cache misses on the whole conversation, every turn.** Also changes semantics: mid-conversation instructions become part of the global system prompt. | #53393, #48874, #41114, #46710; PRs #53501, #56520, #52978, #47681 (competing approaches) |
| 2 | **The `thinking` request field is silently dropped.** `AnthropicMessagesRequest` has no `thinking` field and pydantic ignores extras. `output_config.effort` → `reasoning_effort` then forces `enable_thinking=True` (`chat_completion/protocol.py:585`). Anthropic's default when `thinking` is absent is *off*, but we use the template default, which is usually *on*. | `protocol.py:121` | Side queries (title generation, classifier) reason and spend their `max_tokens` budget before answering. `display: "omitted"` is ignored. | PRs #58613, #53058 |
| 3 | **Stop strings are matched against reasoning text.** `check_stop_strings` runs over the full detokenized output. | `v1/engine/detokenizer.py:130` | The classifier's `</block>` / `</severity>` can match inside `<think>` and end the request with no verdict. | #51669 (related) |
| 4 | **Context-overflow errors are not in Anthropic's format.** vLLM returns "This model's maximum context length is …". Claude Code decides whether to auto-compact or retry with a smaller `max_tokens` based on Anthropic's context-limit error messages *(exact strings unverified)*. Claude Code always sends `max_tokens=32000`, so a 128k-context deployment rejects prompts once they pass ~99k tokens. | `renderers/params.py:357,499` | Long sessions fail hard instead of compacting. | none found |
| 5 | **Unknown content-block types reject the whole request (422).** `AnthropicContentBlock.type` is a closed `Literal`. `document` (PDFs from the Read tool), `search_result`, `tool_addition` / `tool_removal` and server-tool blocks all fail. Once one is in the history, every later request in the session fails. | `protocol.py:41` | Session becomes unrecoverable. | #57324, #46790; PRs #45653, #57693, #46797, #47747, #47877 |
| 6 | **Images in a `tool_result` become a separate `user` message** inserted between tool messages. | `serving.py:445-455` | Gemma 4 silently drops later tool results. items.title: L1 eviction races async L2 store: chunks discarded before offload are never stored (persistent re-prefill under L1 pressure)
items.author: ShreyasBaasri07
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**
Bug

**Describe the bug**
In LMCache v0.5.5 (MP mode), under L1 (CPU) memory pressure, freshly-computed KV chunks can be evicted from L1 before the asynchronous store controller offloads them to L2, so they are silently dropped and never written to L2 — even when L2 is large enough to hold the entire working set and has no eviction configured.

The result: with a shared-prefix (prefix-caching-style) workload, ~19% of requests permanently retrieve only the shared prefix (first half of the prompt) and re-prefill the unique tail on every recurrence, indefinitely. The half-hits persist through the whole run, not just warmup.

Root cause (confirmed in v0.5.5 source):

L1 eviction destination defaults to EvictionDestination.DISCARD — L1 eviction does not offload to L2 (lru.py, eviction_controller.py:193).
The StoreController offloads L1→L2 by reserve_read-ing keys received from an L1_WRITE_FINISHED notification. If a key was already discard-evicted in the meantime, reserve_read returns KEY_NOT_EXIST, the key is silently skipped from the store (only surfaced as an L1_READ_FAILED / lmcache_mp.l1_read_failure "not_found" anomaly), and it never reaches L2 (lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/store_controller.py:600-627).
So there is a race between L1 DISCARD eviction and the async L2 offload; the loser is silently never stored.

**To Reproduce**
Environment: LMCache v0.5.5, MP mode, L1 + L2 where L2 is sized to hold the full working set and has no L2 eviction, and L1 is smaller than the shared-prefix working set.

Start the LMCache MP server with a small L1 and one large L2 adapter (e.g. S3/filesystem), no L2 eviction:
lmcache server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 6555 --chunk-size 256 \
  --l1-size-gb 60 --eviction-policy LRU \
  --l2-adapter '{"type":"s3", ... ,"max_capacity_gb":500}'

Start vLLM with LMCacheMPConnector (kv_role: kv_both), --no-enable-prefix-caching --enforce-eager.
Run a shared-prefix benchmark whose prefix pool exceeds L1. With aiperf/genai-perf
--prefix-prompt-length 4096 --num-prefix-prompts 150 \
--isl 4096 --osl 100 --num-dataset-entries 200 \
--concurrency 10 --random-seed 42 --benchmark-duration 1200

Here 150 prefixes × 4096 tokens ≈ 75 GB of prefix KV > 60 GB L1. Each request = 8192 tokens (4096 shared prefix + 4096 unique tail).

Grep the server log for Retrieved N tokens.

Observed — persistent prefix-only half-hits throughout the run (not just warmup)
Half-hits occur at ~20–32/min even in steady state, long after every one of the 200 fixed prompts has been served many times. Since retrieval is a contiguous match from token 0, Retrieved 4096 means "prefix found, tail missing → prefill." (Optionally, lmcache_mp.l1_read_failure / L1_READ_FAILED "not_found" events fire in the same window.)

Control: setting --num-prefix-prompts 10 (prefix pool now fits in L1) eliminates the half-hits — all requests become full 8192-token hits. So the trigger is specifically L1 < shared-prefix pool.

**Expected behavior**
Once a chunk is computed and admitted to L1, it should reliably be offloaded to L2 and remain retrievable regardless of L1 pressure. A chunk should not be silently dropped from the L2 store just because it was evicted from L1 before the async offload read it. Subsequent requests for the same prompt should be full L2 hits, not re-prefills, when L2 has capacity and no eviction.

**Screenshots**
N/A (server-side KV-cache behavior; log evidence included above).

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**
OS: Linux
LMCache: v0.5.5
vLLM: 0.26.0
PyTorch: 2.11.0+cu130
Python: 3.12.3
GPU: NVIDIA L40S
Mode: MP (LMCacheMPConnector, kv_role: kv_both), --chunk-size 256, --l1-size-gb 60, L2 sized to hold full working set with no L2 eviction

**Smartphone (please complete the following information):**
N/A (not a mobile/browser issue)

**Additional context**
Add any other context about the problem here.

items.title: [Bug] P2P load timeout can report terminal failure while the transfer is still active
items.author: 0andy
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`P2PL2Adapter.query_load_result()` returns a terminal all-zero `Bitmap` as soon as `load_timeout_s` expires, without querying or cancelling the underlying `TransferChannelClient` read ([p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336)). The read may still be in flight at that point, so the adapter reports "finished (failed)" for a load whose transfer has not reached a terminal state.

The existing test `test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure` asserts exactly this behaviour, so I am raising it as a contract question rather than a regression: is a terminal load result allowed to precede the end of the transfer?

**To Reproduce**

On `dev` @ 8d7d2c47, add this test to `tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py`:

```python
def test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight():
    keys = [_key(0)]
    now = [100.0]
    in_flight = TransferChannelReadResult(finished=False)
    with (
        _adapter(load_timeout_s=0.01) as (adapter, _mq, _tc_ctx, tc_client, _n),
        patch.object(p2p_mod.time, "monotonic", side_effect=lambda: now[0]),
    ):
        adapter._remote_addresses[keys[0]] = TransferChannelAddress(offset=100, size=10)
        tc_client.submit_read.return_value = 123
        tc_client.query_read_status.return_value = in_flight
        task_id = adapter.submit_load_task(
            keys, [MagicMock(shm_offset=0, shm_byte_length=10)]
        )
        now[0] = 100.02  # past the 0.01 s load deadline
        assert not in_flight.is_finished()
        assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
```

```
pytest -v tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py -k "deadline or not_finished"
```

Result (CPU-only build, transfer channel mocked):

```
>           assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
E           assert 0 is None
E            +  where 0 = query_load_result(0)

LMCache WARNING: P2P load task 0 timed out; treating as a failure (p2p_l2_adapter.py:335)

test_lookup_deadline_expired_yields_miss PASSED
test_load_not_finished_returns_none PASSED
test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure PASSED
test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight FAILED
1 failed, 3 passed
```

(`0` is the repr of a one-key, all-zero `Bitmap`, i.e. a terminal failure.)

This test only demonstrates the current behaviour; its assertion would need adjusting depending on which direction below is preferred.

**Expected behavior**

Either the adapter does not report a terminal load result while its transfer-channel read may still access the destination buffers, or the contract states explicitly that a terminal result does not imply the transfer has quiesced and callers handle that.

**Additional context**

To be clear about what is and is not shown:

*Reproduced (unit test above):* the read is modelled as unfinished, and after the deadline `query_load_result()` returns a terminal failure.

*Derived from reading the code, not reproduced:*
- On that result, `PrefetchController._poll_load_results()` calls `finish_write_and_delete()` for the failed keys and then `submit_unlock()` ([prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395)); for P2P, `submit_unlock()` sends `p2p_unlock_objects` to the peer ([#L277-L280](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L277-L280)). So both the destination staging buffer and the source-side lock are released.
- The NIXL transfer channel registers the whole L1 buffer once ([nixl_impl.py#L344](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L344)). This creates a window in which a late read may write into memory that has since been reassigned to another key.
- After the timeout the adapter no longer queries the read, so the `NixlTransferChannelClient._tasks` entry and its xfer handle are only released on `close()` ([#L178-L181](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L178-L181), [#L202-L206](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L202-L206)).

*Not reproduced:* actual stale or corrupted KV data end to end. I have not run a two-instance NIXL test for this.

**Possible directions** (not proposing a specific fix yet)

- **A. Stay pending until the transfer is terminal.** After the deadline, keep polling `query_read_status()` and only report once it finishes. Simple ownership model; a hung transfer would hold its buffers and locks indefinitely.
- **B. Add per-task cancellation to `TransferChannelClient`** ([abstract.py#L52-L88](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/abstract.py#L52-L88) has only `submit_read`, `query_read_status`, `close`), and report terminal only once the cancel is confirmed. For NIXL this would map to `releaseXferReq`, which the BackendGuide says "can return error, meaning it was not successful in aborting the request", so it still needs A as a fallback. The Mooncake wrapper has no cancel today; I have not checked the engine itself.
- **C. Drop the adapter-level load deadline** and rely on the controller-level deadline from #5255, which already keeps late loads' buffers and locks until the load result arrives.

The P2P adapter is the runtime caller of `submit_read()`; the transfer-channel benchmark also calls it directly, so an API change in B would touch both.

**Related**

- #5263 — same ownership family, on the shutdown / TTL paths rat
items.author_work_intent: If maintainers agree this is a contract gap, I'm happy to work on the fix. I'd especially appreciate guidance on whether the preferred direction is to keep timed-out reads pending until terminal, add a TransferChannel cancell

comments.author: holtwood
comments.body:
I checked another timeout case at [`1ca53a8`](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/1ca53a8aadca1d054f171fd67350be35797cfddc/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L326-L347) using the original query methods with mocked dependencies. I haven't run a real NIXL transfer.

Even when the transfer is already marked `DONE`, polling after the deadline returns a zero bitmap without calling `query_read_status`. The adapter removes its task, so later adapter polls return `None`. The client's `close()` still has a separate cleanup path.

This seems worth covering in the timeout tests, including cleanup of an already-completed transfer. I can help add that case if it's useful.

items.title: [Bug]: Paused streaming sessions deadlock the scheduler when the KV cache is full
items.author: damienlaine
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

Scheduler-level repro on CPU, no model or GPU needed. Main at `89a00995c9`. Also hit on GPU with Voxtral realtime, V1 and V2 model runners.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

A paused streaming session (`resumable`, `WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ`) keeps its KV blocks. When its next chunk arrives it goes through `kv_holding_waiting`. If the pool is full, `allocate_slots` fails and the waiting loop breaks. Preemption only takes from `running`, which is empty because every session is between chunks. Nothing gets freed, and every session stays waiting forever.

So once the sessions' KV goes over the pool, all of them freeze, not only the one that doesn't fit.

Repro (4 sessions, 7 usable blocks of 16 tokens, each chunk adds one block):

```python
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

import torch

from vllm.config import DeviceConfig, VllmConfig
from vllm.sampling_params import SamplingParams
from vllm.v1.core.sched.scheduler import Scheduler
from vllm.v1.kv_cache_interface import FullAttentionSpec, KVCacheConfig, KVCacheGroupSpec
from vllm.v1.outputs import ModelRunnerOutput
from vllm.v1.request import Request
from vllm.v1.structured_output import StructuredOutputManager

STOP = 128001
BLOCK = 16
NUM_BLOCKS = 8
NUM_SESSIONS = 4


def make_scheduler():
    cfg = VllmConfig(device_config=DeviceConfig("cpu"))
    cfg.model_config = MagicMock()
    cfg.model_config.skip_tokenizer_init = True
    cfg.model_config.is_multimodal_model = False
    cfg.model_config.supports_multimodal_inputs = False
    cfg.model_config.is_encoder_decoder = False
    cfg.model_config.is_diffusion = False
    cfg.model_config.max_model_len = 1024
    cfg.model_config.enable_return_routed_experts = False
    cfg.cache_config = MagicMock()
    cfg.cache_config.num_gpu_blocks = NUM_BLOCKS
    cfg.cache_config.enable_prefix_caching = False
    kv = KVCacheConfig(
        num_blocks=NUM_BLOCKS,
        kv_cache_tensors=[],
        kv_cache_groups=[KVCacheGroupSpec(["layer"], FullAttentionSpec(
            block_size=BLOCK, num_kv_heads=1, head_size=1, dtype=torch.float32))],
    )
    return Scheduler(vllm_config=cfg, kv_cache_config=kv, log_stats=False,
                     structured_output_manager=StructuredOutputManager(cfg),
                     block_size=BLOCK, hash_block_size=BLOCK)


def chunk(rid, n):
    # One streaming update: n new prompt tokens, generation stops after 1 token.
    return Request(request_id=rid, prompt_token_ids=list(range(1, n + 1)),
                   sampling_params=SamplingParams(stop_token_ids=[STOP], max_tokens=16),
                   pooling_params=None, resumable=True)


s = make_scheduler()
ids = [f"s{i}" for i in range(NUM_SESSIONS)]
for rid in ids:
    s.add_request(chunk(rid, BLOCK - 1))

for step in range(12):
    out = s.schedule()
    sched = list(out.num_scheduled_tokens)
    free = s.kv_cache_manager.block_pool.get_num_free_blocks()
    print(f"step {step}: scheduled={sched} free_blocks={free} "
          f"waiting={len(s.waiting) + len(getattr(s, 'kv_holding_waiting', []))}")
    if not sched:
        continue
    # Every scheduled session ends its chunk (STOP) and pauses, keeping its KV.
    s.update_from_output(out, ModelRunnerOutput(
        req_ids=sched, req_id_to_index={r: i for i, r in enumerate(sched)},
        sampled_token_ids=[[STOP] for _ in sched], logprobs=None,
        prompt_logprobs_dict={}, pooler_output=[]))
    # The client sends the next chunk for each of them.
    for rid in sched:
        s.add_request(chunk(rid, BLOCK))
```

```
step 0: scheduled=['s0', 's1', 's2', 's3'] free_blocks=3 waiting=0
step 1: scheduled=['s0', 's1', 's2'] free_blocks=0 waiting=1
step 2: scheduled=[] free_blocks=0 waiting=4
...
step 11: scheduled=[] free_blocks=0 waiting=4
```

On GPU, Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime with a 256 sliding window (~128 MiB KV per session) and `--kv-cache-memory 1GiB`: 7 sessions run fine, with 9 every session stops after a few seconds, 0 tok/s, no preemption, all 9 transcriptions cut. `--max-num-seqs 7` avoids it, the extra sessions just wait.

Expected: preempt a paused session (free its KV, recompute on resume) instead of blocking the queue.

Related: #58776 (a preempted resumable session is dropped). The encoder cache has the same pattern: a paused session keeps its last multimodal item cached until it resumes, and when the cache can't hold them all the waiting loop breaks the same way (seen with a small encoder cache in #45022).

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Reproduced on current main (`31e2443c90`, CPU scheduler-level, exact script from the report): deadlock from step 2 on, `scheduled=[]` for the remaining 10 steps with `free_blocks=0` and all 4 sessions waiting.

This is the deadlock #59339 already fixes: it reclaims KV blocks from paused/`kv_holding` sessions at the waiting loop's allocation-failure point, which is the gap described here (preemption only scans `running`, and `running` is empty). I ran the same repro on #59339's head (`a0f422aa`): continuous progress from step 2 through 8 as paused sessions get reclaimed and resumed. The repro then stalls again at steps 9-11, but that is genuine capacity exhaustion, not deadlock: each session's prompt grows one block per round, so by then a single chunk needs ~9 blocks against an 8-block pool and nothing can legitimately fit.

One note for whoever picks up review: #59339's only red check is the pre-run gate (author has 2 merged PRs, needs a `verified`/`ready` label), not a code failure.

comments.author: divyuuu
comments.body:
Checked this on current main (`1e5d0ea`).

Static trace matches the report: the running-loop only preempts from `self.running` (`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:776-782`), and the waiting-loop `allocate_slots` failure path just `break`s (`1241-1248`) with no reclaim from `kv_holding_waiting`. So once all sessions are paused holding KV and `running` is empty, every `schedule()` stalls with nothing scheduled and nothing freed.

I also checked #59339 (reclaim at the waiting-loop failure point, updated Oct 6) to avoid duplicating it. Validating next whether it covers this exact 4-session repro on a Linux runner (my Windows host can't build vLLM -- no AMD64 precompiled wheel, only manylinux). Repro script ready from the issue body.

If a regression-test gap remains after #59339, may I take it? Happy to contribute the repro as a scheduler regression test. AI assistance used for the trace; will run the repro and tests before any PR per the contribution guide.

comments.author: damienlaine
comments.body:
Ran #59339 (`a0f422aa`) against its base (`21d93d0d8c`) on GPU with Voxtral realtime: RTX 4090, 256/256 sliding windows, `--max-num-batched-tokens 256`, `--kv-cache-memory-bytes 1GiB` (11,915 tokens), 120 s streams sent in real time.

| | completed | generation | words/stream |
|---|---|---|---|
| base, 9 sessions | 0/9, stalled after ~20 s | 0 tok/s | ~15 |
| #59339, 9 sessions | 0/9 | 65 → ~7 tok/s (~110 needed) | ~60 |
| #59339, 8 sessions | 0/8 | ~6 tok/s | ~80 |
| #59339, 7 sessions (fit in pool) | 7/7 | same output as reference | ~275 |
| default pool (49,152 tokens), 9 sessions | 9/9 | 112 tok/s | ~280 |

The stall is gone and reclaimed sessions produce correct output (97-100% word match with the reference on the same audio). Under overcommit, throughput collapses for all sessions, not only the extra one: a reclaimed session restarts from `num_computed_tokens = 0` and recomputes its full history, encoder included, so the cost per reclaim grows with session age.

Also tried restricting victims to sessions with lower `(priority, arrival_time)` than the requester, as the running-loop preemption does: 0/8 and 0/9, ~10 tok/s, and it breaks 3 of #59339's tests. Victim selection is not the issue.

Regression tests for this case are already in #59339 (14 tests, pass locally).

items.title: [SM120] Field report: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash in production on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (PCIe, no NVLink) - working config, measured throughput, rejected topologies
items.author: Lei-010
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Field data from running **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash** as a production SGLang backend on **8× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (SM120, 96 GB, PCIe-only — no NVLink)**, including the *only* topology we could get to start, measured prefill/decode, a speculative-decoding A/B, and the configuration traps that cost us real experiments. Posting because SM120 + V4.1-Flash users currently have to rediscover all of this from scratch.

Full write-up (with methodology and reproduction artifacts): https://github.com/Lei-010/hermes-agent/blob/main/docs/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-SM120-Performance-and-Production-Config.md

Related: vLLM field report https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56700 (same hardware, vLLM side), vLLM https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56892 (SM120 bug/perf tracker).

## What works

```bash
docker run --gpus all -d --name dsv41 \
  --shm-size=64g --ipc=host --network host \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  -e TP_SIZE=8 -e DP_SIZE=1 -e EP_SIZE=8 \
  -e SPEC_ALGORITHM=dspark -e DSPARK_BLOCK_SIZE=6 \
  -e CHUNKED_PREFILL_SIZE=2048 \
  -v /ssd/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash:/model \
  <sglang image>
```

Effective `server_args` (verified at runtime via `/get_server_info`):

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| `tp_size` / `ep_size` / `dp_size` | 8 / 8 / 1 |
| `speculative_algorithm` | DSPARK, `speculative_dspark_block_size = 6` |
| `chunked_prefill_size` | 2048 |
| `context_length` | 1,048,576 |
| `kv_cache_dtype` | `fp8_e4m3` |
| `mem_fraction_static` | 0.72 |
| `max_running_requests` | 16 |
| `attention_backend` / `moe_runner_backend` | `dsv4` / `flashinfer_mxfp4` |
| CUDA graph decode / prefill | full (max_bs 16) / **disabled** |

**TP8/EP8 is not a preference — it is the only layout that starts** (see "Topologies SGLang rejects" below).

## Measured throughput (cold, single stream, tokens from `usage`, not SSE chunk counts)

128K cold prefill:

| Config | tok/s |
|---|---|
| `chunked_prefill_size=2048` (production) | **6,853** |
| same config re-run | 6,765 (−1.3%) |
| flashmla prefill backend | 6,845 |
| fused-MoE all-reduce | 6,828 |
| `chunked_prefill_size=4096` | 6,301 |
| `chunked_prefill_size=1024` | 6,012 |

32K prompt: ≈7,196 tok/s. GPU util ≈87% at 220 W of 600 W → **communication-bound on PCIe**, not compute-bound. ~7K tok/s looks like the ceiling for this board without NVLink.

Radix/prefix cache is the only large multiplier: cache-hit prefill **0.34 s for a 112K-token prefix ≈ 325K tok/s (≈39×)**.

Decode (client path over SSH tunnel, production config): prose 93.9 tok/s, structured/JSON 134.1 tok/s, TTFT 143–169 ms.

## DSPARK A/B (block_size=2, clean legs, each verified via `server_info` + acceptance length)

| Prompt class | DSPARK ON | DSPARK OFF |
|---|---|---|
| prose | 76.5–78.9 tok/s | 36.4–36.5 tok/s |
| structured | 120.3–120.5 tok/s | 36.5 tok/s |
| `accept len` | 3.0 tokens/step | 1.0 |

With DSPARK off the model flattens to ~36.5 tok/s regardless of prompt class — speculation is the difference between usable and unusable latency on this hardware. Production ships `block_size=6` (structured ≈237–252 tok/s vs 120 at block 2).

## Traps that cost us experiments (SGLang-specific)

1. **`--enable-expert-parallel` is a vLLM flag** — SGLang takes `ep_size`; the vLLM spelling is rejected outright.
2. **`docker run` must pass `TP_SIZE`/`DP_SIZE`/`EP_SIZE` explicitly.** Without `-e`, the container silently serves TP8 defaults and your "new" config never happens (we recorded a full sweep of false data this way before adding a config gate).
3. **`ep_size ≤ tp_size`** or the MoE rank computation divides by zero: `moe_ep_rank = tp_rank % (tp_size // moe_dp_size) // (tp_size // moe_dp_size // ep_size)`.
4. **DSPARK + DP attention requires `--enable-dp-lm-head`** — but is unreachable on this model anyway (next section).

## Topologies SGLang rejects on this model

| Attempt | Result |
|---|---|
| DP2 × TP4 (any EP) | `ValueError: V4.1 vision currently supports TP/EP without DP, CP, PP or MoE A2A` — both replicas die within ~70 s |
| prefill context-parallel | same class of rejection |
| `--enable-dp-attention` alone | silently no DP group (`dp_size: 1`) — looks fine, isn't |

Other SM120 gaps we hit: MSCCL++ (`_tune` kernel crash), FlashInfer all-reduce fusion, `flashmla_sparse_q8`, and CUDA-graph capture for **prefill** (crashes even with DSPARK off, i.e. unrelated to speculation).

## Operational notes

- A defunct container can survive a single `docker rm -f`; the next `docker run` then fails on the name conflict while an orphaned engine process keeps the port and answers health checks — which silently mislabels the next experiment. Loop `docker rm -f` until the container is gone **and** nothing listens on the port.
- A parse failure must never satisfy an "expected config" assertion, or a server that has not started yet gets recorded as "spec disabled".
- Verify intended config from the server (`/get_server_info`) before timing anything; discard legs that fail the gate rather than recording them.

## Not established

No 24 h soak (numbers come from a working day of production use), block sizes 4/8/12 not re-measured with the fixed sweep tool, and >32K prefill/long-context degradation not characterised.

items.title: [RFC] Torch Ops Improvements and Backend Routing
items.author: hlin99
items.body_excerpt:
## Background

Today, Torch ops and C ops are separate implementations. This RFC proposes to:

1. Close the functional gap between Torch ops and C ops.
2. Reorganize the Torch ops file layout to align with C ops.
3. Route ops through per-device `DeviceOps` implementations.

## Step 1: Close the Gap Between Torch Ops and C Ops (https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/4370)

The first step is to complete the missing Torch ops functionality and close the gap with C ops. A related PR already exists.

### Motivation

1. **Hybrid model convergence**

   Complete Torch ops support is required for converging hybrid models in the LMCache engine-driven path.

2. **Complete fallback support for device vendors**

   A complete Torch ops implementation provides a functional fallback, allowing device vendors to evaluate LMCache software support quickly before implementing or optimizing native C ops.

## Step 2: Reorganize the Torch Ops File Layout

The second step is to reorganize the Torch ops file layout and align it with the C ops layout.

### Motivation

Currently, Torch ops are concentrated in a single large file. The file is difficult to maintain and becomes increasingly hard to extend as more ops are added.

Aligning the Torch ops layout with C ops will improve maintainability and make the relationship between the two implementations clearer.

## Step 3: Route Ops Through Per-Device `DeviceOps`

### Current Design

Today, `bind_native()` directly replaces a `DeviceOps` method with a native function. Once bound, the original `DeviceOps` method is bypassed.

An op can therefore only use one implementation: native ops or Torch ops.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Before["Before: function replacement"]
        A["DeviceOps.op()"] -->|"bind_native() overwrites op"| B["native_op()"]
        C["DeviceOps.op()"] -->|"no native binding"| D["torch_op()"]
    end
```

### Proposed Design

After this change, `DeviceOps` methods are always retained. Each device-specific `DeviceOps` subclass intercepts the call, performs necessary device-specific handling, and forwards the call to native ops or Torch ops dynamically.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph After["After: DeviceOps interception and forwarding"]
        E["DeviceOps.op()"] --> F{"platform / device routing"}
        F --> G["native_op()"]
        F --> H["torch_op()"]
    end
```

### Motivation

1. **Use Tensor as the unified upper-layer interface**

   Upper-layer code should always pass Tensors and should not need to know whether the selected backend is native ops or Torch ops.

   If native ops are selected, the device-specific `DeviceOps` subclass can convert Tensors to pointers as needed. If Torch ops are selected, it forwards Tensors directly.

2. **Route based on KV format**

   A device vendor may support only a subset of KV formats in its native ops, while Torch ops provide complete functional coverage.

   The device-specific `DeviceOps` subclass can select native ops for supported formats and fall back to Torch ops for unsupported formats.

   For example, the vLLM path can use the optimized native path when supported. The SGLang path may prioritize functional coverage and fall back to Torch ops when a native implementation does not support the requested KV format.

3. **Simplify the current code structure**

   There is currently a significant amount of logic under `platform` that exists because upper layers pass pointers and need to reconstruct Tensors.

   Moving backend-specific conversion and routing into the device-specific `DeviceOps` subclass will simplify the platform code structure.

4. **Make multi-op composition easier**

   The device-specific `DeviceOps` subclass can combine multiple low-level ops into a single API for upper layers.

   For example, `multi_block_transfer` and `memcpy_async` can be composed behind one API, while the upper layer does not need to know the composition details.

5. **Support multiple backends per device**

   This design allows a device to select among multiple backends, such as native ops, Torch ops, TorchMUSA, Triton, or other vendor-specific implementations.

   For example, MUSA can dynamically select between its `torchmusa` and native backends. The same structure can support additional backends in the future.

items.title: [Bug] from_env/from_file set fields to None instead of the default when the value is invalid or empty
items.author: devteamaegis
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`LMCacheEngineConfig.from_env()` and `from_file()` set a config field to `None` — not its documented default — whenever the value fails conversion, or when a YAML key is present without a value.

**Root cause**

`_apply_env_converter_safely` (`lmcache/v1/config_base.py:28`) returns `None` when `env_converter` raises. The `except` handler in `_from_env` that is supposed to fall back to `config["default"]` never runs — the helper already swallowed the exception, so that handler is dead code. `_from_file` has no fallback at all, and the `if value is None: return None` short-circuit means a key present with an empty value (the common "commented out the value" state) nulls the field even when its type is not Optional.

**Reproduce** (`dev` @ 0373a57, CPU-only, no vLLM needed)

```python
import os
from lmcache.v1.config import LMCacheEngineConfig

os.environ["LMCACHE_CHUNK_SIZE"] = "invalid_number"
print(LMCacheEngineConfig.from_env().chunk_size)   # None — expected 256

# YAML with empty values:
#   chunk_size:
#   local_cpu:
#   max_local_cpu_size:
cfg = LMCacheEngineConfig.from_file("c.yaml")
print(cfg.chunk_size, cfg.local_cpu, cfg.max_local_cpu_size)  # None None None
cfg.validate()                                     # passes — nothing catches it
```

**Why it matters**

- `chunk_size=None` crashes far from the config: `range(0, end, None)` → `TypeError` inside `token_database.py`, at request time rather than at load time.
- `local_cpu:` with no value is worse: `None` is falsy, so `storage_backend/__init__.py` silently skips creating the CPU backend — no error, just a cache that never hits.
- `max_local_cpu_size=None` → `TypeError` at backend construction.

**Expected behavior**

The intent is already in the codebase twice: the dead fallback handler in `_from_env`, and `update_config_from_env`, which keeps the previous value when conversion fails (`tests/v1/test_config.py::test_update_config_from_env_error_handling` encodes this). Loading paths should warn and fall back to the field default; an explicit `null` for an Optional-typed field (e.g. `remote_serde: null`) should stay `None`; `validate_and_set_config_value` should keep rejecting bad runtime updates as it does today.

I have a small fix with unit tests; PR incoming.

items.title: [Bug] KV-event token_ids carries one extra token per chunk; hashes variant slices the chunk-hash list with token offsets
items.author: devteamaegis
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

Two related defects in how `CacheStoreEvent`s are built during store. Verified on `dev` @ 0373a57, CPU-only.

**1. Off-by-one: every non-final chunk's event carries `block_size + 1` tokens**

`ChunkedTokenDatabase.process_tokens` yields half-open `[start, end)` bounds (`token_database.py`: `end_idx = min(start_idx + self.chunk_size, total_len)`), and every consumer treats them that way — except the KV-event path. `convert_tokens_to_list` (`lmcache/utils.py:303`) is inclusive of its end index by design — `tokens[token_start : token_end + 1]`, pinned by `tests/test_utils.py` — and both store paths (`cache_engine.py:535` and the layerwise path at `:718`) pass the exclusive `end` straight through. Each emitted event therefore contains its chunk's tokens **plus the first token of the next chunk**; the final chunk is only correct because the slice clamps at the sequence end.

With `chunk_size=4` and 10 tokens:

```
start=0 end=4  block_size=4  len(token_ids)=5  token_ids=[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
start=4 end=8  block_size=4  len(token_ids)=5  token_ids=[4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
start=8 end=10 block_size=2  len(token_ids)=2  token_ids=[8, 9]
```

`CacheStoreEvent` mirrors vLLM's `BlockStored` and is published externally through `get_kv_events()` (vLLM adapter and SGLang adapter), so the event is self-inconsistent (`len(token_ids) != block_size`) and any subscriber that recomputes block hashes from `token_ids` derives different hashes than LMCache stored under.

**2. The hashes variant indexes the chunk-hash list with token offsets** (`cache_engine.py:543`)

```python
stored_event.token_ids = hashes[start : end + 1]
```

`hashes` has one entry per **chunk**, but `start`/`end` are **token** offsets. For 2 chunks of 256 tokens: chunk 0 gets `hashes[0:257]` = both hashes; chunk 1 gets `hashes[256:513]` = `[]`.

**Repro** (no GPU):

```python
from lmcache.utils import convert_tokens_to_list
from lmcache.v1.token_database import ChunkedTokenDatabase

db = object.__new__(ChunkedTokenDatabase)
db.chunk_size = 4
tokens = list(range(10))
for start, end, _ in db.process_tokens(tokens=tokens, make_key=False):
    ids = convert_tokens_to_list(tokens, start, end)
    assert len(ids) == end - start   # fails: 5 != 4 for non-final chunks
```

**Expected behavior**

`len(token_ids) == block_size` for every event, and the hashes variant should select the single chunk hash for the chunk index.

Happy to send the patch with unit tests if useful.

items.title: [Bug] fs_native L2: files left by a previous process are never counted toward max_capacity_gb or evicted (disk grows unbounded across restarts)
items.author: OscarSavNS
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With the `fs_native` L2 adapter, chunk files persist across a server restart and are still served (lookup is a `stat` on the file), but the new process never registers them. They don't count toward `max_capacity_gb`, and the eviction policy never sees them, so **they are never evicted**. Each restart can strand up to a full cap of untracked files, and disk usage grows without bound until the filesystem fills.

## Observed

`lmcache/vllm-openai` image, LMCache `0.5.6rc1` (commit `9a7b6050`), MP server with:

```
--l2-adapter '{"type":"fs_native","base_path":"/lmcache/l2","num_workers":32,"use_odirect":true,
  "max_capacity_gb":1000,"eviction":{"eviction_policy":"LRU","trigger_watermark":0.9,"eviction_ratio":0.1}}'
```

1. Wrote ~1.2 TB of KV. LRU eviction worked as documented: usage hit the 0.9 watermark three times and dropped to 871 GB each time (`L2 usage 0.90 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction`).
2. Restarted the server with the same `base_path`: 298,340 files, 911.7 GB on disk.
3. After the restart, `GET /status` reported `l2_eviction_controller.adapters[0].total_bytes_used = 0`.
4. Requests over the pre-restart prefixes were served from those files: 16.76M tokens, every full chunk, `lookup_hit_l2_tokens_total` +16,760,832. After that, tracked usage was 0.49 GB, i.e. only the new writes, while 911.7 GB of served files stayed untracked.

## Root cause (on `dev` at dc68527c)

- Byte accounting and eviction order are fed only by stores that the current process completes: `_notify_keys_stored` in `l2_adapters/base.py`, called from the native adapter's store completions. Neither `fs_native_l2_adapter.py` nor `native_connector_l2_adapter.py` scans `base_path` at startup.
- Reads of pre-existing files fire `on_l2_keys_accessed`, and `LRUEvictionPolicy.on_keys_touched` ignores keys it doesn't track (`if key in self._order`).
- `NativeConnectorL2Adapter` decrements usage on delete only for keys in `_key_sizes`, i.e. stored by this process.
- Re-storing an existing key is a no-op on disk (`csrc/storage_backends/fs/connector.cpp`: "Skip if already stored on disk").

RFC #4738 mentions this in passing ("Restart recovery: ... Existing files on disk are not automatically registered again"), but as part of a larger multi-disk design, and there is no standalone bug for it.

## Impact

With `max_capacity_gb` sized to the disk (the natural configuration), one restart with a full cache followed by a refill exceeds the disk. Any deployment that restarts routinely (rollouts, crashes) accumulates untracked files. Operators have to choose between wiping `base_path` on every start, which loses the persistence, and eventually running out of space.

## Proposed fix (prototyped, tested)

File names are already reversible: `fs_l2_adapter._filename_to_object_key` inverts the names the C++ connector writes. The prototype:

- adds `L2AdapterInterface.recover_persisted_objects() -> int` (default no-op), delegated by the serde and fault-inject wrappers;
- `StorageManager` calls it for each adapter **after** the L2 eviction states have registered their listeners, at init and in `add_l2_adapter`;
- `NativeConnectorL2Adapter` takes an optional `persisted_object_scanner`. `recover_persisted_objects` records each object in `_key_sizes` (so eviction deletes decrement usage) and announces it through `_notify_keys_stored`. It goes newest-first, so LRU's reverse insertion puts the oldest file at the eviction head. Keys already tracked are skipped;
- `fs_native` gains `recover_on_start` (default `true`) and a scanner that `os.scandir`s `base_path`. It decodes `.data` names, takes `st_size` and `st_mtime`, and skips `.tmp` files, undecodable names and directories.

Tests: 13 new (scanner, adapter recovery/ordering/delete/double-count, config, and `StorageManager` end-to-end: leftover files are accounted, over-cap leftovers are evicted oldest-first, `recover_on_start: false` keeps today's behaviour). The existing tests in `test_native_connector_l2_adapter`, `test_fs_native_l2_adapter_config`, `test_runtime_adapters`, `test_l2_adapter_base`, `test_fault_inject_l2_adapter`, `test_storage_manager_l2_keys` and `test_l2_adapter_factory` still pass (185 passed). Run on the 0.5.6rc1 commit; the patch also applies cleanly to current `dev`.

**Validated on a real cache:** 0.5.6rc1 plus the patch, restarted over the 911.7 GB directory above, with the cap lowered to 800 GiB:

```
fs_native: found 298492 persisted objects (849.44 GiB) in /lmcache/l2 in 3.0 s (0 entries skipped)
L2 adapter 0: registered 298492 objects recovered from persistent storage (usage 912076931072 bytes)
L2 usage 1.06 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction.
L2 usage 0.96 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction.
```

- **Settled usage:** 0.86. The disk went from 912.2 GB to 738.85 GB, with 738.78 GB tracked, within 0.01% of `du`.
- **Oldest first:** the evicted files were the oldest by mtime; the newest were kept.

Open questions for maintainers:

- **Default:** should `recover_on_start` default to `true`? It changes startup behaviour, since eviction can run immediately when leftovers exceed the watermark.
- **Scan cost:** the scan is synchronous at startup. ~300k files took 3.0 s to scan plus 0.5 s to register here; a very large directory might want a background scan.
- **Other adapters:** the same gap likely applies to other persistent adapters, e.g. `fs` and `nixl_store`; the hook is generic.

Happy to open a PR.

items.title: fs L2: per-rank group payloads collide on shared keys — half-size group-5 objects abort lookup promotion (hybrid groups, PP>1)
items.author: kaka86mm
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On a PP>1 hybrid-KV-group model, the fs L2 tier never survives a server restart: lookups find the keys but abort promotion with `Incomplete read` size mismatches, so `lmcache_mp_lookup_hit_l2_*` stays 0 and everything recomputes. Evidence points to **per-rank group payloads colliding on shared keys** — one PP rank writes group-5 objects at exactly half the size the reader's spec-derived buffer expects.

## Environment

- 4× CMP 170HX (sm80), vLLM fork v0.13.0, PP=4 (`12,12,12,12`), MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL — 6 hybrid groups, `group_tokens_per_block=[256,128,128,128,128,128]`
- `lmcache server --chunk-size 8192 --shm-name ... --max-gpu-workers 4 --supported-transfer-mode engine_driven --l1-size-gb 100 --no-l1-use-lazy --eviction-policy LRU --l2-adapter '{"type":"fs","base_path":"/lmcache-l2","relative_tmp_dir":"tmp"}'`
- lmcache 0.5.6.post4410 (PR #4410 head)

## Repro (deterministic)

1. Send a unique 200K-token prefix (same token ids both times) → prefill completes, objects written to L2.
2. Gracefully restart server and engine (`docker stop -t 60` both; no kills).
3. Resend the identical prefix.

Result: full recompute (~57 s), `lookup_hit_l2_tokens_total` / `lookup_hit_l2_keys_total` = **0**, and 27 warnings:

```
Incomplete read for -SEP-model@0x04000400@5@<hash>.data: expected 1310720, got 655360
```

## Evidence for per-rank payload collision

File-size census of the L2 dir after one 200K store:

| group | files × size |
|---|---|
| @0 | 243 × 41,943,040 + 81 × 62,914,560 |
| @1..@4 | 324 × 1,310,720 each |
| @5 | **243 × 1,310,720 + 81 × 655,360** |

- 324 = 4 ranks × 81 chunks; the 81 bad @5 files are exactly one rank's share. The PP ranks carry different layer compositions (rank 0 hosts the vision encoder, rank 3 the lm_head), so per-rank group payloads legitimately differ in size (see @0's 40 MB vs 60 MB classes).
- All 27 lookup-time mismatches are `@5` keys whose on-disk size (655,360) is exactly half of `expected = len(dst_buf)` (1,310,720) — the buffer comes from the engine-side group spec (`fs_l2_adapter.py`, standard async path: `expected = len(dst_buf)`), not from any per-object metadata.
- Atomic writes were enabled (`relative_tmp_dir=tmp`, `os.replace`), and these files were written by a fresh clean process with no interruption — truncation is ruled out; the writer wrote half.
- The reader `continue`s on mismatch, so the first bad object in a chain truncates the contiguous hit to zero → no promotion at all, not even partial.

This also retroactively explains the partial adoption we reported earlier (168/192 keys after a restart) and why `lookup_hit_l2` was 0 all day in production.

## Suggested directions

- Include the rank (or a payload-size discriminator) in the L2 object key, or assemble the full-group payload before writing under the shared key; or
- store the object's true byte length in a sidecar / the key name and size the read buffer from it, instead of deriving `expected` from the model group spec.

Happy to run instrumented builds or share the full server logs / file census on request.

(Prior context from the same rig: #5440 — the per-object cost thread; #4410 review.)

items.title: [Bug][Tests] Worker info API fixture can select duplicate ports
items.author: mohan-zeyu
items.body_excerpt: **Label** bug **Describe the bug** `TestWorkerInfoAPI.controller_urls` in `tests/v1/internal_api_server/test_worker_info_api.py` calls `get_available_port()` separately for the pull, reply, and heartbeat sockets. The observed Buildkite failure assigned both pull and reply to `127.0.0.1:59197`: ```text controller_urls = { 'heartbeat': '127.0.0.1:45599', 'pull': '127.0.0.1:59197', 'reply': '127.0.0.1:59197', } ERROR tests/v1/internal_api_server/test_worker_info_api.py::TestWorkerInfoAPI::test_real_nonexistent_worker zmq.error.ZMQError: Address already in use (addr='tcp://127.0.0.1:59197') ``` **To Reproduce** On a checkout with the original fixture, run: ```bash python -m pytest -q tests/v1/internal_api_server/test_worker_info_api.py ``` This is intermittent: the failure occurs when successive calls select the same released port. A single passing run does not rule it out. It was observed in the Buildkite unit suite for PR #5639 at commit `4d0d06f21a4552db73fa5591aa5e3e1797f57c6a`. **Expected behavior** The controller fixture should bind its three sockets to distinct available endpoints and provide those bound addresses to clients and heartbeat registration. **Environment** - Linux Buildkite runner - Python 3.12.3 - The failure occurs during controller fixture setup, before the test body runs. **Proposed fix** Bind the real controller sockets to `127.0.0.1:0`, read their assigned addresses through `zmq.LAST_ENDPOINT`, and record those addresses before starting handlers or connecting clients. This keeps the selected ports occupied by the sockets that actually use them.

items.title: [Bug] Worker-node enumeration races with controller registrations
items.author: AaravMehta-07
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug

On `dev` at `110caf524c728b7b4489b2d4db40e2c72f79a879`, a fresh `RegistryTree.get_all_worker_nodes_cached(timeout_seconds=0)` can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` while another thread registers a worker.

The underlying `_get_all_worker_nodes_fresh()` iterates `self.instances.items()` and `instance_node.workers.values()` directly. Registrations modify these maps under their registry/instance RW locks, but the reader does not take either lock. The getter is used by `FullSyncTracker`.

### Reproduction

Initialize one registered worker. Pause the fresh getter after it starts traversing the first instance, then have a concurrent thread call the real `register_worker()` API for a second instance. The reader raises the dictionary-size error. Repeat while traversing a single instance's workers and register another worker in that instance: same error.

Two bounded CPU regression tests use an event-gated mapping to force this schedule, a real registration thread, and the public cache getter. Both fail against the unchanged helper with the exact RuntimeError. Snapshotting each map under its owning read lock makes both pass; the registry, full-sync and registration suites then pass 90 tests. The registry lock is released before taking an instance lock, so this does not add nested lock acquisition or promise a globally atomic snapshot.

Validation was source-only on Windows/Python 3.11; no CUDA/native-cache or model-serving integration claim. Two unrelated existing AsyncMock warnings appear in registration tests. Investigation and tests were AI-assisted and independently reproduced by the coordinating agent. A focused fix is prepared for review.
