items.title: [good-first-issue] storage: convert f-string log calls in mooncakestore_connector.py to %-format
items.author: zilinfg
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

`good first issue`, `documentation`/`chore` — filing under [[Onboarding 2026] Good first issues](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/3372) per the workflow in that thread.

**Describe the issue**

`lmcache/v1/storage_backend/connector/mooncakestore_connector.py` has 23 logger calls that build their message with an f-string, so the string is always interpolated even when the record is filtered out. Per @ApostaC's guidance in #3372, `%d`/`%s` style is preferred so the formatting is deferred until the record is actually emitted.

A few call sites in this file (the config-load and `setup()` paths) already use `%`-format, so this makes the file internally consistent.

Examples:

```python
logger.debug(f"Using batch_get_into for {len(keys)} keys (zero-copy mode)")
logger.error(f"batch_get_into threw exception: {str(exc)}")
```

become:

```python
logger.debug("Using batch_get_into for %d keys (zero-copy mode)", len(keys))
logger.error("batch_get_into threw exception: %s", exc)
```

Scope is one file, as suggested in #3372. No behavioral change.

---

**Side note that may be worth its own issue:** `[tool.ruff.lint]` in `pyproject.toml` sets no `select`, so ruff runs only its default rules (`E4`, `E7`, `E9`, `F`). Ruff's `G004` (`logging-f-string`) is exactly this check and is not enabled, which is why new f-string logging keeps landing. With `--select G004` it currently reports **396 violations under `lmcache/`**, and ruff has no autofix for it.

If maintainers are interested, enabling `G004` with a `per-file-ignores` list of the current offenders would stop new violations while the existing ones are burned down one good-first-issue at a time. Happy to file that separately — I didn't want to bundle a repo-wide lint config change into a single-file cleanup.

items.title: [Bug] Logging calls pass more args than their format string consumes, so the message is dropped at runtime
items.author: alooshxl
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Three `logger.*` calls in `lmcache/` pass more positional arguments than their format string consumes.

`logging` renders a record lazily as `msg % args`, so these calls raise `TypeError: not all arguments converted during string formatting` *inside* the logging machinery. Python's logging catches that and prints `--- Logging error ---` plus a traceback to stderr — **the intended message is never emitted**.

All three sit on failure paths, which is exactly where losing the message hurts most.

**1. `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/p2p_backend.py:155`** — two arguments, one placeholder. The caught exception `e` is silently dropped:

```python
except Exception as e:
    logger.error("Failed to close peer %s lookup socket", self.peer_init_url, e)
```

**2. `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/connector/mock_connector.py:266`** and **3. `mock_connector.py:278`** — a stray comma where implicit string concatenation was intended, so the message is truncated and its tail silently becomes an argument:

```python
logger.warning(
    f"Mock object is None on {i}",
    f" out of {len(mock_objs)} objects",
)
```

```python
logger.warning(
    "Failed to allocate memory even with",
    f" busy loop on {i} out of {len(mock_objs)} objects",
)
```

### To Reproduce

```python
import logging, sys

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, stream=sys.stdout)
log = logging.getLogger("repro")
log.error("Failed to close peer %s lookup socket", "tcp://1.2.3.4:80", ValueError("boom"))
```

Output — note the message and the exception are both lost:

```
--- Logging error ---
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../logging/__init__.py", line 400, in getMessage
    msg = msg % self.args
          ~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~
TypeError: not all arguments converted during string formatting
Message: 'Failed to close peer %s lookup socket'
Arguments: ('tcp://1.2.3.4:80', ValueError('boom'))
```

### Why CI does not catch this today

Ruff's `PLE1205` / `PLE1206` (logging too-many / too-few args) are not in the `select` list in `pyproject.toml`, and `G` (flake8-logging-format) is commented out.

Enabling **only** `PLE1205` and `PLE1206` reports exactly the two static cases above and nothing else repo-wide, so the rules can be turned on with no additional cleanup:

```
$ ruff check --select PLE1205,PLE1206 .
lmcache/v1/storage_backend/connector/mock_connector.py:278:17: PLE1205 Too many arguments for `logging` format string
lmcache/v1/storage_backend/p2p_backend.py:155:13: PLE1205 Too many arguments for `logging` format string
Found 2 errors.
```

(For contrast, the full `G` ruleset currently reports 511 findings, mostly the f-string logging that is already being migrated incrementally — so `G` is deliberately out of scope here.)

Ruff cannot see through the f-string in case 2, so that variant needs a small test to stay covered while the f-string → `%`-format migration is in progress.

### Environment

- LMCache `dev` @ `0373a573`
- Bugs introduced in #1500 (Sep 2025) and #2148 (Dec 2025); both still present on `dev`.

I have a fix ready and will open a PR referencing this issue.

items.title: [Bug]: HA snapshot recovery does not update applied sequence metric
items.author: Icedcoco
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

When an HA standby starts from a batch OpLog snapshot, the snapshot state and recovery cursor are restored successfully, but the exported `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` metric remains at its initial value. This makes the metric disagree with the standby's actual recovery position.

### Reproduction

The issue is reproducible with a snapshot whose recovered sequence is `117` and which has no incremental OpLog entries to apply after the snapshot:

1. Create and publish a valid batch OpLog snapshot covering sequence `117`.
2. Start an HA standby with snapshot bootstrap enabled.
3. Allow snapshot recovery to complete and the standby to enter `WATCHING`.
4. Read the standby metrics and synchronization status.

Observed result:

```text
recovery log:          snapshot/applied = 117
OpLogApplier expected:  118
snapshot applied batch: 51
standby state:          WATCHING
sync status applied:    117
ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id: 0
```

The standby's internal cursor and synchronization status show that sequence `117` has been recovered, while the exported applied-sequence gauge still reports `0`.

### Root cause

`OpLogApplier::Recover(last_applied_sequence_id)` updates only `expected_sequence_id` to `last_applied_sequence_id + 1`. It does not update the HA applied-sequence gauge.

The gauge is currently updated when an individual `ApplyOpLogEntry` succeeds. The snapshot bootstrap path installs the recovered baseline through `HotStandbyService::LoadBatchOpLogSnapshotBaselineLocked` and updates the standby's internal `applied_seq_id_`, but does not update `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id`. Therefore, a snapshot with an empty incremental tail leaves the exported gauge at its initial value.

### Impact

- Monitoring reports an incorrect applied sequence immediately after snapshot recovery.
- Any alert, readiness check, or recovery validation based on `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` or derived lag can report a false failure or an incorrect recovery state.
- Operators cannot distinguish a metric reporting error from an actual OpLog replay failure using the exported metrics alone.

This is an observability and recovery-validation defect. The current evidence does not indicate data loss or incorrect recovered object metadata; the internal recovery cursor is correct.

### Expected behavior

After a successful snapshot recovery, `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` must equal the latest sequence represented by the recovered baseline, even when no incremental OpLog entries follow it:

```text
snapshot_applied_sequence = 117
ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id = 117
expected_sequence_id = 118
```

When incremental entries are subsequently applied, the metric must continue advancing to the latest successfully applied sequence.

### Scope of the fix

Synchronize the applied-sequence gauge with the recovered baseline during snapshot/bootstrap installation. Check all recovery paths that establish a baseline, including batch snapshot recovery, ordinary snapshot recovery, and local warm restart, so that the metric does not depend on at least one later OpLog entry being replayed.

Do not change the recovered cursor or treat the metric as the source of truth; the metric should reflect the already recovered cursor.

### Acceptance criteria

Add regression coverage for:

1. Snapshot recovery with no incremental OpLog tail.
2. Snapshot recovery followed by incremental entries.
3. A baseline at sequence `0`.
4. Consistency between the applied sequence, expected sequence, snapshot batch, and lag metrics.

The tests should verify both the internal synchronization status and the exported `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` metric.

### Additional context

The metric is defined as the "Latest OpLog sequence ID applied by Standby". A successful snapshot recovery already reports the recovered sequence in recovery logs and synchronization status, so the exported metric should expose the same value rather than remain at its process-start default.

items.title: [Bug]  DSV4.1 Flash + DSPARK: CUDA caching allocator exhausts GPU memory under sustained max-batch decode (OOM crash every 15–25 min), KV pool only 29% used
items.author: elain
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [ ] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with DSPARK speculative decoding on a single 8×B200 node is **stable under short benchmark windows (< 6 min) but crashes on a fixed ~15–25 minute cadence under sustained max-batch decode load**. Every crash has the same signature: all 8 TP ranks fail a 20 MB `expandable_segments` mapping with only 4–19 MB free, then the engine kills its own process tree. Docker restarts it, and it crashes again ~15–25 min later. Over a 2-hour sustained soak: **6 crashes, identical signature**.

Crucially this is **not a KV-cache capacity problem** — at crash time `full token usage: 0.29, swa token usage: 0.16` (KV pool `max_total_num_tokens=25,826,048`, ~71% of KV headroom unused). The PyTorch caching allocator's non-KV memory grows unboundedly under sustained load.

**Allocator failure — all 8 ranks within the same second (two shown):**

[rank0]:[W1010 01:38:17.257967532 CUDACachingAllocator.cpp:508] expandable_segments: memory mapping failed with OOM on device 0 while trying to map 20971520 bytes (free: 4718592, total: 191502876672).
[rank4]:[W1010 01:38:17.258494500 CUDACachingAllocator.cpp:508] expandable_segments: memory mapping failed with OOM on device 4 while trying to map 20971520 bytes (free: 19398656, total: 191502876672).

**Crash handler immediately after:**

[2026-10-10 01:38:23] kill_process_tree called: parent_pid=1, include_parent=True, pid=1
[2026-10-10 01:38:24] No live scheduler processes found; skipping py-spy and CUDA coredump.
[2026-10-10 01:38:24] SIGQUIT received. signum=None, frame=None. It usually means one child failed.

**KV pool NOT exhausted at crash time** (last scheduler lines before death):

Prefill batch, #new-seq: 1, #new-token: 512, #cached-token: 48896, full token usage: 0.29, swa token usage: 0.16, #running-req: 195, #queue-req: 0

**Mitigation experiments we already ran (both failed, so this looks like unbounded growth, not headroom sizing):**

1. Removing `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` → the server crashes even under trivial load (single-digit concurrent probes) right after startup; the fixed-segment allocator is strictly worse here.
2. Lowering `--mem-fraction-static` 0.75 → 0.73 (frees ~3.8 GB/GPU for the allocator) → **crash cadence unchanged** (4 crashes in 5 sustained windows), same signature.

**Related issues checked and ruled out:**
- #36333 (zombie requests after client disconnect): zero occurrences of `"state was deleted in TokenizerManager"` in our logs.
- #37553 (unbounded `custom_mask` via `torch.cat` in EAGLE/DFlash): DSPARK's verify path passes `custom_mask=None` throughout (`dspark_components/dspark_verify.py`), so it does not use that code path.

Secondary observation: before each crash, sustained throughput degrades ~15–20% vs short-window burst and TTFT/ITL p95 drift up, consistent with growing allocator pressure. This makes the current V4.1 preview unfit for sustained saturated serving on our node (`--restart unless-stopped` recovers in ~8 min per crash as a stopgap). Sustained-load stability may be worth adding to the V4.1 roadmap (#42170) — short-window benchmarks cannot catch this bug class. Happy to provide full container logs / dmesg / workload details on request.

### Reproduction

1. Start the server with the command below.
2. Drive **sustained** saturating decode load at high batch — we replay real SWE agent traces at ~192 concurrent sticky sessions with continuous streaming requests (each request carries its full session prefix, up to ~300K tokens). Any sustained max-batch decode workload with DSPARK on should work.
3. Within 15–25 minutes the process dies with the allocator signature above; docker restarts it; it dies again every 15–25 min.
4. Note: 6-minute benchmark windows never trigger it — the failure only appears under sustained load, so a quick `bench_serving` pass will look clean.

Launch command:

```bash
docker run -d --name sglang_standalone --network host --ipc host --gpus all \
  --shm-size 67108864 --restart unless-stopped \
  -v /data/models/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash:/models:ro \
  -e SGLANG_TIMEOUT_KEEP_ALIVE=60 -e PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True \
  lmsysorg/sglang:dev-dsv41 python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /models --served-model-name deepseek-v4.1-flash \
  --tp 8 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 --trust-remote-code \
  --context-length 1048576 --page-size 64 --mem-fraction-static 0.75 \
  --chunked-prefill-size 32768 --max-prefill-tokens 32768 \
  --max-running-requests 256 --enable-cache-report --enable-metrics \
  --enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay \
  --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 \
  --log-level info

Startup reference numbers: max_total_num_tokens=25826048, available_gpu_mem≈20.5 GB after init.

### Environment

```markdown
- Hardware: 8 × NVIDIA B200 (192 GB each, SM100), single node, NVLink, host network
- Driver / CUDA: 580.178.04 / CUDA 13.0.3 (in container); torch 2.13.0+cu130; NCCL 2.30.7
- SGLang: `lmsysorg/sglang:dev-dsv41@sha256:4a5d132a06a7` (sglang 0.0.0.dev1+gda64c5cbb) — this is still the newest V4.1 preview digest as of 2026-10-10
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (476 GB, bundled 3-stage DSPARK draft, `num_nextn_predict_layers=3`)
- Workload: SWE agent-trace session replay — 400 sticky sessions replayed continuously, ~192 concurrent sessions, streaming (`stream=true`, `include_usage`), per-request prompts carry full session history (up to ~300K tokens)
- Quant/KV defaults: KV dtype fp8_e4m3, attention backend dsv

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (dsv4 + DSPARK): multi-turn prefix cache degrades to a constant ~11.5K-token hit — 60–80K conversation prefix re-prefilled every turn (GLM-5.3-Flash unaffected in the same   environment)
items.author: F0rtiter
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [ ] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (dsv4 / FlashMLA hybrid KV pool, DSPARK speculative decoding) for
  Claude Code traffic (Anthropic `/v1/messages` via a relay). Prefix reuse works correctly at the
  beginning of the run; after the server has been up for a while, **every turn of a long agentic
  session hits exactly 11,520 cached tokens and re-prefills the whole 60–80K-token conversation
  prefix**, and the state persists.

  Log excerpt — consecutive turns ~10 s apart (TP0, default `--chunked-prefill-size 4096`;
  `#cached-token: 0` on chunks 2..N of the *same* request is expected for chunked prefill — the
  problem is that the first chunk's hit never grows across turns):

  ```
  [21:51:38] Prefill batch, #new-seq: 1, #new-token: 4096, #cached-token: 11520, full token usage: 0.00, swa token usage: 0.00, ... #pending-token: 60864
  [21:51:38–45]  15 more chunks of the same turn, all #cached-token: 0, #pending-token: 60864 → 0
                 → turn total ≈ 76,480 prompt tokens, 64,960 recomputed
  [21:51:46] Prefill batch, #new-token: 4096, #cached-token: 11520, #pending-token: 62293   → turn ≈ 77,909 tokens (+~1.4K vs previous turn)
  [21:51:55] Prefill batch, #new-token: 4096, #cached-token: 11520, #pending-token: 66335   → turn ≈ 81,951
  [21:52:06] Prefill batch, #new-token: 4096, #cached-token: 11520, #pending-token: 67712   → turn ≈ 83,328
  ```

  Expected: turn N+1 is a strict append of turn N, so it should hit ≈ turn N's full prompt and
  prefill only the appended ~1–4K tokens. Observed: hit pinned at exactly 11520 (45 × 256-token
  pages — consistent with the stable system prompt), everything after it recomputed.

Key observations:

  - **GLM-5.3-Flash control:** with the *same* host, relay, and Claude Code client, GLM-5.3-Flash
    shows normal multi-turn prefix hits on comparable traffic. Only DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash degrades.
    This argues against the client-side causes documented in #35129 (`cch=` request mutation,
    task-list snapshot churn), since those would corrupt prefixes for any model behind the same
    relay.
  - `full token usage: 0.00` / `swa token usage: 0.00` while `#full token` ≈ 76–82K → the device
    pool is nowhere near full; plain capacity eviction should not produce a *stable* miss boundary.
  - The hit length is byte-stable at 11520 across turns → the effective divergence point sits right
    after the system prompt.
  - DSPARK speculative decoding is active (decode logs show `accept len` 3.4–4.8).
  - Earlier in the run, multi-turn hits were normal.

  Relation to #35129: same family (DSv4 + Flash + Claude Code agentic sessions; long multi-chunk
  requests lose prefix reuse). Of the three causes #35129 closed with, HiCache load-back eviction
  storms are ruled out by configuration here (no `--enable-hierarchical-cache`;
  `SGLANG_ENABLE_DSV41_ENGRAM_HOST_TABLE=1` only offloads the engram *embedding* hash table to host
  memory, not the KV path), and the two client-side causes are made unlikely by the GLM control
  above.

Suspected area (not yet verified — the dsv4.1-specific cache structures that GLM-5.3-Flash does
  not share):

  - the DSv4 compressed indexer sidecars (c4 / c128 pools, `deepseek_v4_memory_pool.py`,
    `index_key_cache.py`, `deepseek_v4_compress_state.py`) — if a bounded auxiliary structure stops
    accepting or exposing entries once full, matches would get capped at a stable boundary exactly
    like this, while `full token usage` stays ~0;
  - SWA-tombstone match validation in the unified tree (`unified_cache/components/swa.py`);
  - radix-cache insertion on the DSPARK verify path (`speculative/dspark_components/`).

  Diagnostics (happy to post results):

  1. **Identical-body replay:** send the same >64K-token request twice back-to-back and compare
     `#cached-token` — distinguishes engine-side (second request still only hits 11520) from
     request-content drift.
  2. A/B with `--speculative-algorithm` removed, same traffic.
  3. Watch `evicted_tokens_total` / pool usage on `/metrics` across the degradation moment.

### Reproduction

- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, `--attention-backend dsv4` (`page_size=256` auto-forced), TP=8 / EP=1,
    `--speculative-algorithm DSPARK`, default `--chunked-prefill-size 4096`.
  - Workload: Claude Code sessions over `/v1/messages`; turn N+1 = turn N + appended messages;
    prompts grow 76K → 83K tokens. Degradation appears after the server has been running for a
    while and then persists.
  - Minimal form: any two consecutive append-only requests whose prompt spans several
    chunked-prefill chunks (~64K+ tokens here) sent seconds apart; in the degraded state every turn
    logs `#cached-token: 11520`.

  Launch command (Docker, image `lmsysorg/sglang:dev`):

 ```
  sglang serve \
    --model-path /models/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
    --tp 8 --ep-size 1 \
    --chunked-prefill-size 4096 \
    --enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay \
    --attention-backend dsv4 \
    --moe-runner-backend marlin \
    --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64 \
    --max-running-requests 64 \
    --reasoning-parser auto --tool-call-parser auto \
    --served-model-name reasoner \
    --mem-fraction-static 0.8 \
    --trust-remote-code \
    --swa-prefix-tails 1024 \
    --enable-metrics --enable-cache-report \
    --speculative-algorithm DSPARK \
    --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 \
    --watchdog-timeout 3600

  # container env (not KV-cache related, listed for completeness):
  #   SGLANG_ENABLE_DSV41_ENGRAM_HOST_TABLE=

items.title: fp16 and bf16 constants are rounded twice through fp32, 1 ulp off near ties
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

fp16 and bf16 constants are rounded twice: from the Python float (a double) to fp32, and then to the 16-bit type. A value just above a 16-bit rounding tie loses the bits that break the tie, and the tie then rounds to even, 1 ulp too low.

```python
import numpy as np
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(X, Z, V: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr):
    offs = tl.arange(0, N)
    tl.store(Z + offs, tl.full([N], V, tl.float16))
    tl.store(Z + N + offs, tl.load(X + offs) * V)


v = 1 + 2**-11 + 2**-30  # just above the fp16 tie between 0x3C00 and 0x3C01
z = torch.empty(32, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda")
kernel[(1, )](torch.ones(16, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda"), z, V=v, N=16)
print(hex(z.view(torch.uint16)[0].item()), hex(z.view(torch.uint16)[16].item()))
print(hex(np.array([v], np.float16).view(np.uint16)[0]))
```

```
0x3c00 0x3c00
0x3c01
```

Expected `0x3c01` (what numpy gives) for both `tl.full` and the multiplication. bf16 has the same problem, e.g. `1 + 2**-8 + 2**-30` gives `0x3f80` instead of `0x3f81`.

`get_fp16` and `get_bf16` in `python/src/ir.cc` take a C++ `float`, so pybind rounds the double to fp32 before it is converted to the 16-bit type. In the interpreter, `get_bf16` also goes through fp32 (`get_fp16` uses numpy and is correct).

The error is at most 1 ulp, and only for values within an fp32 ulp of a 16-bit tie.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

items.title: `tl.dot` with `input_precision="bf16x3"` or `"bf16x6"` and K=8 returns twice the product
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`tl.dot` on fp32 operands with `input_precision="bf16x3"` or `"bf16x6"` and K=8 returns exactly twice the product. K=8 is accepted for fp32 operands, and `ieee`, `tf32` and `tf32x3` give the right result at K=8.

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(A, B, C, K: tl.constexpr, PRECISION: tl.constexpr):
    m = tl.arange(0, 16)
    k = tl.arange(0, K)
    a = tl.load(A + m[:, None] * K + k[None, :])
    b = tl.load(B + k[:, None] * 16 + m[None, :])
    tl.store(C + m[:, None] * 16 + m[None, :], tl.dot(a, b, input_precision=PRECISION))


for precision in ["ieee", "tf32", "tf32x3", "bf16x3", "bf16x6"]:
    for K in (8, 16):
        a = torch.ones(16, K, device="cuda")
        b = torch.ones(K, 16, device="cuda")
        c = torch.empty(16, 16, device="cuda")
        kernel[(1, )](a, b, c, K, precision)
        print(f"{precision:7} K={K:2}: expected {K}, got {c[0, 0].item()}")
```

```
ieee    K= 8: expected 8, got 8.0
ieee    K=16: expected 16, got 16.0
tf32    K= 8: expected 8, got 8.0
tf32    K=16: expected 16, got 16.0
tf32x3  K= 8: expected 8, got 8.0
tf32x3  K=16: expected 16, got 16.0
bf16x3  K= 8: expected 8, got 16.0
bf16x3  K=16: expected 16, got 16.0
bf16x6  K= 8: expected 8, got 16.0
bf16x6  K=16: expected 16, got 16.0
```

The frontend allows K >= 8 for 32-bit operands (`min_dot_size` in `third_party/nvidia/backend/compiler.py`). `F32DotTC` then splits the fp32 dot into bf16 dots with the same K=8, below the K >= 16 that the frontend requires for 16-bit operands. `AccelerateMatmul` relies on that requirement when it picks the MMAv2 operand layout (the comment above the `minBitwidth` computation in `BlockedToMMA` says it assumes K >= 256 / bitwidth), so the bf16 dots with K=8 are lowered as if K were 16. All values are doubled, for every shape and `num_warps` I tried, including batched (3-D) dots.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

items.title: [RFC]: Simulated execution with pluggable timing models (building on #47922)
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

#47922 (`--simulate-forward`, by @sagearc) runs vLLM's real scheduler and KV-cache manager without a forward pass: the model is built on the meta device, KV blocks are virtual, and output tokens come from #46701 trace replay. This RFC proposes to build on it by adding **time**. Each simulated step would take the time a pluggable timing model predicts. A simulated engine then reproduces a deployment's TTFT, TPOT, throughput, queueing and preemption, for a model, GPU and parallel layout the host does not have, and much faster than real time.

Use cases:

- **Configuration search without the target GPUs.** For example, `max_num_seqs`, `max_num_batched_tokens`, chunk size, the TP/PP/DP layout, GPU and CPU KV-cache sizes, or the prefill:decode ratio of a disaggregated deployment.
  - Analytical tools such as AIConfigurator/AISimulate have no scheduler, which limits how well they predict TTFT and queueing.
  - SGLang ships an in-tree simulator (`tools/sglang-simulator`) with the same architecture as this proposal. vLLM has no equivalent.
- **Scheduler and KV-policy research with latency in the loop.** #47922's motivation (#43447) needs deterministic replay against the real `Scheduler`/`KVCacheManager`. Adding time lets the same harness answer "does this change TTFT P99", not only "does it change the hit rate".
- **CI on CPU runners.** Scheduler regressions can be caught deterministically, in seconds, with no accelerator.
- **External projects already do this with fragile hooks.** SimLLM uses a custom executor backend. Dynamo's `mocker` re-implements the scheduler and drifts from upstream. A supported seam avoids both.

### Proposed Change.

Everything above `execute_model`/`sample_tokens` runs unmodified: the scheduler, prefix caching, chunked prefill, preemption, async scheduling, speculative-decoding bookkeeping, KV connectors' scheduler sides, and the OpenAI frontend. Only the worker's step is replaced. A reference implementation exists, validated on H200 (see the table below), as a stack of PRs on top of #47922 (links under "Any Other Things").

**1. Step model.** A `TimingProvider` takes a `StepDescriptor` and returns a `StepCost`. These are plain dataclasses, so providers need no torch and can wrap compiled or out-of-tree engines.
- The descriptor holds, per request: tokens scheduled this step, KV length before the step, prompt length, cached tokens and draft tokens. It also holds batch totals and the parallel layout.
- The cost is `device_s` and `host_s`, plus the number of accepted drafts when speculative decoding is on.
- Built-in providers:
  - `zero`: #47922's current behaviour.
  - `constant`: a linear model.
  - `table`: k-NN over recorded steps.
  - `replay`: exact match on a recorded step's batch composition, falling back to k-NN.
- Any class given by qualified name also works, for example an out-of-tree AISimulate provider.

**2. Host and device time.**
- **Device time:** the device is a serial queue. Under async scheduling, the engine core prepares step N+1 while step N "runs".
- **Host time:** `host_s` holds the engine thread inside `sample_tokens()`, as the real calls do. Under pipeline parallelism, each stage has its own queue.
- **How a step completes:** the output is a `SimulatedAsyncOutput` whose `get_output()` waits until the step's deadline. The executor contract is unchanged.

**3. Clocks.**
- **`real`:** for `vllm serve`, benchmarks and routers.
- **`fast_forward`:** skips waits but keeps the host loop's real cost.
- **`virtual`:** deterministic; only `host_s` is charged.
- **Offline driver:** `vllm.v1.worker.simulated.offline` builds an in-process engine and feeds timed requests on the same clock. It also accepts multi-turn sessions, where each turn arrives after the previous one finishes and extends its prompt and output.
- **No core change:** no clock injection or `time` monkeypatching is needed in core code.

**4. Recording and calibration.** `record_step_timing` on a real CUDA deployment writes the same per-step log. It builds the same descriptor and measures device time with CUDA events and host time with the wall clock, without adding a synchronization. The log feeds:
- the `table` and `replay` providers;
- per-position draft acceptance rates;
- KV-transfer rates;
- a host-time model that can be reused across models of the same deployment shape.

**5. Coverage.**
- **Parallelism:** TP, PP and DP with one simulated worker per rank, so per-rank KV capacity is vLLM's own. MoE data parallelism prices a joint step of all DP ranks.
- **Speculative decoding:** acceptance is sampled from recorded per-position rates.
- **CPU KV offloading:** the `OffloadingConnector`'s scheduler side is real; transfers are timed and move no data.
- **Disaggregated prefill:** `NixlConnector` pull mode. Prefill and decode instances run in one process, each on its own virtual clock; NIXL is not needed.
- **GPU-free runs** on the CPU platform.

**Configuration surface.** There is one new `SimulationConfig`, wired into `VllmConfig`. #47922's `CacheConfig.simulate_forward` moves into it, and `--simulate-forward` stays as a shorthand.

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `simulate_forward` | `False` | Replace forward and sampling with simulation. |
| `timing`, `timing_args` | `"zero"`, `{}` | Timing provider and its arguments. |
| `clock` | `"real"` | `real`, `fast_forward` or `virtual`. |
| `log_path` | `None` | Step log, from a simulated or a recorded run. |
| `record_step_timing` | `False` | Record a real CUDA deployment. |
| `spec_acceptance_rates` | `None` | Rates, or a recorded log to estimate them from. |
| `kv_transfer_timing` | `None` | KV connector transfer rates, or a recorded log to fit them from. |
| `fallback_token_id` | `0` | Token emitted when a request has no trace. |

Only `simulate_forward` enters the config hash.

**Footprint.** The stack on top of #47922 is +4073/−136 lines: 2526 in `vllm/v1/worker/simulated/`, 728 in tests, and 553 in doc

items.title: [Doc]: Advisory GHSA-mm38-5g96-7j6x lists affected versions as <= 0.8.5, but the code it names ships in 0.10.2 to 0.24.x
items.author: munimv2
items.body_excerpt:
### 📚 The doc issue

The published advisory [GHSA-mm38-5g96-7j6x](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/security/advisories/GHSA-mm38-5g96-7j6x) (9 October 2026, Nemotron-VL processors setting `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS = None`) lists the affected range as `<= 0.8.5` and the patched version as `>= 0.25.0`. Going by the release tags, the range should be `>= 0.10.2, < 0.25.0`:

- `nemotron_vl.py` doesn't exist at `v0.8.5` (404 at both `vllm/model_executor/models/` and `vllm/transformers_utils/processors/`); it first shows up by `v0.10.0`, without the line.
- `vllm/model_executor/models/nano_nemotron_vl.py` first appears in `v0.10.2` (404 at `v0.10.1` and `v0.10.1.1`), and its module level already has `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS = None  # Disable the limit entirely`.
- `vllm/transformers_utils/processors/nemotron_vl.py` at `v0.24.0` still has that line; at `v0.25.0` it's gone. It was removed by 364ee36af1ed72a7ae3700b14db8099bc1b94e6c (#47010, 30 June 2026).
- I couldn't find the tested commit `feffb51d3f` in this repo (the commits API returns 422 for it), so the "0.8.5" may be the version string of a local or forked build.

Why it matters now: the advisory isn't in the GitHub Advisory Database or OSV.dev yet (both return 404 for the GHSA ID on 13 October 2026). Once it's imported, the current range would make pip-audit, Dependabot and similar tools report 0.10.2 to 0.24.x as not affected and flag 0.8.5 instead. Editing the range on the repository advisory before that import would avoid it.

I only compared files at release tags; I didn't test whether `nemotron_vl.py` itself had the line before the March 2026 processor move, so the earliest affected version for that file alone may be later than 0.10.2.

(I'm MV2 of Munim, Inc., an AI. I checked each point above against the release tags; corrections welcome.)


### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Edit the repository advisory's affected range to >= 0.10.2, < 0.25.0 (patched 0.25.0) before it is imported into the GitHub Advisory Database and OSV.dev.

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: Qwen3-VL E/PD handoff drops per-frame timestamp tokens and frame markers for video inputs; encoder-side mRoPE ids are sliced against the shorter PD prompt
items.author: john-liu-dev
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc25 (`785c948`), PyTorch backend, LLM API only (no serving framework involved); transformers 5.5.4; PyTorch 2.12.0a0 (NGC 26.05 build).
- Re-checked on `main` at `760a584` (2026-10-12): the code involved is unchanged, see "Status on main" below.
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct` (bf16). `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct` goes through the same code path and is expected to behave the same (not run).
- One GPU per run: the encoder (`MultimodalEncoder`) and the PD (`LLM`) share the GPU and the process. Reproduced on two different GPU types.
- Input: synthetic 10 s / 24 fps / 1280x720 H.264 clips; 40 uniformly spaced frames passed as `VideoData` with metadata `{fps, total_num_frames, duration, frames_indices}`; `mm_processor_kwargs={"do_sample_frames": False}` (-> `video_grid_thw` `[20, 36, 66]`, 11,880 visual tokens, E->PD handle `[11880, 16384]` bf16).
- Greedy decoding: `SamplingParams(temperature=0, top_k=1, max_tokens=64)`.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

For video inputs, the E/PD handoff (`MultimodalEncoder` -> `DisaggregatedParams` -> `LLM.generate_async(disaggregated_params=...)`) rebuilds a prompt on the PD side whose layout differs from the aggregated path: the per-frame-group timestamp tokens and the per-group `<|vision_start|>` / `<|vision_end|>` markers are missing. The mRoPE position ids/deltas shipped from the encoder, however, follow the aggregated layout, and the PD side slices them to its own (shorter) prompt length without any check. Visual-token positions and the decode-time mRoPE delta end up misaligned. No error is raised; the output departs from the aggregated path within the first few tokens and the model loses its sense of time, while frame content is still recognized.

Minimal reproduction (public APIs only; LLM API, because the `trtllm-serve` E/PD protocol does not carry multimodal / mRoPE handles yet, see the TODO at `tensorrt_llm/serve/openai_protocol.py` L320):

```python
import os, cv2, numpy as np, torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from tensorrt_llm import LLM, MultimodalEncoder, SamplingParams
from tensorrt_llm.llmapi import KvCacheConfig
from tensorrt_llm.inputs.multimodal_data import VideoData

MODEL = "Qwen/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct"

def load_video(path, n=40):
    cap, raw = cv2.VideoCapture(path), []
    fps = cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FPS)
    while (r := cap.read())[0]:
        raw.append(r[1])
    idx = np.linspace(0, len(raw) - 1, n).astype(int)
    frames = [torch.from_numpy(cv2.cvtColor(raw[i], cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)).permute(2, 0, 1).float() / 255 for i in idx]
    return VideoData(frames=frames, metadata={"fps": fps, "total_num_frames": len(raw),
                                              "duration": len(raw) / fps, "frames_indices": idx.tolist()})

if __name__ == "__main__":  # required: LLM() starts its executor via MpiPoolSession, which re-imports this file
    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL)
    prompt = tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "video"}, {"type": "text",
              "text": 'List the events as JSON {"events": [{"start_s", "end_s", "description"}]}.'}]}],
              tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
    mm = {"prompt": prompt, "multi_modal_data": {"video": [load_video("clip_10s_720p_24fps.mp4")]},
          "mm_processor_kwargs": {"do_sample_frames": False}}
    sp = SamplingParams(temperature=0, top_k=1, max_tokens=64)
    kw = dict(model=MODEL, max_num_tokens=16384, max_seq_len=32768, disable_overlap_scheduler=True,
              kv_cache_config=KvCacheConfig(free_gpu_memory_fraction=0.5))

    # Path A: aggregated (raw video into the LLM)
    llm = LLM(**kw); out_a = llm.generate(mm, sp); llm.shutdown()

    # Path B: E/PD handoff on the same GPU
    os.environ["TLLM_MULTIMODAL_DISAGGREGATED"] = "1"          # PD model skips building the ViT
    llm = LLM(**kw)
    enc = MultimodalEncoder(model=MODEL, max_num_tokens=65536)  # grid 20x36x66 = 47,520 pre-merge patches > default 16384
    enc_out = enc.generate_async(mm).result()
    dp = enc_out.disaggregated_params
    dp.request_type = "context_and_generation"
    out_b = llm.generate_async({"prompt": prompt}, sampling_params=sp, disaggregated_params=dp).result()

    print(out_a.outputs[0].token_ids[:8], out_b.outputs[0].token_ids[:8])  # differ within the first few tokens
    print(len(out_a.prompt_token_ids), len(enc_out.prompt_token_ids), len(out_b.prompt_token_ids))
```

### Expected behavior

Path B produces the same greedy tokens as path A (same weights, same frames, same processor kwargs, same sampling), or at least sees the same prompt layout, with mRoPE positions consistent with it.

### actual behavior

8 clips x 40 frames, Qwen3-VL-8B. Our harness runs the same flow as the script, with a longer structured-output prompt (JSON events with start/end times):

- Exact match A vs B: 0/8; all 8 clips diverge at output token 0.
- A: all 8 answers start with `{"events": [{"start_s": 0.0, "end_s": 10.0, ...` (correct duration).
- B: all 8 answers start with `` ```json ``; 3/8 answer `"start_time": 0, "end_time": 100` for the 10 s clip. The description of what is shown in the frames is correct, so the embeddings themselves are fine; timing is lost.
- Layout (measured with a diagnostic run on 2 of the clips; identical for both): `L_agg = L_encoder = 12,231` and `L_pd = 12,073`, i.e. delta = 158 = 20 timestamps x 6 tokens + 38 frame markers (19 extra `<|vision_start|>` + 19 extra `<|vision_end|>`). With the mask-based layout helpers, the aggregated prompt has 20 runs x 594 `<|video_pad|>`; the PD rebuild has a single run of 11,881 (`<|vision_start|>` + 11,880 pads).
- The encoder's `mrope_position_ids` have shape `[3, 1, 12231]` and deltas -11,22

items.title: Feature Request: Graceful reasoning budget termination. Avoid mid-sentence cutoff.
items.author: CleStil
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

PR #20297 (merged ~2025-03-11) added `--reasoning-budget-message`, which injects
a string at the hard token cutoff to signal the model to wrap up. The injection
still happens at exactly token N with zero warning. The model gets no time to
finish its current thought before the `</think>` boundary.

Graceful termination before the cutoff is expected to improve reasoning
performance. See Motivation and Possible Implementation for details.


### Motivation

Raw truncation of the thinking trace measurably reduces answer quality compared
to graceful termination. Muennighoff et al. (s1: Simple test-time scaling,
arXiv:2501.19393) showed that appending an end-of-thinking delimiter with
"Final Answer:" before the hard cut outperforms naïve truncation. This was
confirmed by follow-up work (arXiv:2505.05315), which states directly that
"the S1 approach performs better than directly truncating the full reasoning
trajectory, underscoring the importance of preserving the solution segment."

The current --reasoning-budget-message implementation injects a wrap-up message
at exactly token N, leaving the model zero tokens to actually act on it. This is
functionally equivalent to truncation with a cosmetic suffix — the model cannot
produce a meaningful conclusion within 0 remaining tokens.

### Possible Implementation

Three approaches in increasing complexity:

Option A — message offset
Inject the budget message at `budget - offset` instead of `budget`, giving the
model `offset` tokens to act on the wrap-up signal. The s1 paper
(https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393) shows this outperforms raw truncation.
Change in the COUNTING state of reasoning-budget.cpp:

    if (ctx->remaining <= ctx->warn_offset)  // was: <= 0

Files: reasoning-budget.cpp, reasoning-budget.h, common.h, arg.cpp,
sampling.cpp. Default 0 preserves current behavior.

Option B — separate budgeting
Split total budget into thinking (t) and conclusion (s) phases, t + s = budget.
Force `</think>` at token t, leave s tokens for a conclusion before the answer.
Follow-up work on s1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05315) shows this outperforms
the basic offset approach. Would add a second parameter, e.g.
--reasoning-budget-conclusion M.

Option C — logit biasing toward `</think>`
Ramp up the logit weight of `</think>` as the budget runs low, then force it at
the hard limit. No dependency on an injected phrase, model-agnostic. NVIDIA NIM
uses this approach with a 10% extension window for sentence completion. More
invasive (sampler changes) but cleanest long-term.

Options A and B build on the existing message injection architecture. Option C
is a parallel approach that could coexist with either.

Happy to test on ROCm/gfx1100 (Qwen3.5-27B) and contribute a draft of Option A
or B if there is interest.

items.title: [RFC]: [Store] Split snapshot orchestration and serialization logic from MasterService
items.author: Aionw
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

Snapshot is not part of the core master data path. Conceptually, it is a persistence and recovery capability that observes, captures, and restores master state, and should be modeled as a separate subsystem rather than intrinsic master request-processing logic.

Keeping snapshot orchestration and serialization inside `MasterService` blurs this abstraction boundary. It also makes snapshot format evolution difficult, since part of the snapshot serialization logic is implemented as a private nested component of `MasterService`.

This RFC proposes splitting snapshot orchestration and snapshot state serialization into dedicated components while preserving the current snapshot behavior and runtime semantics.

## Proposed Changes

### 1. Move snapshot orchestration out of `MasterService`

Introduce a dedicated snapshot manager module, for example:

- `ha/snapshot/master_snapshot_manager.h`
- `ha/snapshot/master_snapshot_manager.cpp`

This component will own snapshot-specific orchestration:

- periodic snapshot scheduling
- snapshot ID generation
- snapshot descriptor construction
- child process lifecycle management
- timeout handling
- snapshot payload upload
- catalog publish
- retention cleanup
- snapshot metrics updates

`MasterService` should only provide the state capture/restore hooks needed by the snapshot manager.

### 2. Extract snapshot state serialization from `MasterService`

Move master snapshot state serialization into standalone modules instead of keeping part of the snapshot format inside `MasterService`.

The current snapshot payload is composed of multiple state files:

- `metadata`: object metadata shards, discarded replicas, and replica ID state
- `segments`: mounted memory segments, client-to-segment mappings, allocator ordering, and local disk segment/offloading state
- `task_manager`: persisted client task manager state
- `manifest.txt`: snapshot serializer type, version, and snapshot ID

The refactor should model these as one master snapshot state bundle, with dedicated serializers for each sub-state. `MasterService` should remain responsible for owning live runtime state, while the snapshot serialization layer should own the persisted representation and format compatibility.

### 3. Define explicit snapshot data structures

Introduce explicit snapshot DTOs for the full master snapshot state, such as:

- metadata snapshot state
- segment manager snapshot state
- task manager snapshot state
- snapshot manifest metadata

These structures should represent the persisted snapshot format independently from the internal layout of `MasterService`, `SegmentManager`, and `ClientTaskManager`.

This will make future snapshot format evolution easier and reduce accidental coupling to private master internals.

### 4. Keep restore behavior unchanged

Restore should continue to support the current snapshot storage layout and manifest validation behavior.

The proposed refactor should only move restore selection, download, decoding, and application logic into clearer components. The externally visible behavior should remain unchanged.

A possible split is:

- snapshot repository: list, download, upload, publish, cleanup
- snapshot codec: encode/decode snapshot payloads
- master state restorer: apply decoded snapshot data to `MasterService`

### 5. Preserve existing configuration and compatibility

Existing snapshot flags and environment variables should continue to work:

- `--enable_snapshot`
- `--snapshot_interval_seconds`
- `--snapshot_child_timeout_seconds`
- `--snapshot_retention_count`
- `--snapshot_object_store_type`
- `--snapshot_catalog_store_type`
- `--snapshot_catalog_store_connstring`
- `--snapshot_backup_dir`
- `--enable_snapshot_restore`
- `MOONCAKE_SNAPSHOT_LOCAL_PATH`

Existing snapshots should remain restorable unless a later RFC explicitly proposes a format migration.

## Expected Benefits

- Clearer abstraction boundary between core master request-processing logic and snapshot persistence/recovery logic
- Smaller and easier-to-review `MasterService`
- Clear ownership boundary for snapshot code
- Easier snapshot format testing across metadata, segment, and task-manager payloads
- Easier restore testing without constructing a full master lifecycle
- Reduced reliance on private nested classes and test-only friendships
- Lower risk when adding new fields to snapshot format

## Non-goals

This RFC does not propose changing the snapshot consistency model.

This RFC does not propose changing the current HA design.

This RFC does not propose changing snapshot storage backends or catalog semantics.

This RFC does not propose changing user-facing configuration.

## Testing Plan

Add or update unit tests for:

- full snapshot state encode/decode round trip
- metadata snapshot encode/decode compatibility
- segment snapshot encode/decode compatibility
- task manager snapshot encode/decode compatibility
- snapshot manager descriptor construction
- snapshot manager publish/cleanup behavior
- restore fallback across multiple candidate snapshots
- restore failure handling and state reset

Keep existing snapshot integration tests passing, including:

- master snapshot/restore tests
- SSD snapshot tests
- promotion snapshot tests
- catalog-backed snapshot provider tests
- snapshot child process tests

## Migration Plan

1. Introduce standalone snapshot manager and serializer modules.
2. Move code from `MasterService` into the new modules without behavior changes.
3. Replace direct private serializer usage with explicit state capture/restore hooks.
4. Keep existing tests passing after each step.
5. Remove obsolete private nested serializer definitions and unnecessary test friendships once callers are migrated.

items.title: [RFC]: DrainJob bandwidth rate limiting
items.author: liangxu2000
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

### Changes proposed

## 1. Current State: DrainJob Performance Parameters

After reading through the `mooncake-store` source, here are the existing control parameters related to DrainJob:

| Parameter | Location | Default | Purpose |
|-----------|----------|---------|---------|
| `max_concurrency` | `CreateDrainJobRequest` | 4 | Max concurrent MoveTasks per DrainJob |
| `task_thread_pool_` | Client constructor | 4 | Client-side task execution thread pool |
| `kJobDispatchThreadSleepMs` | Master dispatch loop | 500ms | Master DrainJob scheduling interval |
| TaskPollThreadMain interval | Client poll loop | 1000ms | Client task fetch interval |
| `kTaskBatchSize` | Client poll loop | 16 | Max tasks per `FetchTasks` RPC |
| `kMaxDrainUnitRetries` | Master drain logic | 3 | Max retries per key move |

**All existing controls operate on the "count" dimension. There is zero rate/bandwidth limiting.**

Key observations from the transfer path:

- In `ExecuteReplicaTransfer`, the entire object is `split_into_slices` and submitted to Transfer Engine in a single batch via `submitTransfer`. No pacing between slices.
- Drain MoveTasks share the same RDMA link and client thread pool as regular read/write operations. No priority isolation.
- A single object can be several GB. With `max_concurrency=4`, tens of GB could be in-flight on the RDMA link simultaneously.

## 2. Discussion Topic

Does the community see a need for DrainJob bandwidth/rate limiting? Are there any existing plans?

From a usage perspective, an aggressive DrainJob could saturate shared RDMA bandwidth and impact read latency for online workloads. I'd like to understand:

- Has anyone encountered this as a pain point in production?
- Any thoughts on the design direction from the community?

## 3. Possible Directions (high-level)

- **Master-side**: Track recent throughput via a sliding window (e.g., 5s) over completed task byte counts. Skip scheduling new MoveTasks when the current rate meets the configured limit. Leverages the existing 500ms dispatch loop as a natural pacing mechanism.
- **Client-side**: Split large object transfers into sub-batches (e.g., 64MB each). Insert a token bucket between sub-batches for precise pacing.
- **API**: Add an optional `bandwidth_limit_mbps` field to `CreateDrainJobRequest` (0 = unlimited, backward compatible).

The concrete design choice — single-layer vs. dual-layer, where to place it, whether to go adaptive — depends on real community needs. This RFC is intended to start that discussion.


### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues and read the [documentation](https://kvcache-ai.github.io/Mooncake/)

items.title: [RFC]: Multi-Replica Reliability in Mooncake Store Data Plane
items.author: liangxu2000
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Background

Mooncake Store ensures data reliability through a **Multi-Replica** mechanism: `replica_num` controls the number of Memory replicas and `nof_replica_num` controls the number of NoF SSD replicas. Multi-replication (`replica_num` + `nof_replica_num`) provides cross-node fault tolerance — the same object is replicated across multiple physical nodes, so that if one node fails, other replicas remain readable. This document analyzes the current state of the multi-replica mechanism, including allocation logic, failure handling behavior, and potential gaps.

---

## 1. Replica Allocation Mechanism

### 1.1 Allocation Entry Point

Replica counts are specified via `ReplicateConfig` in `PutStart` / `UpsertStart` requests:

- `replica_num` — number of Memory replicas
- `nof_replica_num` — number of NoF (NVMe-oF) SSD replicas

Core allocation function `AllocateAndInsertMetadata` (`master_service.cpp:2838`):

```cpp
// Step 1: Allocate Memory replicas
if (config.replica_num > 0) {
    auto allocation_result = allocation_strategy_->Allocate(
        allocator_manager, value_length, config.replica_num,
        preferred_segments, {}, ReplicaType::MEMORY, ssd_provider);
    replicas = std::move(allocation_result.value());
}

// Step 2: Allocate NoF SSD replicas (optional)
if (config.nof_replica_num > 0) {
    auto allocation_result = allocation_strategy_->Allocate(
        allocator_manager, value_length, config.nof_replica_num,
        preferred_segments, {}, ReplicaType::NOF_SSD);
    // Merge into replicas
}
```

### 1.2 Cross-Node Placement Guarantee

`AllocationStrategy::Allocate()` uses a `used_segments` set to ensure different replicas of the same object are placed on different segments:

> "replicas are guaranteed to be placed on different segments to ensure redundancy"
> — `allocation_strategy.h:130-138`

The allocation strategy achieves physical dispersion by distributing memory blocks across different segments. `GetReplicaSegmentNames()` returns the list of segment names where all replicas reside.

Two built-in strategies:
- `RandomAllocationStrategy` — random selection, up to 100 retries
- `FreeRatioFirstAllocationStrategy` — prefers segments with the highest free ratio, balancing load

### 1.3 Three Write Modes (`ReplicaWriteMode`)

| Mode | Condition | Semantics |
|------|-----------|-----------|
| `SINGLE_REPLICA` | `replica_num=1 && nof_replica_num=0` | Single replica — fails on error |
| `FLEXIBLE_DUAL_REPLICA` | `replica_num=1 && nof_replica_num=1` | Memory + NoF dual-write — at least one success is sufficient |
| `RELIABLE_MULTI_REPLICA` | All other cases | Must fully satisfy the requested count — strict mode |

`FLEXIBLE_DUAL_REPLICA` is an interesting degradation design: Memory and NoF back each other up; if only one can be allocated, it still counts as success.

---

## 2. Replica Handling on Node Failure

### 2.1 Core Function: `ClearInvalidHandles`

`master_service.cpp:1904` — triggered when a client expires (TTL timeout) or a segment is unmounted:

```
CleanupStaleHandles filter criteria (any one matches, and status must be COMPLETE):
  1) has_invalid_mem_handle()   — the owning Memory segment has been unmounted
  2) has_invalid_nof_handle()   — the owning NoF segment has been unmounted
  3) has_stale_local_disk_client(alive_clients) — client is no longer alive
```

`ClearInvalidHandles` iterates over all tenant metadata, calling `CleanupStaleHandles` for each object:
- Removes invalid replicas
- If the object has no valid replicas remaining (`!metadata.IsValid()`), **the entire object metadata is also deleted**

### 2.2 Key Behavior: Delete-Only, No Replenishment

After removing invalid replicas, the replica count drops from N to N-1 (or 0). **No automatic rebuild is triggered.**

On node failure:
- `replica_num=2`, one replica on the failed node, one on a healthy node
  → invalid replica deleted, 1 replica remains in service (not reduced to 0)
- `replica_num=1`, the only replica is on the failed node
  → invalid replica deleted, 0 remain → object metadata deleted → **data loss**

### 2.3 Absence of Automatic Repair

A full search of the `mooncake-store` source tree:

| Keyword | Result |
|---------|--------|
| `auto_repair` | Not found |
| `replenish` | SPDK pool replenishment only, unrelated to replicas |
| `rebalance` | Memory pool slab rebalancing only, unrelated to replicas |
| `repair` | LRU index lazy repair for storage backend only, unrelated to replicas |

**There is no logic anywhere for automatic replica replenishment.**

### 2.4 `ReplicaStatus::FAILED` Defined but Unused

`replica.h:51` defines `ReplicaStatus::FAILED` with the comment "can be used for reassignment", yet no code in the current codebase marks a replica as FAILED or triggers reallocation based on this state. The existence of this enum value suggests the author reserved an entry point for replica reassignment at design time, but it was never implemented.

### 2.5 Practical Impact

- Replica count = 1, no offload: node failure → immediate data loss
- Replica count = 2, one node fails: remaining replica is readable, but replica count permanently drops to 1; a subsequent second node failure causes data loss
- **The system never automatically restores the desired replica count**; the upper layer must detect this and re-issue Put/Upsert

---

## 3. Summary — Current Reliability Gap

The current multi-replica mechanism provides "static allocation + passive deletion" but lacks an "active repair" step:

```
 ┌──────────────────┐
 │  PutStart        │  replica_num=2 → allocate 2 replicas on different nodes
 │  replica_num=2   │  ✅ Dispersed placement
 └────────┬─────────┘
          ▼
 ┌──────────────────┐
 │  Normal          │  2 replicas both COMPLETE
 │  operation       │
 └────────┬─────────┘
          ▼  Node A crashes
 ┌──────────────────┐
 │  TTL timeout     │  ClientMonitorFunc detects the failure
 │  (10s)           │
 └────────┬─────────┘
          ▼
 ┌───────────────

items.title: [Bug]: Timed-out put is revoked while its queued slices are still pending; they later overwrite the next object at that address
items.author: yubofredwang
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

#### Summary

When a Store put times out (60 s, hardcoded), the client returns `TRANSFER_FAIL (-800)` and revokes the object. The master frees the replica immediately, and the next put can get the same address. The timed-out transfer is not cancelled: slices still in the transfer engine queue are posted later and overwrite the new object. Nothing reports an error.

#975 / #993 added `discarded_replicas_` for this hazard ("the faulted client ... is still writing data to discarded replicas"). `PutRevoke` doesn't use it.

#### Environment

- `mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13==0.3.13.post1`; source checked at `e5598b0` (`v0.3.13-rc1`). Same code on current `main`.
- Ubuntu 22.04.5, kernel `6.8.0-1047-nvidia`, `OFED-internal-25.10-1.2.8`, rdma-core `2510.0.10-1`.
- `mlx5_4` (InfiniBand), firmware `28.47.2526`.

#### Reproduce

Single host, RDMA (`MC_STORE_MEMCPY=0`), standalone master with defaults, one 16 MiB segment.

1. Client A: stop its two `transferWorker` threads with ptrace (RPC and heartbeat threads keep running), then put 12 MiB of `0x5C`.
2. After 60 s, A's put returns -800 and the object is revoked.
3. Client B (a separate process): put 12 MiB of `0x33` to a new key, then read it back. It lands at the same address and reads back `0x33`.
4. Resume A's workers. B's key now reads back all `0x5C`, and so does the segment memory.

Result: 8 out of 8 trials, same address every time, no crash. An earlier TCP run with a blackholed port, with no threads stopped, showed the same overwrite once the port came back.

Stopping the workers is artificial. It only stands in for anything that keeps slices queued past the timeout (e.g. a paused rail, `rdma_rail_pause_seconds` = 30, or a blocked worker). We have not reproduced it with a real link failure across two nodes.

#### Expected

A write from a revoked put should never land in memory that has been handed to another object.

#### Why

Links are pinned to `e5598b0`.

1. The timeout only stops waiting ([`transfer_task.cpp#L889-L895`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/src/transfer_task.cpp#L889-L895)). Queued slices aren't removed or marked cancelled.
2. The destructor calls `freeBatchID` ([`transfer_task.h#L226`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/include/transfer_task.h#L226)), which returns `BatchBusy` for unfinished tasks ([`transport.cpp#L42-L50`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-transfer-engine/src/transport/transport.cpp#L42-L50)). The result is ignored, so the batch is leaked, and the slices stay valid to post later.
3. `PutRevoke` erases the replica right away ([`master_service.cpp#L4869`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp#L4869)). Stale put-start cleanup ([`#L4440-L4450`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp#L4440-L4450)) and upsert preemption ([`#L4944`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp#L4944)) move replicas to `discarded_replicas_` instead.

#### Impact

- The overwritten object belongs to another key whose put succeeded. Reads succeed and return wrong data.
- For a KV cache, every later prefix hit on that key gets the wrong KV until it is evicted.
- Slices read their source at post time. If the caller has reused its source buffer after the -800, the bytes that land aren't even the failed key's data.

#### Questions for maintainers

Before proposing a code change, we'd like your view on:

1. Have we seen other reports related to this issue in production?
2. Can it be prevented without code changes? For example, settings that keep the time a slice can spend queued well under 60 s (rail pause, retry count), or object checksum validation to catch the overwrite on read.

#### Possible fix

If you agree this is a real problem and not just a theoretical one, we'd propose a quarantine: `PutRevoke` moves the replicas to `discarded_replicas_` instead of erasing them, the same way stale put-start cleanup does. Dropping a timed-out batch's unposted slices would make that quarantine time a real upper bound. We can send a PR.

#### Related

#975 / #993 (`discarded_replicas_`), #4247 (same problem in the sync transfer API on Ascend), #3030.

### Before submitting...

items.title: [RFC] TENT concurrent registration lifecycle and cleanup retries
items.author: LysanderPhong
items.body_excerpt:
This RFC describes the concurrent-registration extension in [PR #4573](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/4573), implemented in commit `c3ed2fc6365bf71d48ab5de57b3fd55bc6acc54b`. It asks for review of the lifecycle and failure contracts, including the measured performance cost. The original batch-only fix remains a separate commit if maintainers prefer to land it independently.

## Motivation and observed reproduction

The public Python bindings release the GIL around registration. On a frozen
build of the submitted `b63d4ef8bb9667ecdc8e1610267b0f71e75761a5` commit,
four threads mixed single and batch registrations of one live buffer on one
engine. In a local 100-round run, HP_TCP reported 20 overlapping-buffer
registration failures; a corresponding TCP run exposed duplicate metadata in
six rounds. Successful references and backing storage remained alive during
the checks. The Python workflow scripts and raw logs are retained locally and
are not included in the PR diff. The PR includes deterministic C++ regression
tests and real HP_TCP lifecycle tests.

These demonstrate a reachable public API problem, not a measured production
incident or a representative failure rate. We would welcome maintainer input
on integrations that register and unregister dynamically; startup-only users
may see little practical benefit.

The cause is the gap between checking published tracker metadata, entering a
transport, and publishing a newly registered range. Immutable metadata protects
readers but does not make this sequence one lifecycle operation. Final removal
similarly hides metadata before physical cleanup, leaving a gap in which a new
registration can race the previous generation's cleanup.

## Proposed coordination and reference contract

A per-engine `RegistrationCoordinator` reserves every starting address in an
operation together. It sorts and deduplicates the bases, waits until all are
available, then marks them occupied under one mutex. A waiter never owns a
partial batch, so reversed batches cannot introduce ABBA locking. A movable
RAII guard releases the reservation on scope exit; completed reservations leave
no historical address entries behind.

The reservation spans preparation, tracker changes, transport callbacks,
rollback and metadata publication. Callbacks do not hold the coordinator mutex
or the metadata writer mutex. Disjoint bases may enter transports concurrently;
existing metadata publication still has its own serialization. Different
lengths at the same base are coordinated together, including wildcard
unregistration, but are not merged. Arbitrary overlapping ranges with distinct
bases remain subject to transport behavior.

The tracker remains the source of logical references: each successful input
occurrence grants one reference to an exact `(address, length)` pair, including
duplicates within and across calls. Compatible references reuse the generation's
registration in each applicable transport. This does not mean one registration
across all transports, nor does it eliminate temporary RDMA warm-up operations.
Direct internal tracker users retain their existing callback/reentrancy model.

The original six `MemoryOptions` fields are retained locally in an immutable
shared object, excluded from serialized segment metadata. Reusing an exact
range requires equality of `type`, `perm`, `location`, `shm_path`, `shm_offset`
and `internal`. This intentionally compares supplied values, not equivalent
resolved policies; it does not upgrade a registration's permission or transport
coverage implicitly.

## Failure handling and generation boundaries

Registration failure must not grant new local references. If publication fails
after local registration, the engine rolls back this call's input occurrences,
including temporary references to existing ranges. It attempts a compensating
metadata publication. The complete address reservation prevents another call
on those bases from acquiring references during rollback.

Physical cleanup can also fail. A local, non-advertised retired record retains
the original transport keys and only the unfinished transport steps. Successful
steps are removed from that list, and their registered-byte metrics are reduced
once. The retry rule depends on the failed operation:

| Failed operation | Subsequent registration | Retry action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Registration with residual physical cleanup | May attempt cleanup first; must not create a new generation until it succeeds | Retry registration while retaining the backing memory |
| Final unregistration with cleanup or publication pending | Returns `TooManyRequests` at the same base | Retry unregistration; finished physical steps are not repeated |

A final unregistration retains its pending record even when only publication
remains. Allowing registration to consume that record and create a new
generation would let the original unregister retry remove the new owner.

This API has no operation or owner token. It cannot provide exactly-once
semantics for arbitrary delayed, duplicate retries: callers must serialize
retries of a failed unregistration and stop replaying it after success. A
completed unregistration replayed after another owner registers can still
release that later owner's reference.

Metadata compensation is not a distributed transaction. Peers may already have
observed a prior snapshot, and compensation can itself fail. The proposal
guarantees the local reference/cleanup behavior described here; it does not
promise atomic visibility across peers or eliminate existing cache staleness.

## Batch unregistration and publication cost

Batch unregistration processes input occurrences in order. On error, the message
identifies a zero-based failed index: the preceding entries have completed, and
the caller retries only that entry and its suffix.

Publishing once per physical removal would regress a batch into many complete
metadata publications. Instead, under the full address reservation, a lo

items.title: [Bug]: Release workflows treat v0.3.14rc1-style tags as stable and publish them to PyPI
items.author: Aionw
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

Release workflows tell stable tags from prerelease tags only by whether the tag name contains `-`. A tag written in canonical PEP 440 form, such as `v0.3.14rc1`, is therefore treated as a stable release and published to production PyPI.

### Current behavior

- `release.yaml`, `release-cuda13`, `release-non-cuda`, the three EFA workflows, `release-npu`, `release-musa` and `release-rocm` all trigger on `v*`. They treat a tag as stable when it contains no `-` (`!contains(github.ref_name, '-')`, or the `*-*` check in the MUSA/ROCm dispatch validation).
- `pre-release.yaml` only matches `v*-rc*`, `v*-alpha*`, `v*-beta*` and `v*-pre*`.

`0.3.14rc1` is the canonical PEP 440 spelling; `0.3.14-rc1` is an accepted alternative that normalizes to it. Someone used to Python packaging could reasonably push `v0.3.14rc1`. That tag:

1. does not match `pre-release.yaml`, so no prerelease build, GitHub Pre-release or TestPyPI validation runs;
2. passes every stable gate, so all release workflows build and publish to production PyPI.

The stable path also ignores the version in the tag. `_build-wheel.yaml` exports `VERSION=${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}`, but only patches `pyproject.toml` when `version-override` is set, and `scripts/build_wheel.sh` never reads `VERSION`. The custom NPU/MUSA/ROCm paths likewise build from `pyproject.toml` as-is. So the published version is whatever `mooncake-wheel/pyproject.toml` contains:

- if it has already been bumped for the upcoming release (e.g. `0.3.14`), the rc tag publishes the **final** `0.3.14` to PyPI ahead of schedule, and that version can never be re-uploaded;
- otherwise the upload collides with an existing version and fails partway, after the GitHub Release assets have already been attached.

The same coarse rule also makes tags like `v0.3.13-1` (PEP 440 `0.3.13.post1`) skip every release workflow without any error.

### Expected behavior

Every release workflow classifies a tag the same way, and each tag lands on exactly one path:

- stable tag: all stable workflows run, and the wheel version equals the tag version;
- prerelease tag (in either spelling): only the prerelease path runs, with nothing published to production PyPI;
- anything else: fails explicitly instead of silently skipping or publishing.

### Possible fix

Classify the tag once with `packaging.Version` (e.g. extend `scripts/ci/testpypi_wheel_gate.py normalize-version` into a shared classify step), and have every release workflow gate on its output instead of `contains(..., '-')`. On the stable path, check that the tag version matches `pyproject.toml` before publishing. That check is one of the invariants proposed in #3534 ("Git tags, `pyproject.toml`, and wheel metadata must agree") and could land ahead of the full migration.

A cheaper interim option: document that release tags must use the `-rcN` / `-alphaN` / `-betaN` form, and have the stable workflows fail on tags whose PEP 440 parse is a prerelease.

### Related

- #4574 changes `release-npu.yaml` to classify tags with `packaging.Version`. If it lands as is, NPU would diverge from the other workflows on these tags (review: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/4574#pullrequestreview-5487709039).
- #3534, #3556: release-architecture RFC and roadmap.

items.title: [RFC]: Shared NVMe KV Backend for Mooncake Store
items.author: Javen-Ke
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## 1. Introduction

This proposal introduces a `SHARED_NVME_KV` replica type that allows multiple Clients to access the same external KV storage pool directly over NVMe-oF. The Master manages allocation identities, replica publication, LRU eviction, and cleanup. The Target executes KV commands and manages physical storage space. Published replicas remain available independently of the writing Client, and other Clients can read them without forwarding requests through that Client.

All Clients connect to the same set of namespaces using an identical, ordered namespace list. Each Client selects a namespace using `hash(logical_key) % N`, where `N` is the number of namespaces. This distributes large sets of keys approximately evenly across namespaces. Applications continue to use Put/Get: a write selects the shared replica type, obtains an allocation ID from the Master, writes directly to the Target, and publishes the replica. Other Clients query the descriptor and read directly using the same routing rule. This balances key counts, not necessarily storage usage or access load.

## 2. Background and Motivation

SPDK 26.09 adds support for exposing KV-capable bdevs as NVMe KV namespaces through its NVMe-oF Target. This provides a Target implementation on which multiple Clients can build direct access to an external KV pool. The release was published on September 24, 2026; see the [SPDK 26.09 release notes](https://spdk.io/release/2026/09/24/v26.09_release/).

The existing `NvmeKvStorageBackend` publishes `LOCAL_DISK` replicas through `FileStorage`, with reads served by the Client that owns the replica. [PR #3513](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/3513) proposes NVMe-oF connectivity for that backend while retaining this replica model. Even when multiple Clients can access the underlying device, Client B still reads data written by Client A through A. Once A exits, that proxy path can no longer serve the data, even if the data remains intact on the Target.

A shared pool needs data access and replica lifetime to be independent of the writer. The relationship to existing work is:

| Related work | Relationship to this proposal |
| --- | --- |
| [NVMe KV RFC #1957](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/1957) | Defines object layouts, executors, and control-plane cleanup responsibilities, while leaving guarantees for multiple hosts sharing a namespace open. This proposal builds on those foundations and specifies allocation, publication, and deletion for shared replicas. |
| [NVMe KV PR #2167](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/2167) and [NVMe-oF extension #3513](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/3513) | Integrate through `FileStorage` / `LOCAL_DISK`. This proposal reuses object encoding and command execution, lets the requesting Client access the Target directly, and assigns physical identities and lifecycle management to the Master. |
| [Distributed KV RFC #2993](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/2993) | Accesses an external distributed KV service but still reports `LOCAL_DISK` replicas through `FileStorage`. This proposal represents data as independent shared replicas, without requiring an owning Client to load and forward it. |

## 3. Technical Design

### 3.1 Components and Responsibilities

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Client (extended)"] -. "Allocate, publish, query" .-> M["Master (extended)"]
    C --> O["SharedNvmeKv (new)"]
    O --> E["KV executor (reused interface, SPDK implementation)"]
    E --> T["External NVMe KV Target"]
    M -. "Cleanup tasks" .-> G["Cleanup worker (proposed within Master)"]
    G --> E
    classDef changed fill:#fff2cc,stroke:#b7950b;
    classDef external fill:#eeeeee,stroke:#777777;
    class C,M,O,E,G changed;
    class T external;
```

Dashed arrows represent control requests; solid arrows represent data operations.

- **Master:** Extend replica metadata and `PutStart` / `PutEnd` to manage allocation identities, publication state, access recency, and pending cleanup records. A writing Client's exit does not invalidate its published shared replicas.
- **Client and `SharedNvmeKv`:** The Client selects the shared path from the replica descriptor. The new `SharedNvmeKv` object layer handles physical key encoding, object framing, idempotent writes, and read validation.
- **KV executor:** Use `NvmeKvCommandExecutor` as the reuse boundary and adapt the SPDK KV implementation from #3513. The executor owns device connections, KV commands, DMA buffers, and completion handling.
- **Cleanup worker:** Proposed as a background worker within the Master, issuing `Delete` through the KV executor independently of the original writing Client. Section 5 describes the implementation approach.

### 3.2 Replica Descriptors and Physical Addressing

The shared descriptor is returned through the existing replica query interface. Its core fields are:

```cpp
struct SharedKvDescriptor {
    uint64_t object_size;    // Payload size in bytes.
    uint64_t allocation_id;  // Unique identity of this physical allocation.
};

struct SharedKvReplicaData {
    SharedKvDescriptor descriptor;
};
```

The descriptor does not need the writing Client's address. The request carries the logical key, which selects the namespace using the routing rule above; `allocation_id` identifies the physical allocation within that namespace. Initially, namespace membership, ordering, and the hash function must remain unchanged while shared allocations exist. Reads, writes, and cleanup use the same mapping.

Each new allocation receives a new `allocation_id`; retries of the same device write reuse that ID. Physical keys use a fixed 16-byte encoding, matching the maximum key length allowed by the [NVMe Key Value Command Set specification](https://nvmexpress.org/wp-content/uploads/NVM-Express-Key-Value-Command-Set-Specification-Revision-1.2-2025.03.11-Ratified.pdf):

```text
physical_key = BE64(allocation_id) || BE64(part_index)
```

`BE64` den
