items.title: Assertion in TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers: "expected then yield to report fat ptr indices" on a pointer select inside a runtime scf.if
items.author: O1iveira7
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Compiling a legal Triton kernel fails with a C++ assertion in the AMD `TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers` pass. The kernel merges two pointer bases with `tl.where` under a tensor condition inside a runtime `if`; the pass then hits a mixed representation between the two `scf.if` arms and aborts compilation.


**Error log**
```
CanonicalizePointers.cpp:1445: ... ConvertSCFIfOp::matchAndRewrite_(scf::IfOp, OneToNOpAdaptor, ...):
Assertion ifOp.thenYield()->hasAttr(kSCFIfOpYieldFatPtrOffsets) &&
          "expected then yield to report fat ptr indices" failed.
note: Pipeline failed while executing [TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers` on 'tt.func' operation: @kernel]
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed

Failure is in `make_ttgir` (MLIR), before LLVM codegen; exit code 1.
```

The generated TTGIR is:

```
%5 = scf.if %4 -> (tensor<2x!tt.ptr<f32>>) {
  %11 = tt.addptr %10, %0          // base = splat(arg1)
  %12 = arith.select %9, %11, %2   // tensor condition, different bases
  scf.yield %12
} else {
  scf.yield %2                     // base = splat(arg2)
}
%8 = tt.load %5
```
TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers is a 1:N conversion to fat pointers (scalar base, tensor offset). scf.if is only rewritten after both scf.yields are rewritten (tracked via internal then/else-rewritten attributes). ConvertSCFYieldOp sets kSCFIfOpYieldFatPtrOffsets on a yield only when one of its remapped operands is a 2-element fat pointer, while ConvertSCFIfOp unconditionally asserts that the then-yield has that attribute.

Here ConvertArithSelectOp takes its special case for a tensor condition with differing scalar bases and materializes both arms into full tensor pointers instead of a (base, offset) pair. So the then-yield carries a single materialized pointer and gets no fat-pointer index attribute, while the else-yield (a plain tt.addptr) converts to a fat pointer pair and does get the attribute. Both yields are marked rewritten, the scf.if becomes illegal, ConvertSCFIfOp fires, and the assertion fails on the inconsistent arms.

**Reproducer**
```
import os

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(sw, a_ptr, b_ptr, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    p = b_ptr + offs
    if tl.load(sw) == 0:
        p = tl.where(offs >= 0, a_ptr + offs, b_ptr + offs)
    tl.store(a_ptr + offs, tl.load(p))


def _main() -> None:
    device = "cuda"
    N = 2
    a = torch.randn(N, device=device)
    b = torch.randn(N, device=device)
    sw = torch.tensor([0], dtype=torch.int32, device=device)
    print(f"REPRO_START N={N} buffer_ops={os.environ.get('AMDGCN_USE_BUFFER_OPS', 'default')}", flush=True)
    kernel[(1,)](sw, a, b, BLOCK=N, num_warps=1)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print("REPRO_DONE (no crash)", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    _main()
```

### Environment details

- AMD Instinct MI308X (gfx942), ROCm 7.2.3
- triton-rocm 3.8.0, torch 2.14.0+rocm7.2, Python 3.12.13

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Picking this up; the earlier attempt #12182 is closed unmerged and the assert is still in place on current main (2a514c0f).

The mechanism in the report checks out. The trigger is the tensor-condition case of ConvertArithSelectOp: with different scalar bases it materializes both arms into full tensor pointers, so the then yield carries one plain pointer and ConvertSCFYieldOp records no fat-ptr offsets for it, while the else yield still carries a (base, offset) pair and does get the attribute. Once both yields are marked rewritten, ConvertSCFIfOp fires and asserts on the asymmetry. Reproduced locally with triton-opt on an asserts-enabled build, same assert as the report (CanonicalizePointers.cpp:1450).

That asymmetric shape is legal output of the select conversion, and downstream consumers already accept a materialized pointer (MaterializeFatPointer passes through any pointer operand that does not arrive as a pair), so the natural place for the fix is the scf.if boundary: for each result where the two yields disagree on the representation, materialize the (base, offset) side into a tensor pointer before rebuilding the op. Results that stay fat on both sides keep the pair form and the existing attribute propagation. The same hole exists when both arms materialize (neither yield reports offsets and the old code asserts on the then yield all the same); the fix covers that shape too.

PR coming with lit coverage for both. No AMD hardware here, so verification is at the MLIR level only.

items.title: [RFC] Joint text+image variant of fused_qk_rmsnorm_rope for MMDiT joint attention
items.author: yuweih205
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

`flashinfer.norm.fused_qk_rmsnorm_rope` fuses QK RMSNorm + 3D RoPE + V copy for a *single* stream with RMSNorm across all heads (Wan-style). The MMDiT family (FLUX.1/FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, HunyuanVideo-1.5, SD3) runs joint attention over a text stream and an image/video stream, with **per-head** RMSNorm (`nn.RMSNorm(head_dim)`), RoPE on the image tokens only (text ids are zero in FLUX/HunyuanVideo, offset positions in Qwen-Image), and `torch.cat` of the two streams before attention. With today's FlashInfer that prologue is 8 launches: `rmsnorm` x4, `apply_rope_with_cos_sin_cache_inplace` on the image stream, and three `torch.cat`s into the joint buffers.

## Proposal

Add `fused_joint_qk_rmsnorm_rope(qkv_txt, qkv_img, q_weight_txt, k_weight_txt, q_weight_img, k_weight_img, *, ppf, pph, ppw, num_{frame,height,width}_channels, num_heads_{q,k,v}, head_dim, eps, base, interleave, norm_per_head=True, txt_first=True, txt_rope="identity"|"offset", txt_pos_offset=0, is_qk_norm, output_fp8, ...)` returning Q/K/V directly in the joint layout `[batch, seq_len_txt + seq_len_img, H, D]`.

Implementation: the existing kernel body is kept and parameterised by a small `Layout` functor (`SingleStreamLayout` = current behaviour, bit-identical; `JointStreamLayout` = stream select + per-stream weights + text/image positions), plus a `PER_HEAD_NORM` template flag (warp-level reduction instead of the block-level one). The two input streams may be strided views of one joint `[B, S_txt+S_img, hidden]` buffer, so FLUX.1 single-stream blocks are covered too. Text tokens with the identity rotation are exact (angle 0). YARN is not exposed on the joint path to keep instantiations down (24 new kernels).

## Measured (1x H200, CUDA 13.2, `benchmarks/bench_fused_joint_qk_rmsnorm_rope.py`, `bench_gpu_time` medians)

| joint-attention prologue, per block | eager torch | composed FlashInfer chain | fused joint | vs composed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FLUX.1 512², B=1 (txt 512 + img 1024) | 0.342 ms | 0.090 ms | 0.049 ms | 1.83x |
| FLUX.1 1024², B=1 (txt 512 + img 4096) | 0.879 ms | 0.192 ms | 0.093 ms | 2.07x |
| FLUX.1 1024², B=2 | 1.648 ms | 0.359 ms | 0.179 ms | 2.00x |
| Qwen-Image 1024² (txt 128 + img 4096) | 0.859 ms | 0.185 ms | 0.086 ms | 2.17x |
| HunyuanVideo-1.5 480p 33f (txt 256 + video 14040) | 2.642 ms | 0.569 ms | 0.275 ms | 2.07x |

The joint kernel over txt+img costs about the same as the stock single-stream kernel over img alone (per-head norm needs no block-level reduction). The refactored single-stream path is bit-identical to the current kernel on 6 shapes (bf16/fp8, interleaved/NeoX, head_dim 64/128/256) with timing unchanged (within ±2% run-to-run noise). Correctness of the joint path: with `norm_per_head=False` and no text tokens the output is bit-identical to `fused_qk_rmsnorm_rope`; text-first vs image-first are bit-identical row permutations; vs an fp32 reference the error is <= 1 bf16 ulp on ~0.03% of elements (same class as the composed chain). The same fusion inside vllm-omni (Triton version) gave FLUX.1 full-forward -15% and -3..-5% end-to-end for FLUX.2-klein / Qwen-Image / HunyuanVideo-1.5 at 1024².

## Questions before a PR

1. Is a hand-written CUDA extension of `fused_qk_rmsnorm_rope.cuh` acceptable, or should new DiT kernels go through Cake?
2. API placement: `flashinfer.norm` + re-export from `flashinfer.diffusion_ops` like the existing kernel?
3. FLUX.2's four-axis RoPE and SD3 (no RoPE) are out of scope for the first version; fine?

Branch with kernel, binding, Python API, tests (tolerance + bitwise parity) and benchmark is ready; happy to open the PR if the direction is OK.

items.title: [PD] Runtime role switch: engine launched with --disaggregation-mode decode crashes with illegal memory access after decode -> prefill -> decode
items.author: athrael-soju
items.body_excerpt:
**Version:** sglang 0.5.21 (`lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21-cu130`), mooncake transfer backend, TP 1, one node.

**Model:** Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B (hybrid linear and full attention). Every engine runs with
`--max-running-requests 256 --page-size 1 --attention-backend triton --enable-pd-role-switch --disaggregation-transfer-backend mooncake`.

**Steps**

1. Start engine A with `--disaggregation-mode prefill` and engine B with `--disaggregation-mode decode`, each with its own `--disaggregation-bootstrap-port`.
2. Serve requests A -> B: they work.
3. With both engines idle, `POST /pd_role_switch {"new_role": "decode", "decode_cuda_graph_memory_gb": <B's value from /server_info>}` on A, then `{"new_role": "prefill"}` on B. Serve B -> A: it works.
4. Switch A back to prefill and B back to decode (passing `decode_cuda_graph_memory_gb`). Both switches return `success: true`.
5. Serve A -> B.

**Expected:** B decodes as it did in step 2.

**Actual:** B's scheduler exits on its first decode with `torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered`, then SIGQUIT. Prefill requests fail after the bootstrap timeout. This reproduced in 4 of 4 runs, including with a larger model from the same family.

**Workaround:** launch every engine with `--disaggregation-mode prefill` and switch the decode engines to decode at startup. With that, engine A and engine B each switched both ways through three full cycles and served every request (2 of 2 runs). So the failure seems tied to an instance whose launch role was decode.

items.title: [Interpreter] bfloat16 arithmetic returns wrong values (computed on raw bits)
items.author: roy6n23
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Under `TRITON_INTERPRET=1`, bfloat16 kernels silently produce wrong results. The interpreter stores bf16 tensors as raw `uint16` bits, and only the bf16 <-> fp32/fp16 casts decode them. Everything else (arithmetic, comparisons, `tl.dot`, `tl.sum`/`tl.cumsum`, `tl.maximum`) runs numpy on the integer bit patterns.

I hit this while testing a FlashAttention-2 forward kernel under the interpreter: every bf16 case was off by about 8e8 while fp16 matched, and the same kernel passes on an H100.

Repro:

```python
import os

os.environ["TRITON_INTERPRET"] = "1"

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, add_ptr, dot_ptr, N: tl.constexpr):
    offs = tl.arange(0, N)[:, None] * N + tl.arange(0, N)[None, :]
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offs)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offs)
    tl.store(add_ptr + offs, x + y)
    tl.store(dot_ptr + offs, tl.dot(x, y))


torch.manual_seed(0)
for dtype in (torch.float16, torch.bfloat16):
    x, y = torch.randn(16, 16, dtype=dtype), torch.randn(16, 16, dtype=dtype)
    add, dot = torch.empty_like(x), torch.empty(16, 16)
    kernel[(1, )](x, y, add, dot, N=16)
    print(f"{dtype}: max |add - ref| = {(add.float() - (x + y).float()).abs().max().item():.3g}, "
          f"max |dot - ref| = {(dot - x.float() @ y.float()).abs().max().item():.3g}")
```

Output on main (596bd30):

```
torch.float16: max |add - ref| = 0, max |dot - ref| = 0
torch.bfloat16: max |add - ref| = nan, max |dot - ref| = 2.44e+10
```

Two related cast issues: fp32 -> bf16 truncates instead of rounding to nearest even (the default in `semantic.cast`), and int -> bf16 writes the integer as bits, e.g. `(1 < 2).to(tl.bfloat16)` gives 9.2e-41.

The test suite doesn't catch this because bf16 is skipped under the interpreter (`check_type_supported`, plus skips in `test_dot`, `test_scaled_dot` and `test_dot_multidim`). With those skips removed, 527 of the 1,338 bf16 interpreter tests fail on main.

I have a patch that keeps bf16 stored as bits but decodes to fp32 for computation and rounds results back to bf16 with round-to-nearest-even, the same fp32 intermediate the interpreter already uses for bf16 <-> fp16 casts (#11699). With it the skips can be removed: 1,836 previously skipped interpreter tests pass with no regressions. Only bf16 atomics would keep a skip, since they already raise "Unsupported data type". Would a PR along these lines be welcome?

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 596bd30 (3.9.0+git596bd304), built from source; also reproduces with the 3.8.0 wheel
OS: macOS 15.7 arm64, CPU only with TRITON_INTERPRET=1 (3.8.0 also checked on Linux aarch64)
GPU: none (interpreter)
Python 3.12.12, numpy 2.5.3, torch 2.14.1 (CPU)

items.title: [Gateway] Add routing support for the /v1/audio/speech API
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
Parent issue: #2989

## Background

AIBrix documents vLLM-Omni as exposing OpenAI-compatible multimodal APIs, including `/v1/audio/speech`. The Gateway currently supports audio transcription and translation but not speech generation.

Speech generation has a different transport contract: a JSON request, a binary audio response, potentially multiple streamed response chunks, no JSON usage or SSE processing, and no async job registration.

## Proposed behavior

Support `POST /v1/audio/speech`.

The Gateway should:

1. parse the JSON request;
2. require a non-empty `model`;
3. require a non-empty textual `input`;
4. preserve all other request fields;
5. use existing non-PD model routing;
6. stream successful binary responses without parsing or mutation;
7. preserve upstream audio headers.

## Validation

Add a focused validator such as:

```go
func validateAudioSpeechRequest(
    requestID string,
    requestBody []byte,
) (model, message string, errRes *extProcPb.ProcessingResponse)
```

Validate only a JSON object root, a non-empty string `model`, and a non-empty string `input`.

Forward fields such as `voice`, `response_format`, `speed`, `instructions`, `language`, and `stream_format` without duplicating engine validation. A request-level `stream` field must not cause the Gateway to interpret the response as SSE.

## Response handling

Classify `/v1/audio/speech` as a non-language response.

Do not pass successful binary responses through language JSON parsing, SSE parsing, token usage extraction, video job rewriting, or full response buffering.

Preserve `Content-Type`, `Content-Length`, `Content-Disposition`, and `Transfer-Encoding`. Do not invent token usage for audio output.

## Envoy routing

Add the endpoint to path constants, JSON validation dispatch, non-language response classification, ModelRouter default paths, the shared reserved HTTPRoute, and vLLM-Omni documentation.

No dedicated EnvoyExtensionPolicy is needed because the shared route already streams response bodies.

## Testing

Cover valid requests, field preservation, invalid model/input, malformed JSON, query parameters, model routing, binary and invalid UTF-8 payloads, multi-chunk responses, content header preservation, upstream JSON errors, cancellation and cleanup, no token parsing, no video job registration, and reserved/model route presence.

## Non-goals

- Do not implement speech synthesis in AIBrix.
- Do not add multipart input.
- Do not buffer the complete audio response.
- Do not add async speech jobs.
- Do not add PD support.
- Do not add a dedicated response mode or HTTPRoute.
- Do not change transcription or translation behavior.
- Do not introduce an endpoint registry.

## Acceptance criteria

- Speech requests route by model to an eligible backend Pod.
- Unknown engine-specific fields remain intact.
- Successful audio responses stream byte-for-byte.
- Binary responses never enter JSON or SSE processing.
- Audio response headers are preserved.
- Error, cancellation, and cleanup behavior is tested.
- Both reserved and model routes expose the endpoint.

items.title: [Bug]: Prefix caching silently inert on hybrid Mamba2 models when max_model_len < auto-selected block size
items.author: Majid-Taheri
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

- vLLM main (0.23.1rc1.dev, commit 429f40574 base)
- GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm_120), single GPU
- Model: `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4` (`NemotronHForCausalLM`, hybrid Mamba2 + attention)

</details>

### Describe the bug

On hybrid Mamba2 models (e.g. NemotronH), `--enable-prefix-caching` is silently inert whenever `max_model_len` is smaller than the attention block size that vLLM auto-selects for the hybrid KV layout. Prefix caching is accepted without warning, but the cache never records a single hit, so users get none of the expected TTFT benefit and no indication why.

**Mechanism.** For hybrid models, `Platform.check_and_update_config` (`vllm/platforms/interface.py`, the "Setting attention block size to N tokens" path) raises `cache_config.block_size` up to `attn_block_size` so the attention page size is >= the mamba page size:

```python
if cache_config.block_size < attn_block_size:
    cache_config.block_size = attn_block_size
    logger.info("Setting attention block size to %d tokens ...", attn_block_size)
```

For this model that yields `block_size = 8320`. Block-hash prefix caching only registers a **complete** block, so if `max_model_len < block_size` no request can ever fill one block, and the prefix cache is structurally unable to hit. Nothing warns the user that enabling prefix caching will do nothing in this configuration.

### Reproduction

Same model and GPU, only `--max-model-len` differs. Send the same prompt three times (temperature 0), measure streaming TTFT and read `/metrics`.

**Inert — `--max-model-len 4096` (< block_size 8320):**

```
--enable-prefix-caching --max-model-len 4096   # block size auto-set to 8320
```
| request | TTFT |
|---|---|
| 1 (cold) | 0.349 s |
| 2 (repeat) | 0.249 s |
| 3 (repeat) | 0.259 s |

```
vllm:prefix_cache_queries_total  10608.0
vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total     0.0      # zero hits across 10.6k queries
```

**Working — `--max-model-len 16384` (> block_size 8320), same prompt (~12.8k tokens):**

| request | TTFT |
|---|---|
| 1 (cold) | 1.510 s |
| 2 (repeat) | 0.313 s  (4.8x faster) |
| 3 (repeat) | 0.315 s |

```
vllm:prefix_cache_queries_total  38448.0
vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total     16640.0   # ~43% hit rate
```

Same model, same `block_size = 8320`; the only difference is `max_model_len`. Below the block size, hits are impossible; above it, prefix caching works as expected.

### Impact

Any hybrid-Mamba user (NemotronH, and likely other MambaMixer2 models whose page-size coupling inflates `block_size`) who runs with `max_model_len` below the auto-selected block size gets prefix caching that is enabled but completely inert, with no log message pointing at the cause. `max_model_len 4096` is a common setting, so this is easy to hit unknowingly.

### Suggested fix

At config validation, when `enable_prefix_caching` is set and the resolved `cache_config.block_size > max_model_len` for a hybrid model, emit a warning that prefix caching will be ineffective in this configuration (block size exceeds max model len, so no full block can form), and suggest raising `--max-model-len` at or above the block size. A warning is the minimal fix; auto-adjusting or erroring could be discussed.

Happy to send a PR for the warning if that direction is agreeable.

items.title: [Performance][NIXL] BLHNC MLA caches lost whole-row registration in #53781 and now need more NIXL descriptors than LBHNC
items.author: stu-cao
items.body_excerpt:
## Your current environment
- GLM-5.3 (78 MLA + 21 indexer layers) with a DFlash2 draft (6 layers, GQA, 8 KV heads, fp8 KV, k=4).
- Prefill DEP8 (TP1 per rank). Decode TP4. Pull-mode `NixlConnector`, GPU-resident KV (no host buffer).
- vLLM main @ `4e0a414c44`, plus #58471 (GQA draft head slicing under an MLA target), the NVFP4
  prefill-context gather from #58744, and our NVFP4 KV decode path (`nvfp4_ds_mla` on
  `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE`, #59342).
- GB200 NVL72 (NIXL over NVLink), and B300 HGX (NIXL over RDMA).

## Describe the issue

### 1. Whole-row transfer is unreachable for page-contiguous BLHNC MLA caches
#53781 (HiSparse host-resident hot-buffering) put `not page_contiguous` in front of the
"packed MLA layouts transfer the complete storage row" branch of
`NixlConnectorWorker.register_kv_caches`:

```python
# before #53781
elif storage_is_block_major and (
    (packed_storage and is_mla_region)
    or (not hnc_contiguous and not self._is_csa_linear)
):
# after #53781
elif storage_is_block_major and (
    not page_contiguous
    and ((packed_storage and is_mla_region) or not self._is_csa_linear)
):
```

The gate is needed so a HiSparse decoder can land host-resident and device-only layers separately.
But `page_contiguous` is true for every GLM-5.3 layer, so a device-resident BLHNC cache registers one
region per layer. Every transfer then carries one descriptor per layer per block, and BLHNC
ends up costing more than LBHNC, the opposite of its purpose.

Registration on one GB200 decode rank, from the `prepared N descriptors into M strides` log line:

| layout | strides | descriptors |
|---|---:|---:|
| LBHNC, block 1024 | 62 | 2,488,080 |
| BLHNC, block 64, current main | 104 | 2,714,816 |
| BLHNC, block 64, whole row | 1 | 26,104 |

End to end, the whole-row run looked like this. GB200 runs: DEP8 prefill → 10× TP4 decode;
AgentX agentic traffic, 128 concurrent sessions, 1800 s per arm; 29,088 transfers.

| | LBHNC bs1024 | BLHNC bs64, whole row |
|---|---:|---:|
| NIXL xfer, mean | 85.23 ms | 22.30 ms |
| NIXL post, mean | 57.88 ms | 6.96 ms |
| TTFT p50 | 848 ms | 730 ms |

With fp8 KV on GB200 (DEP8 prefill → 1×TP8 decode, 32 sessions), current main's BLHNC took
2.0–3.6 s per transfer. Restoring the pre-#53781 gate brought that to 78 ms, against 146 ms for
LBHNC.

### 2. A naive re-enable misregisters a head-sharded draft
Under BLHNC, every KV cache group starts at byte 0 of the shared block row, so the first draft page
has the same base address as the first target page. Regions are deduplicated by base address.
So if the draft also takes the whole-row branch, it folds into the target's single replicated
region. Then #58471's per-rank head slice never runs, and each TP4 rank receives the TP1 prefill's
8-head draft pages unsliced. We shipped exactly that by narrowing the gate to
`(not page_contiguous or not self.use_host_buffer)`.

The same aliasing folds draft layer 0 into a target region even without whole-row: 104 strides
for 105 layers. That is #57661, fixed by #57662's `(base_addr, block_len)` key.

## Proposal (PR to follow, stacked on #58471 and #57662)
- Opt-in `kv_connector_extra_config.whole_row_regions` (default false).
- Replicated (MLA) layers of a block-major row register as one whole-row region.
- Head-sharded layers (a GQA draft under an MLA target) keep per-layer SPLIT regions, so each rank
  reads its own head slice.
- The flag is rejected with `kv_buffer_device=cpu` and with HiSparse host-resident groups, so
  #53781's case is untouched.
- With `--disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager`, BLHNC packs the head-sharded draft pages inside the
  target's block row. Their size depends on TP, so a whole-row region would differ between a TP1
  prefill and a TP4 decode (2,721,312 vs 2,131,360 bytes; the handshake asserts). The flag must reject
  that layout at registration with a clear error.

Open question for maintainers: should this be opt-in, or automatic whenever no group is
host-resident?

## Not this issue: DFlash2 acceptance under BLHNC
BLHNC deployments with a DFlash2 draft also lose about 5.5 points of draft acceptance. That loss is
tracked in #60560. It comes from the hybrid KV cache manager turning the sliding-window draft into a
real SWA group, not from NIXL registration: the corrected registration proposed here (B300, 34.18%)
loses as much as the misregistration described above (GB200, 34.8%).

## Before submitting a new issue...
- [x] Searched open issues and PRs: #57661, #57662, #50717, #58471, #59586, #60368.
  - Related: #60560 (DFlash2 acceptance under BLHNC + HMA).

AI assistance (Claude) was used to analyze logs and draft this issue. A human reviewed and edited
every line.

items.title: GLiNER2.5-Decide support
items.author: sandrohanea
items.body_excerpt:
I'd like to discuss adding GLiNER2.5-Decide classification support to llama.cpp through the existing `/v1/systemone` decision API.

I already implemented this model in g[gliner.cpp](https://github.com/sandrohanea/gliner.cpp) as a successful proof of concept. I think it would be more useful in llama.cpp, where it could reuse the existing runtime, backends and decision API, but initially, when I added it, there was no support for decision models in llama.cpp.

The initial scope would cover:
- The DeBERTa-v2/v3 encoder variant used by GLiNER2.5-Decide.
- Its Linear-ReLU-Linear classification head on contextual `[L]` marker states.
- Conversion of the original checkpoint to GGUF.
- Classification through `/v1/systemone`, without spans, records or other GLiNER checkpoints.

A prerequisite is NFC normalization for the Unigram tokenizer. The checkpoint's tokenizer explicitly uses NFC, which normalizes canonically equivalent Unicode sequences consistently. For example, U+00E9 (`é`) and U+0065 followed by U+0301 (`é`, an `e` plus a combining acute accent) should produce the same normalized text. Omitting this step can produce different token IDs from the reference tokenizer. 

The proposed implementation adds NFC as a reusable Unicode utility, enabled through optional GGUF metadata and disabled by default. It uses generated Unicode tables, iterative decomposition and algorithmic Hangul handling, without a new runtime dependency.

I'd split this into two dependent PRs: NFC normalization first, then GLiNER2.5-Decide support. GPU precision validation would remain follow-up work.

Does this scope and approach fit the project?

items.title: Misc. bug: [SYCL] GET_ROWS returns wrong values or NaN on weights reordered by MUL_MAT
items.author: skipzx-lab
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

llama.cpp master cbe28bb (13 Oct 2026). Also present in acestep.cpp's ggml fork (synced 7 Oct).
SYCL build: oneAPI 2026.1, icx/icpx, -DGGML_SYCL=ON
Hardware: Intel Arc Pro B60 24 GB, Level Zero driver 1.14.37020

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

Other (Please specify in the next section)

### Command line

```shell

```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

ggml, SYCL backend (ggml/src/ggml-sycl/getrows.cpp)

With `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_OPT=1` (the default), ggml-sycl reorders Q4_0, Q8_0, Q2_K, Q3_K, Q4_K, Q5_K and Q6_K weights in place the first time they're used in a small-batch MUL_MAT (8 tokens or fewer), and marks the tensor with `extra->optimized_feature.reorder`. GET_ROWS never checks that flag. If the same tensor goes through GET_ROWS afterwards, it decodes the reordered bytes as if they were normal blocks and returns wrong values or NaN.

You need one tensor used by both ops on the device, which is what happens with tied embeddings when the embedding isn't kept on the CPU. llama.cpp mostly avoids this because its input embeddings stay on the CPU and a tied output gets its own copy, but other ggml-based programs run into it.

**Real-world case.** acestep.cpp's 4B LM (Q8_0, tied embeddings). Seed 42 with a 240 s request, which should produce about 1,200 audio codes:

| Backend | Codes generated |
|---|---|
| SYCL, default | 16 / 299 / 388 / 521 / 1,300 (5 runs) |
| SYCL, `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_OPT=0` | 1,196 / 1,200 / 1,198 |
| Vulkan | 1,197 |

Full logs: https://github.com/ServeurpersoCom/acestep.cpp/issues/54

**Minimal repro.** One graph with `mul_mat(w, x)` where `x` is a single column, followed by `get_rows(w, ids)` on the same `w`, compared against CPU. I've written this up as a test-backend-ops case (`test_get_rows_after_mul_mat`) and will open a PR with it and the fix.

1. Build with `-DGGML_SYCL=ON`.
2. Add the test case and run `test-backend-ops -b SYCL0 -o ADD`.

On unpatched master it fails for all 7 types on SYCL. Q8_0 and Q6_K give NaN, the rest give wrong values. The same test passes on Vulkan.

AI disclosure: the investigation was done with Claude Code Assistance. I've verified the results on my own hardware.

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

[GET_ROWS] NaN at index 608 (SYCL0=nan CPU=-0.251465)  ADD(type=q8_0,n=256,m=16,r=4): FAIL
[GET_ROWS] ERR = 1.000000865 > 0.000000100            ADD(type=q4_0,n=256,m=16,r=4): FAIL

items.title: [RFC] An Extensible Collective Framework for Mooncake PG
items.author: caozhanhao
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

This RFC proposes an extensible GPU collective framework for Mooncake PG. The framework separates PG-level backend dispatch from group-wide algorithm selection, rank-local planning, GPU execution, and device data movement, while preserving the existing PG APIs and elastic semantics.

This proposal builds on #2716 by turning its device-collective direction into a concrete framework for GPU collectives. The framework is introduced incrementally alongside the legacy implementation, and the new collective path remains opt-in during the rollout.

## Motivation

The legacy GPU collective path couples collective protocols with host workers, transfer submission, synchronization, and failure handling. Adding several algorithms per operation and tuning them for different message sizes and topologies would otherwise duplicate these concerns and make cross-rank consistency harder to maintain.

The new framework gives GPU collective algorithms a narrower responsibility: implement a protocol against a rank-local plan and a device transfer interface. Membership, capability negotiation, backend dispatch, algorithm selection, resource ownership, and recovery remain framework responsibilities.

## Goals

- Define reusable planning and execution boundaries for GPU collective operations.
- Define algorithm selection within the new path so every rank receives the same policy and runs a consistent collective protocol.
- Decouple device collective algorithms from route-specific transfer details.
- Allow membership or algorithm changes to reuse a CUDA Graph capture.
- Migrate incrementally with explicit opt-in while the legacy path remains the default.

## Non-Goals

- Replacing all legacy collectives during the initial rollout.
- Switching to another route after a transfer failure in the initial implementation.

## Architecture

```
                                      +-------------------+
                                      | torch.distributed |
                                      +---------+---------+
                                                |
                                                v
+===================================================================================================+
| Mooncake PG                                                                                       |
|                                                                                                   |
|                                  +-------------------------+                                      |
|                                  | Mooncake Communicator   |                                      |
|                                  +------------+------------+                                      |
|                                               |                                                   |
|              +--------------------------------+-----------------------+                           |
|              |                                |                       |                           |
|              v                                v                       v                           |
|   +-------------------+        +---------------------------------------------------+              |
|   | Legacy Collective |        | New Collective Runtime                            |              |
|   | Runtime           |        |                                                   |              |
|   +---------+---------+        | +----------------+          +--------------+      |              |
|             |                  | | Device Runtime |          | CPU Runtime  |------+-------+      |
|             |                  | +--------+-------+          +--------------+      |       |      |
|             |                  +----------|----------------------------------------+       |      |
|             |                             |                                                |      |
|             |                             v                                                |      |
|             |        +-----------------------------------------------------------+         |      |
|             |        | Device Transfer Service                                   |         |      |
|             |        |                                                           |         |      |
|             |        | +-----------+ +------------+ +-----------+ +------------+ |         |      |
|             |        | | P2P Route | | RDMA Route | | GIN Route | | Host Proxy | |         |      |
|             |        | +-----+-----+ +-----+------+ +-----+-----+ +------+-----+ |         |      |
|             |        +-------|-------------|--------------|--------------|-------+         |      |
|             |                |             |              |              |                 |      |
+=============|================|=============|==============|==============|=================|======+
              |                +-------------+--------------+              |                 |
              |                              |                             |                 |
              |                              v                             v                 |
              |                 +--------------------------+   +------------------------+    |
              |                 | Transfer Engine (Device) |   | Transfer Engine (Host) |<---+
              |                 +--------------------------+   +------------------------+
              |                                                            ^
              |                                                            |
              +------------------------------------------------------------+
```

The public collective APIs remain unchanged. The Coordinator owns authoritative membership and publishes group-wide decisions. `MooncakeCommunicator` dispatches operations to the selected legacy or new backend

items.author: shakilahmedemon

### 🐛 Describe the bug `F.scaled_dot_product_attention` on float32 CUDA inputs of shape (8192, 4, 4) is about 3x slower on recent nightlies than on 2.9.1 and 2.11.0. items.title: `_scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention_backward` segfaults when the dropout seed/offset are CUDA tensors and the stream is not capturing (CUDA graph replay)
items.author: todd427
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

With `dropout_p > 0`, `aten._scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention_backward` reads the philox seed and offset on the host whenever the current stream is not capturing. A forward that was captured in a CUDA graph and then replayed returns the seed and offset as CUDA tensors. Calling the backward on them outside capture dereferences a device pointer on the CPU and the process dies with SIGSEGV (exit 139). No Python exception is raised.

I found this through `torch.compile(mode="reduce-overhead")`, where cudagraph trees run a backward partition eagerly after the forward was recorded. The reproduction below needs neither `torch.compile` nor a model.

```python
import torch

dev = "cuda"
q, k, v = (torch.randn(2, 4, 128, 64, device=dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16) for _ in range(3))
op = torch.ops.aten._scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention
bw = torch.ops.aten._scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention_backward

# eager forward: seed/offset are CPU tensors
out, lse, seed, off = op(q, k, v, None, True, 0.1, False)
print("eager forward seed device:", seed.device, flush=True)
bw(torch.ones_like(out), q, k, v, None, out, lse, seed, off, 0.1, [True, True, True, False], False)
print("eager backward ok", flush=True)

# forward captured in a CUDA graph: seed/offset are CUDA tensors
s = torch.cuda.Stream()
with torch.cuda.stream(s):
    op(q, k, v, None, True, 0.1, False)
torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(s)
g = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
with torch.cuda.graph(g):
    out, lse, seed, off = op(q, k, v, None, True, 0.1, False)
g.replay()
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print("captured forward seed device:", seed.device, "capturing:", torch.cuda.is_current_stream_capturing(), flush=True)
bw(torch.ones_like(out), q, k, v, None, out, lse, seed, off, 0.1, [True, True, True, False], False)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print("backward outside capture ok", flush=True)
```

Output (the last line is never printed; the process exits with 139):

```
eager forward seed device: cpu
eager backward ok
captured forward seed device: cuda:0 capturing: False
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

Reproduced with torch 2.14.1+cu130 and torch 2.16.0.dev20261012+cu132 (also 2.12.0+cu130 with the `torch.compile` version).

### Where it crashes

Under `gdb` (nightly build), SIGSEGV on the autograd thread:

```
#0  at::native::_efficient_attention_backward(...)
#3  at::native::_scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention_backward_cuda(...)
=> mov (%rax),%r13        # straight after a call to TensorBase::data_ptr<long>
si_addr = 0x7ffc37e9c200  # equal to rax, in the range CUDA uses for device allocations
```

### Cause

In `aten/src/ATen/native/transformers/cuda/attention_backward.cu` (read on `main`), with `dropout_p != 0`:

```cpp
if (at::cuda::currentStreamCaptureStatus() == at::cuda::CaptureStatus::None) {
  rng_engine_inputs = at::PhiloxCudaState(*philox_seed.data_ptr<int64_t>(),
                                          *philox_offset.data_ptr<int64_t>());
} else {  // dropout + capture
  rng_engine_inputs = at::PhiloxCudaState(philox_seed.data_ptr<int64_t>(),
                                          philox_offset.data_ptr<int64_t>(), 0);
}
```

The branch is chosen by the capture status of the current stream, but what matters is where `philox_seed` and `philox_offset` live. Note [Seed and Offset Device] in `attention.cu` says they are on the device only "if we are currently in graph capture mode". A graph that is replayed keeps returning those CUDA tensors after capture has ended, so the backward can legitimately receive them outside capture.

I confirmed this in the `torch.compile` case by printing the two arguments from inductor's generated code just before the call: on step 0 the seed is a CPU tensor and the call works; on step 1 it is `cuda:0`, `is_current_stream_capturing()` is False, and the call crashes.

### Possible fix

Branch on the tensor's device instead of the capture status (host read when the tensors are on the CPU, device pointers when they are CUDA tensors). I have this change and a regression test in my fork, but have not built or run them yet. I will open a PR once a maintainer confirms this is worth fixing and marks the issue actionable.

### Workarounds

`dropout_p=0` in the attention call, the math attention path, or not running the backward of a captured forward outside capture.

### Related

I searched the issue tracker and pull requests for the function names, `philox_seed`, and the crash and found no report of this. Related: #99905 (dropout in SDPA under `torch.compile`), #196586 and #197563 (a ROCm flash-attention path that read dropout seed tensors through device pointers on the host).

## Agent details (AI-generated)

This issue was investigated and drafted with Claude Code (Claude Sonnet 5.5) working on my machine. The assistant ran the reproductions, the `gdb` session and the instrumentation of the generated code, and wrote the text above. I have read the text and the reproduction. The explanation of why cudagraph trees run the backward eagerly comes from reading `cudagraph_trees.py` and was not tested separately.

## Versions

<summary>collect_env output (torch 2.16.0.dev20261012+cu132)</summary>

```

items.title: [docs] Slurm: fix multi-node example, add single-node and offline batch examples
items.author: holtwood
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

Contributes to #3244.

The existing multi-node example expands `$SLURM_NODEID` in the batch shell, before `srun` creates its per-task environments. Both launches can therefore receive the same node rank. The existing readiness loop also checks only whether a TCP port is open.

This PR covers basic multi-node serving, single-node serving, and offline batch inference. #29991 has a separate scope around PD disaggregation and Apptainer.

## Changes

- Evaluate `$SLURM_PROCID` inside each `srun` task and use Slurm `%n` patterns for per-node logs.
- Use configurable HTTP and distributed-init ports, a bounded `/health` check, and early process-exit detection.
- Add a single-node serving job with cleanup and an SSH forwarding hint.
- Add an offline job that writes a real Python file with a `__main__` guard, as required by the Engine multiprocessing setup.
- Document the log-directory prerequisite and cluster-specific scheduler, network, port, and model-cache settings.

## Validation

- `bash -n` on all three batch scripts.
- `mint validate`.
- `mint broken-links`.
- Parsed and mock-executed the offline Python example, including Engine context cleanup.
- Checked task-side rank expansion with `SLURM_PROCID=0` and `SLURM_PROCID=1`.
- Cross-checked the Engine `spawn` setup, context-manager support, `/health` behavior, and referenced server arguments against the PR base revision.

I did not run these examples end to end on a Slurm GPU cluster. The `#SBATCH` resource values, partition name, network interfaces, and port availability remain site-specific.

items.title: [HiCache] Track HybridLinear/Mamba pipeline-parallel correctness and support
items.author: alphabetc1
items.body_excerpt:
HybridLinear/Mamba models such as Nemotron-H have a pre-existing HiCache correctness issue with pipeline parallelism (`PP > 1`). On non-first stages, cache-transfer completion and consumers use different layer indices, so forward may read cached state before host-to-device restoration finishes.

PR #37870 fixes sparse layer-ID coverage for `PP=1`. PP support needs a separate correctness review and end-to-end validation; this issue tracks that follow-up.

items.title: Why does num_warps affect numerical precision?
items.author: yaozhenghangma
items.body_excerpt:
I'm testing a Flash Attention kernel, and I've placed the test code at the end. In short, when performing an attention operation using q, k, and v matrices with `num_batchs = 8`, `seq_len = 128`, `num_heads = 128`, and `head_dim = 128`, I observed that setting `num_warps = 4` and `num_warps = 8` produce different output results. The maximum difference between the output matrices is `0.00048828125`, and this difference remains consistent across repeated runs. Moreover, when keeping all other parameters the same and setting `seq_len` to 32 or smaller, the discrepancy disappears. 

I'm using an Nvidia T4 GPU, with CUDA version 12.4 and Triton version 3.1.0.

```python
import math
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def flash_attention_kernel(
    q_ptr, k_ptr, v_ptr, o_ptr,
    start_loc, seq_len,
    q_stride_batch_seq, q_stride_head, q_stride_dim,
    k_stride_batch_seq, k_stride_head, k_stride_dim,
    v_stride_batch_seq, v_stride_head, v_stride_dim,
    o_stride_batch_seq, o_stride_head, o_stride_dim,
    num_head,
    kv_group_size,
    d_scale,
    BLOCK_SIZE_M: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_SIZE_N: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_SIZE_D: tl.constexpr
):
    # q k v: [batchs*seq, heads, dim]
    q_block_id = tl.program_id(0) # m id
    batch_and_head_id = tl.program_id(1)
    batch_id = batch_and_head_id // num_head
    head_id = batch_and_head_id % num_head
    kv_head_id = head_id // kv_group_size

    batch_start = tl.load(start_loc + batch_id)
    batch_seq_len = tl.load(seq_len + batch_id)

    m_ranges = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_M)
    n_ranges = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_N)
    m_start = q_block_id * BLOCK_SIZE_M
    m_offsets = m_ranges + m_start
    embed_offsets = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_D)

    q_offsets = (
        (batch_start + m_offsets[:,None]) * q_stride_batch_seq
        + head_id * q_stride_head
        + embed_offsets[None,:] * q_stride_dim
    )

    k_offsets = (
        (batch_start + n_ranges[:,None]) * k_stride_batch_seq
        + kv_head_id * k_stride_head
        + embed_offsets[None,:] * k_stride_dim
    )

    v_offsets = (
        (batch_start + n_ranges[:,None]) * v_stride_batch_seq
        + kv_head_id * v_stride_head
        + embed_offsets[None,:] * v_stride_dim
    )

    o_offsets = (
        (batch_start + m_offsets[:,None]) * o_stride_batch_seq
        + head_id * o_stride_head
        + embed_offsets[None,:] * o_stride_dim
    )

    q_mask = m_offsets[:,None]  < batch_seq_len
    q = tl.load(q_ptr + q_offsets, mask=q_mask, other=0.0)

    acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M, BLOCK_SIZE_D), dtype=tl.float32)
    m_i = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M,), dtype=tl.float32) - float("inf")
    l_i = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M,), dtype=tl.float32)

    m_mask = tl.where(m_start < batch_seq_len, 1, 0) # loop for m > seq_len is ignored
    n_size = tl.minimum(m_start + BLOCK_SIZE_M, batch_seq_len) # inter block casual mask

    for n_idx in range(0, n_size * m_mask, BLOCK_SIZE_N):
        k_mask = n_idx + n_ranges[:,None] < n_size
        k = tl.load(k_ptr + k_offsets + n_idx * k_stride_batch_seq, mask=k_mask, other=0.0)
        v = tl.load(v_ptr + v_offsets + n_idx * v_stride_batch_seq, mask=k_mask, other=0.0)

        qk = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M, BLOCK_SIZE_N), dtype=tl.float32)
        qk += tl.dot(q, tl.trans(k))

        # intra block casual mask
        q_off = m_offsets
        k_off = n_idx + n_ranges
        mask = q_off[:,None] >= k_off[None,:]
        qk = tl.where(mask, qk * d_scale, -float("inf"))

        pad_mask = n_idx + n_ranges < n_size
        qk = tl.where(pad_mask[None,:], qk, -float("inf"))

        m_j = tl.max(qk, axis=1)
        m_new = tl.maximum(m_i, m_j)
        alpha = tl.exp2(m_i - m_new)

        P_j = tl.exp2(qk - m_new[:,None])
        l_j = tl.sum(P_j, axis=1)
        l_i = l_i * alpha + l_j

        o_scale = alpha
        acc = acc * o_scale[:, None]
        P_j = P_j.to(v_ptr.dtype.element_ty)
        acc += tl.dot(P_j, v)

        m_i = m_new

    acc = acc / l_i[:, None]

    tl.store(o_ptr + o_offsets, acc, mask=q_mask)


def flash_attention(q: torch.Tensor, k, v, start_loc, seq_len, num_warps):
    _, num_head, d_size = q.shape
    _, num_kv_head, _ = k.shape
    kv_group_size = num_head // num_kv_head
    num_batch = seq_len.shape[0]
    max_seq_len = int(torch.max(seq_len).item())
    d_scale = 1.0 / math.sqrt(d_size) * 1.4426950408889634

    grid = lambda meta: (
        triton.cdiv(max_seq_len, meta["BLOCK_SIZE_M"]),
        num_batch * num_head,
        1
    )
    num_stages = 1

    o = torch.empty_like(q, dtype=q.dtype, device=q.device)
    flash_attention_kernel[grid](
        q, k, v, o,
        start_loc, seq_len,
        *q.stride(), *k.stride(), *v.stride(), *o.stride(),
        num_head=num_head,
        kv_group_size=kv_group_size,
        d_scale=d_scale,
        BLOCK_SIZE_M=64,
        BLOCK_SIZE_N=64,
        BLOCK_SIZE_D=d_size,
        num_warps=num_warps,
        num_stages=num_stages,
    )

    return o


class TestFlashAttention:
    def test_flash_attention(self):
        num_batchs = 8
        seq_len = 32
        num_heads = 128
        head_dim = 128
        dtype = torch.float16
        device = 'cuda'
        tensor_shape = (num_batchs, num_heads, seq_len, head_dim)

        q = torch.rand(tensor_shape, dtype=dtype, device=device)
        k = torch.rand(tensor_shape, dtype=dtype, device=device)
        v = torch.rand(tensor_shape, dtype=dtype, device=device)

        qt = q.permute(0,2,1,3).contiguous().view(-1, num_heads, head_dim)
        kt = k.permute(0,2,1,3).contiguous().view(-1, num_heads, head_dim)
        vt = v.permute(0,2,1,3).contiguous().view(-1, num_heads, head_dim)
        start_loc = torch.arange(0, num_batchs*seq_len, seq_len, device=device)
        seq_len_list = torch.full((num_batchs,), seq_len, device=d

items.title: Constexprs that compare equal but differ in type or sign (1 and 1.0, 0.0 and -0.0) reuse each other's binary
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

When a kernel is launched with a constexpr that compares equal to the value of an earlier launch but has a different type or sign (`1` and `1.0`, or `0.0` and `-0.0`), the second launch reuses the binary compiled for the first one. The result depends on which value was launched first.

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(X, out, C: tl.constexpr):
    tl.store(out, tl.load(X) * C)


x = torch.tensor([2**30 + 1], dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
for order in [(1, 1.0), (1.0, 1)]:
    kernel.device_caches.clear()
    results = []
    for c in order:
        out = torch.zeros(1, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
        kernel[(1, )](x, out, c)
        results.append(out.item())
    print(order, results)
```

```
(1, 1.0) [1073741825, 1073741825]
(1.0, 1) [1073741824, 1073741824]
```

Expected: `x * 1` is `1073741825` and `x * 1.0` (computed in fp32) is `1073741824`, regardless of launch order. In the same way, launching with `C=0.0` and then `C=-0.0` stores `0.0` for the second launch.

The on-disk cache is not affected: the string key built from the specialization differs (`1` vs `1.0`, `0.0` vs `-0.0`). The problem is the in-memory lookup in `compute_cache_key` (`python/triton/runtime/jit.py`):

```python
key = (tuple(specialization), str(options))
cache_key = kernel_key_cache.get(key, None)
```

The specialization contains `("constexpr", value)`, and tuple equality treats `1 == 1.0 == True` and `0.0 == -0.0` (with equal hashes) as the same key, so the string key of the first launch is returned. This cache was added in #7768.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

items.title: `tl.reduce` over a tuple with `axis=None` pairs values with the wrong indices
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`tl.reduce` over a tuple with `axis=None` can pair values with the wrong indices. An argmax written as `tl.reduce((x, idx), None, combine)` returns the right maximum but the wrong index. The same reduction with `axis=0` on the same 1-D input is correct.

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def combine(v1, i1, v2, i2):
    gt = (v1 > v2) | ((v1 == v2) & (i1 < i2))
    return tl.where(gt, v1, v2), tl.where(gt, i1, i2)


@triton.jit
def argmax(X, O, N: tl.constexpr, AXIS_NONE: tl.constexpr):
    off = tl.arange(0, N)
    x = tl.load(X + off)
    if AXIS_NONE:
        v, i = tl.reduce((x, off), None, combine)
    else:
        v, i = tl.reduce((x, off), 0, combine)
    tl.store(O, i)
    tl.store(O + 1, v)


N = 1024
torch.manual_seed(0)
x = torch.randperm(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32)
for axis_none in (False, True):
    o = torch.zeros(2, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
    argmax[(1, )](x, o, N, axis_none, num_warps=4)
    print(f"axis={'None' if axis_none else 0}: max={o[1].item()} index={o[0].item()} (expected index {x.argmax().item()})")
```

```
axis=0: max=1023 index=535 (expected index 535)
axis=None: max=1023 index=901 (expected index 535)
```

For `axis=None`, `reduction` in `python/triton/language/semantic.py` flattens each operand separately with `reshape(..., can_reorder=True)`. The two reshapes are free to reorder their elements independently, and here the loaded `x` and the `arange` end up in different orders, so the combine function sees `x[p]` together with `idx[q]`, `q != p`.

This is the same failure as #12099; its fix (#12124) covers the reshape the compiler inserts, not this frontend path. Reshaping the operands with `can_reorder=False`, or reshaping them together, would keep the pairing.

### Environment details

items.title: In-kernel tensor descriptor with a dimension >= 2^31 reads zeros when lowered to pointers
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

A tensor descriptor created in the kernel with `tl.make_tensor_descriptor` and a dimension in [2^31, 2^32) reads zeros and writes nothing, on GPUs where descriptors are lowered to pointers (sm_89 here). A host-side `TensorDescriptor` with the same shape works.

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl
from triton.tools.tensor_descriptor import TensorDescriptor


@triton.jit
def load_in_kernel_desc(X, Y, M):
    desc = tl.make_tensor_descriptor(X, shape=[M], strides=[1], block_shape=[16])
    tl.store(Y + tl.arange(0, 16), desc.load([0]).to(tl.int32))


@triton.jit
def load_host_desc(desc, Y):
    tl.store(Y + tl.arange(0, 16), desc.load([0]).to(tl.int32))


triton.set_allocator(lambda size, align, stream: torch.empty(size, dtype=torch.int8, device="cuda"))
n = 2**31 + 64
x = torch.ones(n, dtype=torch.int8, device="cuda")  # the whole extent is allocated
for M in (2**31 - 64, n):
    y = torch.zeros(16, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
    load_in_kernel_desc[(1, )](x, y, M)
    y_host = torch.zeros(16, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
    load_host_desc[(1, )](TensorDescriptor(x[:M], [M], [1], [16]), y_host)
    print(f"M={M}: in-kernel descriptor {torch.unique(y).tolist()}, host descriptor {torch.unique(y_host).tolist()}")
```

```
M=2147483584: in-kernel descriptor [1], host descriptor [1]
M=2147483712: in-kernel descriptor [0], host descriptor [1]
```

Expected all ones in both cases.

`make_tensor_descriptor` in `python/triton/language/semantic.py` converts the shape to int32 (`self.make_scalar(x, tl.int32)`), and `RewriteTensorDescriptorToPointer` sign-extends it, so the extent becomes negative and every element is masked out. The strides are already int64.

### Environment details

GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

items.title: A volatile load is executed several times when its result is needed in several layouts
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

A single `tl.load(..., volatile=True)` can be executed several times when its result is needed in more than one layout. With a concurrent writer, different uses of the loaded value then see different snapshots, which no single load can produce.

```python
import re
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(F, V, Y, ITERS: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    r = tl.arange(0, 4)[:, None]
    c = tl.arange(0, 8)[None, :]
    if pid < 4:  # writers
        for i in range(ITERS):
            tl.atomic_add(F + r * 8 + c, tl.full([4, 8], 1, tl.int32), sem="relaxed")
    else:  # readers: one volatile load
        v = tl.load(F + r * 8 + c, volatile=True)
        base = (pid - 4) * 32
        tl.store(V + base + r * 8 + c, v)
        tl.store(Y + base + r * 8 + c, v + tl.sum(v, 0)[None, :] + tl.sum(v, 1)[:, None])


n = 20000
for num_warps in (1, 4):
    F = torch.zeros(32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32)
    V = torch.zeros(n * 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32)
    Y = torch.zeros(n * 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32)
    k = kernel[(n + 4, )](F, V, Y, ITERS=200000, num_warps=num_warps)
    v, y = V.view(n, 4, 8), Y.view(n, 4, 8)
    inconsistent = ((v + v.sum(1, keepdim=True) + v.sum(2, keepdim=True)) != y).flatten(1).any(1).sum().item()
    print(f"num_warps={num_warps}: {len(re.findall('ld.volatile', k.asm['ptx']))} ld.volatile in PTX, "
          f"{inconsistent} of {n} readers inconsistent with a single load")
```

```
num_warps=1: 1 ld.volatile in PTX, 0 of 20000 readers inconsistent with a single load
num_warps=4: 6 ld.volatile in PTX, 19781 of 20000 readers inconsistent with a single load
```

Expected 0 inconsistent readers: each reader computes `Y` from one loaded value `v`, and `V` stores that value. The check does not depend on the order of the concurrent writes.

With `num_warps=4` the sums need `v` in other layouts, and `RemoveLayoutConversions` rematerializes the load instead of converting its result. `canBeRematerialized` (`lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/Utility.cpp`) returns early for `LoadOp` based on `isExpensiveLoadOrStore`, before the check for write effects that a volatile load would fail. With `num_warps=1` there is one `ld.volatile` and every reader is consistent.

### Environment details

GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

items.title: fp64 downcast with `fp_downcast_rounding="rtz"` fails with "Unsupported rounding mode for conversion"
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Casting fp64 to fp32, fp16 or bf16 with `fp_downcast_rounding="rtz"` fails to compile with `LLVM ERROR: Unsupported rounding mode for conversion.` The frontend accepts it, and the `cast` docstring documents `fp_downcast_rounding` for any float downcast. The interpreter computes the right result.

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def cast_rtz(X, Y):
    offs = tl.arange(0, 16)
    tl.store(Y + offs, tl.load(X + offs).to(Y.dtype.element_ty, fp_downcast_rounding="rtz"))


x = torch.full((16, ), 1 + 2**-30, dtype=torch.float64, device="cuda")
y = torch.zeros(16, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
cast_rtz[(1, )](x, y)
print(y[0].item())
```

```
Unsupported conversion from f64 to f16 with rounding mode rtz
LLVM ERROR: Unsupported rounding mode for conversion.
...
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

Expected `1.0`. fp16 and bf16 destinations fail the same way; the message names f16 for the fp32 destination as well.

For a non-default rounding mode, `cast` in `python/triton/language/semantic.py` emits `tt.fp_to_fp` with that mode, but `FpToFpOpConversion` (`third_party/nvidia/lib/TritonNVIDIAGPUToLLVM/ElementwiseOpToLLVM.cpp`) has no conversion with an f64 source. With the default RTNE the frontend emits `arith.truncf` instead, which works. For fp32, PTX has `cvt.rz.f32.f64`.

items.title: CPU: copy of a transposed 2-D tensor is single-threaded and slow
items.author: icodywu
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Existing tensor transpose is slow, furthermore, permutes which moves the innermost dimension are also slow. 
I have a faster implementation I'd like to contribute. It boosts speed by 2.5-18X.

```
import time, torch

def gbps(f, nbytes, reps=5):
    f()
    best = float("inf")
    for _ in range(reps):
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); f(); best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return 2 * nbytes / best / 1e9  # bytes read + written

print(torch.__version__)
cases = [("2-D x.t()", torch.randn(16384, 16384), (1, 0)),
         ("batched x.transpose(1, 2)", torch.randn(64, 1024, 2048), (0, 2, 1)),
         ("NHWC -> NCHW", torch.randn(64, 56, 56, 256), (0, 3, 1, 2))]
for name, x, p in cases:
    out = torch.empty(x.permute(p).shape)
    row = []
    for t in (1, 8, 32):
        torch.set_num_threads(t)
        row.append("%d threads %5.1f GB/s" % (t, gbps(lambda: out.copy_(x.permute(p)), x.numel() * 4)))
    print("%-26s" % name, " | ".join(row))

```

items.title: b12x W4A16 (BF16) MXFP4: E8M0 scale bias makes weights BF16-subnormal / zero for scale bytes < 121 (rows silently lost, SM12x)
items.author: sjronan
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting
- [x] I have searched existing issues and did not find a solution or an existing report.

### Environment
- FlashInfer `main` @ `ee4de7dfd6` (same code in the archived standalone b12x @ `2cc7f66a`)
- GeForce RTX 5080 (SM120), torch 2.12.1+cu130, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.7.1, driver 610.88
- Also seen on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120), standalone b12x, serving through vLLM

### Bug description

The experimental b12x W4A16 MoE, on the BF16 activation path with MXFP4 weights (`source_format="fp4_e8m0_k32"`), produces wrong output whenever the checkpoint's E8M0 scale bytes are below about 121. Below about 114 small FP4 values are flushed to zero. Rows lose part or all of their expert contribution. There is no NaN or Inf, and the aggregate cosine against the reference can stay at 0.99999, so the existing tests and most accuracy gates do not see it.

**Mechanism** (`flashinfer/experimental/b12x`):

| step | code | value |
|---|---|---|
| FP4 unpack | `_lib/intrinsics.py` `packed_dequant_e2m1x4_to_bfloat2x2` (sign + 3 magnitude bits `>> 6` into a BF16) | `v * 2^-126`. FP4 0.5 is already a BF16 subnormal |
| E8M0 scale | `_lib/intrinsics.py:3378` `packed_dequant_e8m0x4_to_bfloat2x2`: `add.u32 hN, bN, 7; shl 7` (lines 3404-3411) | BF16 exponent field `e + 7`, i.e. `2^(e-120)` |
| MMA weight | `mul.bf16x2` (`_elem2_mul`) | `v * 2^(e-246) = true_weight * 2^-119` |
| epilogue | `moe/_shared/kernels/w4a16/kernel.py:247` `_E8M0_K32_BF16_GLOBAL_COMPENSATION = 2**119`, folded into `global_scale_f32` | restores the true scale |
| clamp | `w4a16/prepare.py:35`, `kernels/reference.py:55`: 247 | keeps the field at 254 or below |

So every nonzero weight is a normal BF16 only for **121 ≤ e ≤ 247**. That window is centred on scales of about 2^57, which no trained checkpoint uses. In real MXFP4 checkpoints the bytes sit at about 100-130:

- **e < 121:** MMA weights are BF16 subnormals. The MMA products `x * w` are carried at 2^-119 of their true value, so for ordinary activations they fall into FP32-subnormal range and lose precision or vanish.
- **e < 114:** FP4 0.5 rounds to zero. At 111, 0.5 to 2 round to zero, and at 110 everything except ±6 does.

Example: MiMo-V2.6-Pro (MXFP4 experts). MoE layers 1-16 have scale bytes 111-117 (dominant 115-117). Layers 17-18 start at 114 (dominant 118-119), and layers 19+ start at 116 (dominant 120). DeepSeek-V4 / V4-Pro sit at 119-122, mostly 120/121. They are at the edge, and in practice we measured no loss there (cosine 0.99999 on the old kernel). The FP16 activation path (`packed_dequant_e8m0x4_to_half2x2` with `_E8M0_K32_FP16_GLOBAL_COMPENSATION = 2**7`) has the same class of problem: weights are normal FP16 only for e ≥ 121, and the scale overflows FP16 above 135. The fix below does not touch it.

### Minimal reproduction

**(a) Bit-level model (NumPy only, no GPU).** It models what the kernel does with one FP4 code and one scale byte. Old constants are `bias=7, clamp=247`.

```python
import math
def bf16(bits):                      # decode a BF16 bit pattern
    s = -1.0 if bits & 0x8000 else 1.0; e = (bits >> 7) & 0xFF; m = bits & 0x7F
    return s * (math.ldexp(m, -133) if e == 0 else math.ldexp(128 + m, e - 134))
def bf16_rn(x):                      # round-to-nearest-even into BF16, subnormals kept
    if x == 0: return 0.0
    q = math.ldexp(1.0, max(math.frexp(abs(x))[1] - 1, -126) - 7)
    return math.copysign(round(abs(x) / q) * q, x)
FP4 = [0, .5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6]
for e in (110, 113, 116, 120, 121):
    s = bf16(((e + 7) << 7) & 0xFFFF)                                 # the scale the kernel builds

items.title: [Bug] FlashInfer autotune cache is discarded every boot under MoE expert parallelism (EP>1): per-rank shapes never agree, so the fused-MoE tactic is re-drawn each start
items.author: ntxf31415
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`_drop_diverged_autotune_cache()` discards the whole FlashInfer autotune cache — on every boot — whenever the per-rank MoE GEMM shapes differ, which is the normal case with **expert parallelism (EP > 1)**. The cache is then re-tuned from scratch each start, so the fused-MoE tactic is re-drawn every boot. Since the tactic selection is timing-based, end-to-end throughput varies across boots with identical config.

### Environment

- 4× GB10 (DGX Spark), SGLang TP4 / EP2, switchless RoCE ring
- MoE runner backend `flashinfer_mxfp4` (MXFP4 experts), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
- `--chunked-prefill-size 4096`, `--mem-fraction-static 0.90`
- FlashInfer 0.6.18, CUDA 13.0, cuDNN 92000

### Root cause

`python/sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/flashinfer_autotune.py`:

```python
def _autotune_cache_digest(cache_path, env):
    ...
    payload = {"file": configs, "env": env}
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()

def _drop_diverged_autotune_cache(cache_path, group, env) -> None:
    digests = [""] * torch.distributed.get_world_size(group)
    torch.distributed.all_gather_object(digests, _autotune_cache_digest(cache_path, env), group=group)
    if len(set(digests)) == 1:
        return
    ...
    cache_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)          # <-- deletes the cache
```

Each rank digests **its own** `rank_tp{N}_pp0_dp0.json` and all four are compared. Under EP sharding each rank owns a different slice of the routed experts, so **the MoE GEMM problem shapes themselves differ per rank** and the files can never be equal. Measured on our four ranks (same boot, same config, caches cleared so all four start from empty):

| rank | distinct shapes in its cache | example expert shape present |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 24 | `(192, 2304, 320)` |
| 1 | 24 | `(64, 2304, 320)` |
| 2 | 24 | `(64, 2304, 320)` / `(192, …)` |
| 3 | 24 | `(16, 5120)`, `(4, 5120)` |

**The intersection of the four shape sets is empty.** So `len(set(digests)) == 1` is never true, the cache is `unlink`ed on every start, and every start re-profiles `trtllm::fused_moe::gemm1` / `gemm2` for all shapes.

Startup log, one boot:

```
Running FlashInfer autotune with cache: /root/.cache/sglang/flashinfer/autotune/0.6.18/sm121/<key>/rank_tp3_pp0_dp0.json
[AutoTuner]: Tuning trtllm::fused_moe::gemm1:   0%|          | 0/8 ...
```

Tuning count is **26–27 profiles per boot** regardless of whether a complete cache file is already present at that path. The shipped image cache contains only `sparse_mla_sm120_decode_dsv4` entries, so the fused-MoE shapes always miss anyway.

Note the digest also includes the environment, so even equal tactics would not be enough — but here the file contents themselves cannot match.

### Impact

The fused-MoE tactic is re-drawn on every start, and it matters a lot. Two consecutive boots of the same configuration, measured with a cold single-stream prefill probe at 8K tokens:

| boot | prefill t/s (8K) |
|---|---|
| A | 3169 |
| B | 2431 |

**−23 % at 8K**, while 100K was essentially unchanged (3266 vs 3164) — i.e. the draw is shape-range dependent, and a bad draw is stable for the whole life of that process. We also saw a full 1.5× swing on longer inputs between boots.

### Workaround we run

We mount a site-patched copy of this file that keeps the digest check and the log line but drops the `unlink`:

```python
    log_info_on_rank0(logger, "[site patch] keeping per-rank autotune caches")
```

With the per-rank caches kept, subsequent boots report **0 tuning profiles** (cache genuinely read and used) and throughput is stable.

⚠️ Caveat we found the hard way: this is only safe if every rank's own cache is **complete**. If some ranks hit and others miss, the missing ranks enter the timing-reduction collective while the others don't — we reproduced that as an NCCL collective timeout at startup with the process hanging, so a partial cache is worse than none.

### Possible fix directions

1. Compare like-for-like per rank (i.e. make the guard per-rank rather than requiring cross-rank equality), given that under EP the shape sets legitimately differ.
2. Or key the digest only on the *tactics for the shapes this rank actually uses*, rather than on the whole file.
3. Or make the reduction group follow the ranks that actually share a shape set.

If the divergence check is load-bearing for a reason we have not understood, it may be worth at least not deleting — logging and continuing — so a partially-cached fleet degrades to slow rather than to a hang.

items.title: [Bug] qwen_vl: literal "<image>" in message text aborts requests with 500 "Mismatch: More IMAGE tokens found than corresponding data provided"
items.author: brushax
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version (`main`, checked 2026-10-13).
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

For models served by `QwenVLImageProcessor` (Qwen2-VL / Qwen2.5-VL / Qwen3-VL / Qwen3.5 / Qwen4-Exp / …), a **literal `<image>` string in ordinary message text** is counted as an image placeholder. When the same request also carries at least one real image part, the placeholder count exceeds the number of image payloads and the request is aborted with HTTP 500:

```text
Mismatch: More 'IMAGE' tokens found than corresponding data provided.
Error in request: An exception occurred while loading multimodal data:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../multimodal/processors/base_processor.py", line ..., in legacy_load_mm_data
    modality, raw_data, frame_limit = next(task_info_iter)
StopIteration
RuntimeError: An exception occurred while loading multimodal data:
INFO: ... "POST /v1/chat/completions HTTP/1.1" 500 Internal Server Error
```

Note the final message is empty (`...multimodal data: `), which makes this hard to attribute from logs alone.

This is easy to hit in agent workloads: GitHub issue/PR pages render user-uploaded screenshots as the literal text `<image>`, and that fetched page content is replayed as a tool message in the conversation. Once such a message is in the history, **every** subsequent request to that model fails identically while any image is present — the conversation is permanently wedged.

**Root cause.** `python/sglang/srt/multimodal/processors/qwen_vl.py` registers the legacy `/generate` sentinel as an alternative inside `image_token_regex`:

```python
# Also match the legacy sglang <image> sentinel used by /generate,
# so the artifact fast path can normalize it before build_input_ids.
self.mm_tokens = MultimodalSpecialTokens(
    image_token="<|vision_start|><|image_pad|><|vision_end|>",
    image_token_id=hf_config.image_token_id,
    image_token_regex=re.compile(
        r"<\|vision_start\|>(?:<\|image_pad\|>)+<\|vision_end\|>|<image>"
    ),
    ...
)
```

`BaseMultimodalProcessor.get_combined_regex()` builds the prompt-splitting regex from `image_token_regex`, and `submit_data_loading_tasks()` pulls one image per match. A plain-text occurrence of the bare string is therefore indistinguishable from a template-generated placeholder. The chat template only ever emits the native `<|vision_start|><|image_pad|><|vision_end|>` sequence, so in the chat path any `<image>` present in the rendered prompt is user text.

Text-only requests carrying the same string are **not** affected (the mm path is only armed when the request contains mm inputs), which makes the failure intermittent and hard to attribute.

**Related:** #37579 reports the same failure mode for the GLM-V (`glm4v`) processor with `<|image|>` / `<|video|>`. The Qwen-VL variant with `<image>` is not covered there (different processor, different sentinel string), so this is a separate manifestation of the same class of bug.

### Reproduction

Start any Qwen-VL-family model (the failure is in the processor, not the checkpoint). Repro used here: Qwen4-Exp NVFP4, 4×V100, `tp=4`.

```python
import requests

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:30000"
MODEL = "<any model served by QwenVLImageProcessor>"
PNG = "iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAYAAAAfFcSJAAAADUlEQVR42mP8z8BQDwAEhQGAhKmMIQAAAABJRU5ErkJggg=="  # 1x1 PNG


def call(text):
    return requests.post(
        f"{BASE}/v1/chat/completions",
        json={
            "model": MODEL,
            "messages": [
                {
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": [
                        {"type": "text", "text": "what is this?"},
                        {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/png;base64,{PNG}"}},
                    ],
                },
                {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c1", "content": text},
                {"role": "user", "content": "go on"},
            ],
            "max_tokens": 8,
        },
    ).status_code


print(call("plain text, no markers"))  # -> 200
print(call("<image>"))                 # -> 500   <-- stray sentinel, identical request otherwise
```

Observed (all against the same server, one image part in every request):

| message text | real image present | result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `plain text, no markers` | yes | 200 |
| `<image>` | yes | **500** (`Mismatch: More 'IMAGE' tokens ...`) |
| `<image>` in a `user` message instead of a `tool` message | yes | **500** |
| `<image>` | **no** | 200 |
| *(none)* | yes | 200 |

So the arming condition is exactly "≥1 real media part **and** ≥1 literal `<image>` occurrence in message text". A full-size real request that reproduces this in production was a 170-message agent conversation whose tool results contained a fetched GitHub issue page (literal `<image>` markers) plus one real image; the request body replays deterministically to a 500 against the worker.

### Environment

```text
$ python3 -m sglang.check_env
Python: 3.12.3 (main, Aug 31 2026, 10:18:26) [GCC 13.3.0]
CUDA available: True
GPU 0,1,2,3: Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB
GPU 0,1,2,3 Compute Capability: 7.0
CUDA_HOME: /usr/local/cuda
NVCC: Cuda compilation tools, release 12.8, V12.8.93
CUDA Driver Version: 580.178.04
PyTorch: 2.9.1+cu128
sglang: 0.0.0.dev0
sglang-kernel: 0.4.9
flashinfer_python: 0.6.12
triton: 3.5.1
transformers: 5.8.1
torchao: 0.17.0+cu128
numpy: 2.3.5
fastapi: 0.141.1
pydantic: 2.13.5
uvicorn: 0.52.4
xgrammar: 0.2.1
openai: 2.6.1
```

Image tag used: `ccr.ccs.tencentyun.com/sglang-sxm2/sglang:20261006.g967bce438` (build of `2026-10-06`
