items.title: [Feature][Training][Rubin] MegaMoE: MXFP8, recomputation, and clamped SwiGLU
items.author: abcdabcd987
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

We need the MegaMoE training backend in [PR #6053](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053) to support activation checkpointing, clamped SwiGLU, and native MXFP8 across Blackwell and Rubin. The target workloads include both 256- and 288-expert models with irregular, unequal per-rank token counts.

The GB200 benchmark at revision `072340e2` also reports 1.4–1.5× slower steps than MoK under uniform routing, and 58.9 GiB of retained output/context per layer at EP32/64 with overflow-safe schedules; the memory figure excludes symmetric workspaces ([benchmark details](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025)). These are results for that revision, not Rubin measurements or claims about later revisions.

## Requested outcome

- **Recomputation:** Add a context-only recompute API for activation checkpointing, similar to MoK's `recompute_forward_context`. Rebuild the state needed by backward without rerunning unnecessary down projections, combine, and output epilogues; validate that recomputed and saved-context backward agree.

- **GLM-5.3-Flash support:** Support 288 routed experts, including EP8 with 36 local experts and EP32 with 9. Implement clamped SwiGLU for both routed and shared experts: `silu(clamp(gate, max=10)) * clamp(up, min=-10, max=10)`, with matching backward semantics; retain the unclamped option for the GLM-5.2 workload ([GLM-5.3-Flash implementation](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/8073e6dcaea9aa4b42acf2d92ec72148786bbaeb/src/transformers/models/glm5_next/modeling_glm5_next.py#L86-L142)).

- **MXFP8:** Add native MXFP8 routed-expert forward, input gradients, and weight gradients, not fake quantization followed by BF16 GEMMs. Use a MoK-compatible recipe with caller-prequantized weights and fused activation/gradient quantization, including both operand orientations where needed; keep the shared expert in BF16 initially ([MoK reference API](https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens/blob/caeb2963f855c7ad53bb50c8bbf211086405cb98/README.md)).

- **Memory and speed:** Address the router-gradient backward overhead, capacity-sized saved routed outputs, and computation on padded source rows identified in the [GB200 benchmark comment](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025). Reduce retained activation memory without trading away numerical quality, and make performance track real work rather than pessimistic reserved capacity.

## Target hardware

Required targets are **`sm_100` (B200/GB200), `sm_103` (B300/GB300), and `sm_107` (Rubin)**. Implement and validate the requested capabilities on all three, rather than treating Blackwell as a comparison-only platform.

Expert-parallel groups must support peers spanning multiple hosts within one NVL72 NVLink domain. An inter-rack transport is not required.

## Inference engine

We use PyTorch native with a custom training integration. This request covers both forward and backward, not an inference-only operator.

## Workload and configuration

- **Data type and quantization:** BF16 baseline and native MXFP8 routed-expert training; BF16 shared expert.
- **Parallelism:** Expert parallelism within one NVLink domain, combined with expert FSDP and activation checkpointing.

`H` is hidden width and `I` is expert intermediate width. Both workloads use top-8 routing and one shared expert of width `I`.

| Workload | H | I | Routed experts | Target EP sizes | Local routed experts |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| [GLM-5.2-shaped workload](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025) | 6144 | 2048 | 256 | 4 / 8 / 16 / 32 / 64 | 64 / 32 / 16 / 8 / 4 |
| [GLM-5.3-Flash](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash/raw/main/config.json) | 4096 | 2048 | 288 | 8 / 32 | 36 / 9 |

**The real input-token count `T_r` is irregular, generally not a power of two, and changes across microbatches and runs.** Ranks in the same EP collective can have different counts, including zero; support this independently of uneven received expert loads, without caller-side activation padding.

Use roughly 8K–32K real tokens per rank as the main benchmark range, including counts such as `8191`, `16172`, `16231`, and `32767`. Token counts and routing must remain runtime inputs.

- **Layouts:** Activations are `[T_r,H]`; routing IDs and coefficients are `[T_r,8]`. Gate and up weights are separate tensors, each `[E_local,I,H]`, used as `gate_e = X_e @ W_gate[e].T` and `up_e = X_e @ W_up[e].T`. Down weights are `[E_local,H,I]`, used as `activation_e @ W_down[e].T`.

## Current workaround

The existing comparison paths are [MoK #17](https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens/pull/17) and DeepEP HybridEP plus grouped GEMMs, as described in the [benchmark setup](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025). For the measured adapter revision, activation checkpointing replays the full forward because it lacks a context-only entry point ([recompute comparison](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025)).

## Acceptance criteria

- **Hardware coverage:** Run correctness and performance qualification on `sm_100`, `sm_103`, and `sm_107` for the listed workloads.
- **Training correctness:** Validate outputs, input gradients, routing-coefficient gradients, and all expert/shared weight gradients against independent references. Include clamp boundaries, uneven/empty ranks, skewed routing, and recomputation; support FP32 weight-gradient accumulation and document the BF16/MXFP8 numerical behavior.
- **Performance:** Compare complete forward/backward and checkpointed execution against MoK and HybridEP plus grouped GEMMs. Include scheduling, quantization, copies, and replay, and report total peak memory with matched ring sizes or an explicit latency-versus-memory comparison.

items.title: [Serve] A batch_size_fn exception stops batching and hangs subsequent valid requests
items.author: ai-yang
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

With `@serve.batch(batch_size_fn=...)`, an ordinary exception from the custom sizing callback terminates the queue's background batching task. The exception is not propagated to the dequeued request futures, and subsequent valid requests to the same batched method also hang. The replica remains alive; the application still reports `RUNNING`.

For example, a string-length sizing callback raises `TypeError` for `None`. The expected behavior is to fail the affected request with that error and continue processing valid strings. Instead, both the invalid request and the next valid request time out. This reproduced on three independently deployed replicas.

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray `3.0.0.dev0`, `master` commit `be4889928d3a396d7a1476d1bac3288dac72f9ab`.
- Official nightly wheel for that exact commit, with Python sources linked using `setup-dev.py`.
- Linux x86_64, Python 3.11.15; one local Serve replica, no GPU or external service.

### Reproduction script

```python
import asyncio
import ray
from ray import serve

@serve.deployment(num_replicas=1, max_ongoing_requests=8)
class Demo:
    @serve.batch(
        max_batch_size=8,
        batch_wait_timeout_s=0.01,
        batch_size_fn=lambda items: sum(len(item) for item in items),
    )
    async def batched(self, items):
        return items

    async def __call__(self, item):
        try:
            return {"result": await asyncio.wait_for(self.batched(item), 1)}
        except Exception as exc:
            return {"error": type(exc).__name__}

ray.init(address="local", num_cpus=2, include_dashboard=False)
try:
    serve.start(http_options={"location": "NoServer"})
    handle = serve.run(Demo.bind(), route_prefix=None)
    for item in ("ok", None, "ok"):
        print(handle.remote(item).result(timeout_s=30))
finally:
    serve.shutdown()
    ray.shutdown()
```

Expected: `{'result': 'ok'}`, `{'error': 'TypeError'}`, `{'result': 'ok'}`.

Actual: `{'result': 'ok'}`, `{'error': 'TimeoutError'}`, `{'error': 'TimeoutError'}`.

The timeout bounds the reproduction; it is not the cause of the batching task's failure. Without it, the request futures remain unresolved. Inspecting `_is_batching_task_alive()` after the sizing exception returns `False` on the baseline and `True` with exception propagation fixed.

### Root cause

`wait_for_batch()` calls `_compute_batch_size()` while examining the first item and while assembling a batch, without an exception boundary. `_process_batches()` directly awaits it, so the exception ends the only queue consumer. Additionally, `_process_batch_inner()` recomputes sub-batch size before the `try` block that completes request futures on failure; an exception at that stage leaves the corresponding sub-batch unresolved.

### Issue Severity

Medium-high availability impact for deployments using custom batch sizing: one input-related callback exception can make the batched method persistently unavailable to otherwise valid requests. Input validation before enqueueing can avoid the trigger, and restarting an affected replica restores service. The default path without `batch_size_fn` does not have this trigger.

### Duplicate-work check

On 2026-09-13, searched `batch_size_fn`, `batch_size_fn exception`, `batch_size_fn hang`, and Serve batching hang across issues and PRs, and inspected nearby discussions:

- #58956 / #59059 introduced custom sizing. A review comment on #59059 already mentions keyword-argument `IndexError`; this reproduction uses positional arguments and concerns ordinary callback exceptions disabling later valid requests. It does not propose a keyword-argument compatibility fix.
- Closed #50046 concerns an earlier cancellation bug, and closed #42593 concerns earlier batching hangs; both predate custom sizing.
- Open #64595 restructures batching into per-model queues. Its patch adds `CancelledError` handling but does not handle these ordinary sizing exceptions. It touches the same file, so a fix may need rebasing if that work lands first.

No matching in-flight fix was found. AI assistance was used to investigate this issue and prepare the reproduction.

items.title: [Core] RESCHEDULING placement group busy-spins the GCS main thread when it can't be scheduled
items.author: dancingactor
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

If scheduling a placement group in the `RESCHEDULING` state fails, `GcsPlacementGroupManager` keeps retrying it immediately(~90k retry/s), which busy-spins the GCS main thread. Until the next resource sync update arrives, every retry is guaranteed to fail the same way, so retrying before then is unnecessary and only blocks the GCS main thread.

Here is the issue in detail:

- Placement group P is already scheduled successfully on nodes A and B, with one bundle on each node.
- Node A dies, so P needs to be rescheduled elsewhere, and P enters the `RESCHEDULING` state.
- `GcsPlacementGroupManager` treats a `RESCHEDULING` placement group as top priority, so it inserts P at the front of the queue.
- The cluster doesn't currently have available resources for P, so `GcsPlacementGroupManager` fails to schedule P.
- `GcsPlacementGroupManager` immediately reinserts P at the front of the queue and retries scheduling it. The cluster resources haven't been updated yet, so it fails again.
- This retry loop keeps running and busy-spins the GCS main thread, starving other tasks. It only stops when a resource sync update finally provides enough available resources for P.

In this case, every retry between two resource sync updates is completely redundant, because it is guaranteed to produce the same result.

### Proposed Change

I think Solution 1 is better because it solves busy-loop and keeps the `RESCHEDULING` PG at top priority.
|            | Solves busy-loop | Keeps `RESCHEDULING` PG top priority |
| ---------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| master     | No               | Yes                                  |
| Solution 1 | Yes              | Yes                                  |
| Solution 2 | Yes              | No                                   |
#### Solution 1
Only retry scheduling a `RESCHEDULING` PG when a resource sync update arrives

#### Solution 2
Back off the `RESCHEDULING` PG the same way as a normal PG when retrying (the first attempt still gets top priority). This also solves the busy-loop problem, but it removes the top priority of the `RESCHEDULING` PG.

These PRs already proposed this change:
- https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65007
- https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65970


### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray: 3.0.0.dev0, built from source at commit a1a2cc64ee

### Reproduction script

``` python
import time

import psutil

import ray
from ray.cluster_utils import Cluster
from ray.util.placement_group import placement_group, placement_group_table

# Head node with 0 CPUs and two 1-CPU workers, both filled by a placement group.
cluster = Cluster(initialize_head=True, head_node_args={"num_cpus": 0})
workers = [cluster.add_node(num_cpus=1) for _ in range(2)]
ray.init(address=cluster.address)
pg_a = placement_group([{"CPU": 1}])
pg_b = placement_group([{"CPU": 1}])
ray.get([pg_a.ready(), pg_b.ready()])

# Remove pg_a's node. pg_a becomes RESCHEDULING: it's feasible, but pg_b holds the
# only remaining CPU.
node_id = placement_group_table(pg_a)["bundles_to_node_id"][0]
cluster.remove_node(next(w for w in workers if w.node_id == node_id))
while placement_group_table(pg_a)["state"] != "RESCHEDULING":
    time.sleep(0.1)
time.sleep(1)

# Nothing in the cluster changes from here on.
gcs = psutil.Process(cluster.head_node.all_processes["gcs_server"][0].process.pid)
start = placement_group_table(pg_a)["stats"]["scheduling_attempt"]
gcs.cpu_percent()
time.sleep(5)
end = placement_group_table(pg_a)["stats"]["scheduling_attempt"]
print(f"pg_a scheduling attempts in 5s: {end - start}, GCS CPU: {gcs.cpu_percent():.0f}%")
```

items.title: [Bug]: multi-node trtllm-serve with the MPI orchestrator (trtllm-llmapi-launch) hangs during executor startup; cause under investigation
items.author: dmvevents
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- CPU architecture: x86_64
- GPU: 2× node, 8× NVIDIA H200 each (16 GPUs total), AWS `p5en.48xlarge`
- Networking: AWS EFA (32 NICs/node), EFA 1.50 userspace + aws-ofi-nccl (GIN); Kubernetes StatefulSet with `hostNetwork: true` (pod IP == node IP on a `10.x.0.0/16` primary CIDR), sshd on :2222 for the `mpirun` bootstrap.
- Libraries:
  - Container: `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc9`
  - TensorRT-LLM: v1.3.0rc9 line (source paths below verified against this line)
  - NCCL 2.30.4, PyTorch as shipped in the container
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (container)
- Orchestrator: MPI (`trtllm-llmapi-launch` → `mpirun`), i.e. the `MpiCommSession`/IPC-executor path (not Ray).

### Who can help?

Leaving blank for a core maintainer to route (executor / IPC / multi-node serving).

### The bug

On a **multi-node** `trtllm-serve` launched with the **MPI orchestrator** (ranks spanning two hosts),
startup **hangs at IPC-executor init**. Rank-0's orchestrator creates its ZMQ IPC queues bound to
**loopback** and advertises that `tcp://127.0.0.1:PORT` endpoint to all workers. The 8 worker ranks on
the *second* host try to connect to `127.0.0.1:PORT`, which resolves to *their own* loopback, never
reach rank-0, and exit — so `MpiSession`/IPC init blocks forever waiting for them to connect.

This is specifically an **IPC-executor** problem, not an MPI / NCCL / EFA problem: the `mpirun`
cross-node bootstrap is clean (all 16 ranks start; `orted` launches on the worker node over ssh), and
the hang is **before** NCCL init.

### The hang (reproduced, frozen 8+ minutes, GPUs idle)

`trtllm-serve` freezes right after these lines and never proceeds:

```
[TRT-LLM] [W] Orchestrator is creating IPC executor
rank 0 using MpiCommSession to bind to external MPI processes
[TRT-LLM] [I] Generating a new HMAC key for server proxy_request_queue
[TRT-LLM] [I] Generating a new HMAC key for server worker_init_status_queue
[TRT-LLM] [I] Generating a new HMAC key for server proxy_result_queue
```

Rank-0 waits for the 16 workers to connect to `worker_init_status_queue`; the 8 worker-node ranks
never connect (they start, fail to reach rank-0, exit → `orted` defunct), so init hangs.

### Root cause (source, v1.3.0rc line)

1. `tensorrt_llm/executor/ipc.py:58` — the queue bind address defaults to a hardcoded loopback:
   ```python
   self.address_endpoint = address[
       0] if address is not None else "tcp://127.0.0.1:*"
   ```
2. `tensorrt_llm/executor/proxy.py:494` — `worker_init_status_queue = IpcQueue(is_server=True,
   name="worker_init_status_queue")` is constructed with **no `address`**, so it uses that loopback
   default; `proxy.py:520` then advertises that `tcp://127.0.0.1:PORT` endpoint to the workers.
   Cross-host workers connecting to `127.0.0.1:PORT` hit their **own** loopback → fail.
3. **No routable-IP override exists.** A whole-tree grep of `tensorrt_llm/executor/` for
   `TLLM_*ADDR|*IP|*HOST`, `0.0.0.0`, `get_local_ip`, `use_hostname` finds nothing that sets the
   orchestrator IPC bind address. (`TLLM_SPAWN_PROXY_PROCESS_IPC_ADDR` is an `ipc://` unix socket for
   the RPC-proxy path — even more node-local — and `MASTER_ADDR` is for the Ray backend, not the MPI
   IPC executor.)

So on a single node everything binds and connects on loopback and works; the moment ranks span hosts,
the loopback-bound orchestrator queues are unreachable by the remote workers.

### Expected behavior

A multi-node MPI-orchestrated `trtllm-serve` should let the orchestrator IPC queues bind to a
**routable** address (or `0.0.0.0`) and advertise rank-0's **routable IP** (not `127.0.0.1`) to the
workers, so cross-host workers can connect and `/health` comes up.

### Reproduction

```bash
mpirun -np 16 -H <node0>:8,<node1>:8 \
  --mca plm_rsh_args "-p 2222 -o GSSAPIAuthentication=no" \
  -x TRTLLM_FORCE_COMM_METHOD=... \
  trtllm-llmapi-launch trtllm-serve <a-MoE-model> \
  --tp_size 16 --ep_size 16 --pp_size 1 ...
# hangs at "Orchestrator is creating IPC executor" (see log above); GPUs idle.
```
(`GSSAPIAuthentication=no` is only needed so ssh doesn't stall on GSSAPI KEX against a no-KDC node —
unrelated to the IPC bug.)

### A candidate direction — and why this is filed as an issue, not a "fix" PR

An env-overridable bind address gets *past* the freeze once, but is **not a reliable fix**, so I am
filing this as a defensive-note issue rather than presenting a patch as done:

```diff
--- a/tensorrt_llm/executor/ipc.py
+++ b/tensorrt_llm/executor/ipc.py
-        self.address_endpoint = address[
-            0] if address is not None else "tcp://127.0.0.1:*"
+        self.address_endpoint = address[
+            0] if address is not None else ("tcp://%s:*" % os.environ.get("TLLM_IPC_BIND_IP", "127.0.0.1"))
```
Run with `-x TLLM_IPC_BIND_IP=<rank-0 routable node IP>`.

**Caveat (measured):** with this change + `TLLM_IPC_BIND_IP=<node0 IP>`, **one** attempt advanced all
the way to `launch_server` (past the IPC freeze); a subsequent clean relaunch (stale procs + port
reaped) **re-hung at the same IPC freeze**. So a routable-IP bind is *necessary but not sufficient*.
Unconfirmed which of: (a) the env did not thread to rank-0 on the relaunch (env propagation), (b) a
second worker-connected queue still binds loopback, or (c) an ephemeral-port node↔node reachability
issue. A complete fix should (i) bind the orchestrator IPC to a routable/`0.0.0.0` address, (ii)
advertise the routable IP (not `0.0.0.0`/`127.0.0.1`) to workers, and (iii) ensure **every**
worker-connected queue (not just `worker_init_status_queue`) uses it — then prove a clean multi-host
`trtllm-serve` reaches `/health`.

### Proven workaround

Switching the orchestrator from MPI to **Ray** (`--orchestrator_type ray` / the Ray-backed launch
path, which uses `MASTER_ADDR` for a routable rendezvous) brings multi-node `trtllm-serve` up cleanly
on the same 2-node substrate. So the defect is specific to the **MPI IPC-executor** bind path, and
there is a working alternative

items.title: [Bug]: Block-scaled FP8 model fails during NVRTC warmup in a pip-less uv environment
items.author: dtemraz
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM: `1.3.0rc29` (PyTorch backend)
- Python: 3.12
- Environment: virtual environment created with `uv venv` (no `pip` installed in the venv)
- GPU: H100 SXM 80 GB
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` (block-scaled FP8)

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [ ] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction


On a machine with a supported NVIDIA GPU and working CUDA dependencies:

```bash
uv venv /tmp/trtllm-uv-repro --python 3.12
uv pip install --python /tmp/trtllm-uv-repro/bin/python \
  --index-strategy unsafe-best-match \
  --prerelease=allow \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.nvidia.com \
  'tensorrt_llm==1.3.0rc29' 'mpmath==1.3.0'

export PATH=/tmp/trtllm-uv-repro/bin:$PATH

/tmp/trtllm-uv-repro/bin/trtllm-serve Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8 --backend pytorch
```

The environment has no venv-local `pip` executable unless it is installed separately. 
The failure is observed during engine warmup, at the first block-scaled FP8 GEMM JIT compilation.


### Expected behavior

TensorRT-LLM should locate the JIT include headers using the installed package's location without requiring the `pip` command to exist in the environment. If the headers cannot be located, the error should identify the missing include path or package-location lookup failure.


### actual behavior

On the tested setup, serving fails during warmup with:

```text
RuntimeError: NVRTC compilation failed
```

The failure originates in JIT include-directory discovery: getJitIncludeDirs() locates the required headers by invoking pip show tensorrt_llm and parsing the Location: field.

In a uv-created virtual environment without pip, this command may resolve to a system-level pip that cannot locate the package installed in the virtual environment. As a result, the required include paths are missing, and compilation of fp8_block_scaling_gemm fails.

The error surfaces as RuntimeError: NVRTC compilation failed, without identifying the missing include paths.

BF16 inference works in the same environment.

## Workaround

Installing `pip` into the same virtual environment and ensuring its executable is first on `PATH` resolves the issue in the tested setup.

### additional notes

.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug] trtllm-bench filters TensorRT-only options from the TensorRT backend
items.author: yufeiwu-nv
items.body_excerpt:
## Product defect

get_llm treats backend != 'tensorrt' as a non-TensorRT backend. However RuntimeConfig represents TensorRT with backend=None, and only accepts 'pytorch', '_autodeploy', or None. Consequently TensorRT runs lose batching_type, normalize_log_probs, and extended_runtime_perf_knob_config before constructing the TensorRT LLM, so requested runtime settings can silently be ignored.

Affected code: `tensorrt_llm/bench/benchmark/__init__.py`.

## Expected behavior

Preserve TensorRT-specific arguments when runtime_config.backend is None, while continuing to remove them for PyTorch and AutoDeploy.

## Root cause and fix

The backend-dispatch sentinel and the filtering condition disagree. The fix changes the condition to backend != None, matching RuntimeConfig's actual representation.

## Reproduction and verification

On the pre-fix revision, invoke get_llm with backend=None and kwargs containing extended_runtime_perf_knob_config (for example cuda_graph_mode=True), using a stub TensorRT LLM constructor to capture its arguments. The old path removes the setting; the fixed path preserves it. Source evidence is the PR diff together with RuntimeConfig at base commit 98453d2bb737356d393c525d96f05a622adadcf6. This is a source-derived procedure; no new test or performance measurement was executed for this filing. The issue covers this product-code defect, separately from the PR's test additions.

## Resolution record

This issue retrospectively records a product defect addressed by merged PR https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/8753.
Merge commit: `b4d17d1a4c273e573d2a5f8be33e77a25a14f5df`; merged at 2025-11-03T05:34:06Z.
The PR is merged; this filing does not claim a new validation run or that the defect affects current main.

items.title: [Bug] trtllm-bench JSON report writing fails when the output parent directory is missing
items.author: yufeiwu-nv
items.body_excerpt:
## Product defect

generate_json_report opens the requested report file without first creating its parent directory. A report path under a missing directory raises FileNotFoundError and loses the requested JSON output after benchmark execution.

Affected code: `tensorrt_llm/bench/benchmark/__init__.py`.

## Expected behavior

Create missing parent directories before opening the JSON report, while preserving existing directories.

## Root cause and fix

The merged product-code change adds report_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) immediately before opening the report file.

## Reproduction and verification

On a pre-fix revision, call generate_json_report(Path('/tmp/trtllm-report-repro/nested/report.json'), lambda: {'ok': True}) when the chosen parent does not exist, in an environment where TensorRT-LLM is importable. Before the fix open() fails; after the fix the parent is created and JSON can be written. Use a fresh writable temporary path. This is a source-derived reproduction; it was not executed for this filing. This issue tracks only the JSON-report defect in the mixed PR, not the separate test watchdog changes or the --iteration_log shutdown hang in #18297.

items.title: [BUG] SM90 blockwise FP8 GEMM reuses modified B scales across M waves
items.author: 1sgtpepper
items.body_excerpt:
## Which component has the problem?

CUTLASS C++

## Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

SM90 cooperative blockwise FP8 GEMM applies the preceding M wave's A scale again when processing the next M wave. With CTA tile 256×128×128 and scale granularity 128×64×128, `D[128,0]` is **1024 instead of 512**.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

In a checkout of `59e3a3338d516ca6ce0e073af8da65289678a35c`:

```sh
curl -fL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/1sgtpepper/cutlass/75e7b4a8a2859c317209d81c91c5ab9158a573e7/test/regression/fp8_scale_wave.cu -o fp8_scale_wave.cu
nvcc -std=c++17 -O3 -lineinfo --expt-relaxed-constexpr \
  -gencode=arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a \
  -Iinclude -Itools/util/include fp8_scale_wave.cu -o fp8_scale_wave
./fp8_scale_wave
```

Inputs are FP8 E4M3 ones, with A scales 2 and 4 across the row bands and B scales 1 and 2 across the column bands.

```text
minimal l=0 m=128 n=0 actual=1024 expected=512
minimal tile=256x128x128 scale=128x64x128 stages=3 problem=256x128x128x1 mismatches=16384 FAIL
```

**Expected behavior**

Each M wave multiplies its own A scale by the original B scale for the current K tile.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**

- CUTLASS `59e3a3338d516ca6ce0e073af8da65289678a35c`, main as of September 8, 2026. The affected collective is byte-identical in `v4.8.0dev` and `v4.7.1`; these releases were not executed.
- H100 80GB HBM3, driver 580.95.05; CUDA 13.1.1.
- Modal cloud GPU, Ubuntu 24.04 container, Linux x86_64.

**Additional context**

The `ScaleMsPerWave == 1 && ScaleNsPerTile > 1` path modifies B-scale registers reused by successive M waves, in both the main loop and drain. Reloading B's original scales makes all ten `--all` cases pass; restoring the old code restores the same six failures.

This leads to very weird issues where a Reload of our Grafana dashboard can show wildly different plots, on the same cluster, same timespan, same everything: We also confirmed by investigating our Prometheus replicas that *one* of them *consistently* is not receiving all metrics: This could be verified by just scraping the `/metrics` endpoint manually; it did in fact return entirely different results depending on which iteration of the scraping it was: With this, it basically makes reliably working on these metrics impossible, since you never know whether you really see "the truth" or not. We got more information that the metrics seem to be "complete" only every 10s, pretty reliably: This also explains why *one* of our Prometheus replicas consistently does see full metrics and the other one doesn't. ### Versions / Dependencies Ray 2.55.0, Python 3.12, Linux ### Reproduction script [no reproduction] ### Issue Severity High: It blocks me from completing my task.

items.title: [core][rdt] Add execution-ucx (Axon) as an RDT backend
items.author: Florentino-Ding
items.body_excerpt: ### Description I would like to propose adding [execution-ucx](https://github.com/MoFHeka/execution-ucx) (via Axon) as a new Ray Direct Transport (RDT) backend. execution-ucx is an asynchronous communication framework built on OpenUCX and the P2300 `std::execution` model. I have integrated it into Ray RDT through Axon, a C++ communication layer with Python bindings. ### Performance Results I benchmarked the execution-ucx backend against GLOO and NIXL using **Ray's official `rdt_single_node_benchmark`**, with CPU tensors ranging from 4 B to 1 GB. The results show that execution-ucx consistently achieves the lowest end-to-end latency across all tested tensor sizes. | Tensor Size | GLOO | NIXL | execution-ucx (Axon) | |---|---:|---:|---:| | 4 B | 5.92 ms | 9.59 ms | **5.63 ms** | | 150 KB | 5.89 ms | 10.20 ms | **5.63 ms** | | 1 MB | 6.43 ms | 11.10 ms | **6.28 ms** | | 100 MB | 179.5 ms | 238.0 ms | **143.1 ms** | | 1 GB | 1.72 s | 2.36 s | **1.37 s** | Compared with the existing backends: - **vs. NIXL:** 1.66–1.81× speedup across all tested tensor sizes. - **vs. GLOO:** Up to 1.26× speedup, with the largest improvements observed for 100 MB and 1 GB tensors. The stage-level breakdown also shows that execution-ucx spends less time in the RDT handoff stage, which accounts for a significant portion of the end-to-end latency. These results suggest that execution-ucx could be a promising alternative RDT backend, particularly for large CPU tensor transfers. **Benchmark stage breakdown:** ### Use Case Provide a lower-latency RDT backend for CPU tensor transfers between Ray actors, with the potential to extend support to GPU tensors and multi-node RDMA communication. ### References - [execution-ucx](https://github.com/MoFHeka/execution-ucx?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - [Related issue: UCCL as an RDT backend](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/60433) I would appreciate feedback from the Ray maintainers on integrating this backend into RDT.

items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

`ExecutionOptions.label_selector` promises to constrain every task and actor created by a Dataset, including shuffle and aggregation tasks. The disk-based `SHUFFLE_V2` map and reduce operators do not merge that selector into the remote options passed to their tasks.

Both disk V2 shuffle map and reduce tasks should carry the Dataset's `label_selector`. Operator-level selectors must win for conflicting keys, consistent with `merge_label_selector()` and legacy shuffle behavior.

The affected implementation:
- `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/shuffle_operators/disk_shuffle_map_operator.py`
- `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/shuffle_operators/disk_shuffle_reduce_operator.py`

### Versions / Dependencies

`master`

### Reproduction script

Start a two-node cluster where only the worker carries the `training` label.
For example, start the worker with:

```bash
ray start --address=<head-address> --labels='{"ray-subcluster":"training"}'
```

Then run the following against that cluster. With a currently nonexistent label selector, correct behavior is for the map/reduce tasks to remain pending; current behavior submits them without the selector and allows them to run on available nodes.

```python
import ray
from ray.data.context import DataContext, ShuffleStrategy

ray.init(address="auto")

ctx = DataContext.get_current()
ctx.shuffle_strategy = ShuffleStrategy.SHUFFLE_V2
ctx.use_disk_based_hash_shuffle = True
ctx.execution_options.label_selector = {"ray-subcluster": "does-not-exist"}

result = ray.data.range(100, override_num_blocks=4).repartition(2, keys=["id"])
print(result.materialize().take_all())
```

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

items.title: Illegal memory access in triton kernel and non-determinism codegen
items.author: xw285cornell
items.body_excerpt:
Hi team, we seem to identified an issue that triton is generating non-deterministic codegen results, and in certain cases (small chances) it seems to have illegal memory access due to out of bound access in shared memory. 
The triton code is fairly simple (shown below). We run the code many times (disabled pytorch's codegen cache) and it seems it produced different shared memory: 
Most of times: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 2560, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}
Sometimes: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 544, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}

So sometimes it only asks for 544 bytes for shared memory space which might lead to out of bound access to shared mem. We checked and ttir is the same across the two runs, but llir is different. Wondering if you can shed some lights on this (and whether the codegen is deterministic. Also this is still on llvm IR - not sure if it repros in MLIR. 

```
from torch._inductor.triton_ops.autotune import pointwise

@pointwise(
    size_hints=[262144, 64],
    tile_hint=TileHint.DEFAULT,
    filename="notebook",
    meta={
        "signature": {0: "*bf16", 1: "*fp32", 2: "*bf16", 3: "i32", 4: "i32"},
        "device": 0,
        "constants": {},
        "mutated_arg_names": [],
        "configs": [instance_descriptor(divisible_by_16=(0, 1, 2, 3), equal_to_1=())],
    },
)
@triton.jit
def triton_(
    in_ptr0,
    in_ptr1,
    out_ptr0,
    xnumel,
    ynumel,
    XBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
    YBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
):
    xnumel = 262144
    ynumel = 62
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:, None]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    yoffset = tl.program_id(1) * YBLOCK
    yindex = yoffset + tl.arange(0, YBLOCK)[None, :]
    ymask = yindex < ynumel
    x0 = xindex % 512
    x1 = xindex // 512
    y2 = yindex
    x3 = xindex
    tmp0 = tl.load(
        in_ptr0
        + (
            512
            + x0
            + (1536 * x1)
            + (786432 * y2)
            + (786432 * (((x0 + (512 * x1)) // 262144)))
        ),
        xmask & ymask,
    ).to(tl.float32)
    tmp1 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (512 + x0), xmask)
    tmp2 = tmp1.to(tl.float32)
    tmp3 = tmp0 + tmp2
    tmp4 = 2.8284271247461903
    tmp5 = tmp3 / tmp4
    tl.store(
        out_ptr0 + (y2 + (62 * x3) + tl.zeros([XBLOCK, YBLOCK], tl.int32)),
        tmp5,
        xmask & ymask,
    )
```

items.title: Tier-aware prefix scoring follow-ups from #2587
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
Follow-up to #2587. Tracking the open items from @varungup90's [review](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pull/2587#pullrequestreview-5463866402).

- [ ] Tier is only set when a (prefix, pod) entry is created, and `ProcessBlockRemoved` drops the pod whatever tier is removed. With CPU offload, vLLM copies a block to CPU while the GPU copy is still there, so `Stored(GPU) → Stored(CPU) → Removed(GPU)` ends with the pod removed instead of scored as CPU. Just overwriting `Medium` doesn't work either, since blocks still on GPU would score as CPU. Plan: track the set of tiers per (prefix, pod) and score with the best one.
- [ ] Decide whether removals should also be scoped by `group_idx`.
- [ ] Fix the `DecodeEventBatch` doc comment. vLLM sends one `EventBatch` per message (`[ts, [map events], dp_rank]`), not one event per message.
- [ ] Add a decoder test fixture in that shape.
- [ ] Share the optional-field parsing between `parseBlockStoredArray` and `parseEventMap`.
- [ ] From @bolubo: should `MatchPrefix` weight the longest match instead of taking the max weighted score?

No impact without offloading, since GPU and empty `medium` both weigh 1.0.

**Area:** Testing (E2E)

## Summary

In the `Installation Tests` workflow, the `Run installation e2e tests` step went from 9m15s in mid-July to 40m36s now, and the whole workflow from about 20 minutes to 54. The `installation-test` job has a 75-minute timeout.

Measured on two runs of the same workflow:

- July 13: https://github.com/Jeffwan/aibrix/actions/runs/29281096831/job/86923371188
- October 8, `a228471` (main at #2930): https://github.com/Jeffwan/aibrix/actions/runs/37735233267/job/113174859334

## Numbers

| | Jul 13 | Oct 8 |
|---|---|---|
| Whole workflow | 20.5 min | 54 min |
| `Run installation e2e tests` step | 9m15s | 40m36s |
| Test packages | 1 (`./test/e2e`) | 13 |
| Top-level tests | 44 | 180 |
| Sum of test time | 486s | 2,123s |
| Compile time before the first test | 47s | 3m08s |

October 8 time per package. All packages run one after another (`go test -p 1`):

| Package | Time |
|---|---|
| gateway/routing | 527s |
| controller/roleset | 360s |
| controller/stormservice | 257s |
| gateway/pd | 218s |
| controller/podset | 206s |
| controller/modeladapter | 169s |
| controller/modelclaim | 163s |
| controller/raycluster | 117s |
| controller/modelwarmup | 46s |
| gateway/api | 32s |
| controller/modelrouter | 25s |
| controller/autoscaling (+ external-metrics) | ~5s |

## Why it grew (about +31 min)

### 1. New controller lifecycle E2E tests: about +19 min

Controller tests went from about 204s (only `TestRoleSetInPlaceUpdate`) to 1,348s. Every new package runs on the same kind cluster, one after another, so each one adds its full time to the step.

| Change | Package time now |
|---|---|
| StormService E2E (#2733, Sep 16) | 257s |
| PodSet lifecycle E2E (#2751, Sep 20) | 206s |
| ModelAdapter E2E no longer skipped (#2657, Sep 3) | 169s |
| ModelClaim E2E (#2460 Jul 18, expanded through #2929 Oct 8) | 163s |
| RayClusterFleet lifecycle E2E (#2753, Sep 20) | 117s |
| ModelWarmup E2E (#2769, Oct 2) | 46s |
| ModelRouter lifecycle E2E (#2743, Sep 19) | 25s |
| RoleSet historical-node (#2628) and drain (#2736) tests enabled in CI | roleset 202s → 360s |

### 2. Gateway tests: about +8 min

Gateway tests went from about 282s to 777s.

- **Each request to the mock is about 3.3× slower (#2383, Jul 14).** That change turned on capacity-aware latency in the mock by default. A request with no `max_tokens` now sleeps about 0.03s + 2ms × `randint(10, 500)` output tokens. That averages about 0.55s, where it used to be a fixed 0.2s.
  - 30 pod-discovery requests: 6.3s → 20.8s.
  - The 8 routing tests present in both runs: 163s → 351s in total. `TestRandomRouting` went 21s → 67s; the VTC tests went from about 21s to 52–61s.
- **New tests:**
  - power-of-two routing: 137s
  - PD failure, bucketing and watchdog tests: `gateway/pd` is 218s now
  - backend-request and API endpoint tests

### 3. Build overhead: about +4 min

#2676 (Sep 8) split the suite into packages and added `go test -p 1`. The `-p` flag limits concurrent compile actions as well as test binaries, so all compilation is now serial:

- compile time before the first test: 47s → 3m08s
- about 5–9s of compiling and linking before each of the 13 packages

items.title: [Bug] PodAutoscaler status is rewritten on every reconcile, alternating between two versions
items.author: AarnavNoble
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

For `scalingStrategy: KPA` or `APA`, the controller writes the PodAutoscaler status on every reconcile, even when nothing about the target or its metrics has changed. Two code paths set the same conditions with different text, and each one overwrites the other:

| Condition | `computeStatus` (start of `Reconcile`) | `reconcileCustomPA` |
|---|---|---|
| `AbleToScale` | reason `Configured`, empty message | reason `SucceededGetScale`, message `successfully retrieved target scale` |
| `ScalingActive` | message `desired=1, actual=1` | message `desired=1, actual=1; reason=stable` |

A reconcile that reads the first version writes the second, and the next one writes the first again.

The controller is set up with `For(&PodAutoscaler{})` and no event filter, and the comment on `hasObservedInvalidSpec` notes that "a status update also enqueues the object". So each of these writes should enqueue the next reconcile immediately, without waiting for the 10s resync. Every reconcile lists the target's pods and fetches metrics from each of them.

`scalingStrategy: HPA` has the same overlap between `computeStatus` and the conditions copied from the HPA in `reconcileHPA`. There the second write uses the object fetched before the first write, so I expect it to fail with a conflict on alternate reconciles; that error is logged and dropped. I have not written a test for the HPA path.

### Steps to Reproduce

The unit test below builds a reconciler on the fake client, reconciles one unchanged KPA PodAutoscaler ten times, and counts status writes. Save it as `pkg/controller/podautoscaler/status_stability_test.go` and run:

```
go test ./pkg/controller/podautoscaler/ -run TestReconcileSettlesWithoutRewritingStatus -v
```

Output on `main` at `6b9ce490`:

```
round  1: status writes=2 AbleToScale.reason="SucceededGetScale" ScalingActive.message="desired=1, actual=1; reason=stable"
round  2: status writes=1 AbleToScale.reason="Configured" ScalingActive.message="desired=1, actual=1"
round  3: status writes=1 AbleToScale.reason="SucceededGetScale" ScalingActive.message="desired=1, actual=1; reason=stable"
round  4: status writes=1 AbleToScale.reason="Configured" ScalingActive.message="desired=1, actual=1"
...
round 10: status writes=1 AbleToScale.reason="Configured" ScalingActive.message="desired=1, actual=1"
status was rewritten 8 times across 8 reconciles of an unchanged PodAutoscaler
```

<summary>status_stability_test.go</summary>

items.title: [Feature]: Thread the explicit NVFP4 4over6 recipe into the TRT-LLM gen, CUTLASS and Prims-TS fused-MoE backends (follow-up to #5152)
items.author: feih-nv
items.body_excerpt:
### Problem

#5152 (merged as 7bcf9183) made the NVFP4 4over6 recipe an explicit argument (`nvfp4_4over6=` / `QuantConfig.nvfp4_4over6`) on the quantization entry points and the CuTe-DSL MoE, but the other fused-MoE backends still resolve the recipe from the process-wide `FLASHINFER_NVFP4_4OVER6*` environment variables at dispatch time. Today only `CuteDslRunner` sets `supports_nvfp4_4over6 = True`; every other unified runner raises `NotImplementedError` on an explicit recipe, so a caller who pins a recipe cannot use those backends at all, and a caller who leaves it unset gets whatever the environment says.

Remaining environment-reading sites on `main` (72f88c79):

- TRT-LLM gen fused MoE: `csrc/trtllm_fused_moe_runner.cu` (per-token GEMM2 activation quant) calls `resolveNVFP4Recipe(kNVFP44Over6FromEnv)`; `TODO(aleozlx, #5141)`.
- CUTLASS fused MoE: `csrc/fused_moe/cutlass_backend/cutlass_fused_moe_kernels.cuh` `dispatchNVFP44Over6Config()` reads `getEnvNVFP4Use4Over6()` and friends; `TODO(aleozlx, #5141)`.
- Prims-TS: `flashinfer/prims_ts/moe/runner.py` `_nvfp4_per_token_global_scale_inv()` reads `FLASHINFER_NVFP4_4OVER6` / `_E4M3_USE_256`, but only from `_quantize_nvfp4_fc1_output_for_fc2`, which no NVFP4 tactic reaches (see below). Prims-TS is out of scope.
- Trace templates: the MoE traces carry no recipe axis, so a replayed trace depends on the environment.

Out of scope here: `moe_ep` (not part of the unified API).

### Requested outcome

Meet #5141 for TRT-LLM gen and CUTLASS: the public flat APIs accept an explicit recipe, and the backends consume it instead of reading process-global state at dispatch.

- Public flat APIs get `nvfp4_4over6=` (unset = environment, `None` = standard, `NVFP44Over6Config` = that recipe), as `cute_dsl_fused_moe` already does since #5152: `trtllm_fp4_block_scale_{,routed_}moe`, `cutlass_fused_moe`.
- Unified runners opt in through `QuantConfig.nvfp4_4over6` on the same shared layer.

Only the GEMM2-input quantization inside the MoE is affected (GEMM1 input is quantized by the caller):

- TRT-LLM gen quantizes it itself only in per-token mode, so it follows `CuteDslRunner`: a pinned recipe only with `per_token_scale=True` on NVFP4×NVFP4, `None` always allowed.
- CUTLASS has no per-token mode, but its `doActivation` quantizer has 4over6 variants, so the recipe applies on the standard path. The caller's `fc2_input_scale` must be built with the same `e4m3_max` (documented; a calibrated value cannot be checked).

The encoder/decoder pair already exists (`nvfp4_4over6_code()` in Python, `resolveNVFP4Recipe(int64_t)` in `nvfp4Recipe.h`):

1. **TRT-LLM gen** - `int64` recipe code in `MoERunnerArgs`, trailing FFI argument of `trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe`, decoded at the GEMM2 quant site in `trtllm_fused_moe_runner.cu` (`globalScaleInv()` keeps the per-token scale consistent, so no extra scale check). Python: `core.py` op and fake op, `TrtllmMoERunner` (`backends/trtllm/sm100_runner.py`), public flat kwarg; opt in `TrtllmFp4RoutedRunner`.
2. **CUTLASS** - recipe in `QuantParams::FP4`, trailing argument on `run_moe` / `run_moe_min_latency`, `dispatchNVFP44Over6Config()` dispatches on it (two call sites: `expandInputRowsKernelLauncher`, `doActivation`; all instantiations already exist). `cutlass_fused_moe` op, fake op and public kwarg (the unified CUTLASS runner calls it); opt in `CutlassNvfp4Runner`.
3. **Trace templates** - add the recipe to the FP4 MoE templates (TRT-LLM flat / routed / shared experts, CUTLASS), present only when non-default so existing definition names do not change.

**Not in scope: Prims-TS.** Its NVFP4 MoE path never requantizes the GEMM2 input: `map_trtllm_nvfp4_moe_tactic` fixes `fc1_dtype_c=E2M1` and `fc2_use_per_token_sf_b=False` for every tactic, so FC1's epilogue emits NVFP4 (no 4over6 variant) and `_quantize_nvfp4_fc1_output_for_fc2` is unreachable (confirmed on B200: environment on/off gives bit-identical output, the requantizer is never called). A recipe there would first need a selectable per-token FC2 config, which is a kernel-selection change rather than plumbing. `PrimsTsRunner` keeps rejecting explicit values through the base `MoERunner` check.

Each backend gets the config-equals-env bit-exactness test pattern from `tests/utils/test_fp4_quantize.py::test_nvfp4_quantize_config_equals_env` (explicit recipe with the environment off must equal unset recipe with the equivalent environment), plus CPU `check_support` rejection tests.

### Target hardware

SM100 / SM103 (Blackwell); hardware-independent API change.

### Inference engine

- TRT-LLM
- PyTorch native
- Custom / other

### Affected model or model family

Any NVFP4 model using the 4over6 recipe through the TRT-LLM gen or CUTLASS fused-MoE backends.

### Current workaround

Set the four `FLASHINFER_NVFP4_4OVER6*` variables process-wide and leave `QuantConfig.nvfp4_4over6` unset. Two recipes in one process, or one recipe per backend, are not possible.

### Impact

- API usability or integration complexity
- Correctness or numerical-quality risk (a pinned recipe silently differing from the environment would rescale activations by 448/256)

### Related work

- #5141 (parent request), #5152 (first half: quantization entry points, CuTe-DSL MoE, `QuantConfig` field), #3264 / #3448 (4over6 implementation and `NVFP44Over6Config`).

items.title: Five conv filter tile access iterators invert the byte scaling in add_pointer_offset (8/sizeof_bits instead of sizeof_bits/8)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Five conv filter tile access iterators invert the byte scaling in `add_pointer_offset`: they compute `pointer_offset * 8 / sizeof_bits<Element>::value` where every sibling iterator uses `pointer_offset * sizeof_bits<Element>::value / 8`.

Affected sites:

- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h:194
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_fixed_channels.h:165
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_few_channels.h:167
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv3d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h:160
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/depthwise_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_direct_conv_optimized.h:162

For fp32 (32 bits) the inverted form is a silent no-op multiplier of 8/32 vs the correct 4; for fp16 it scales offsets by 1/2 instead of 2. All 30+ sibling iterators (activation/dgrad/wgrad variants) use the correct form, e.g. conv2d_dgrad_filter_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h:187.

Currently latent: no in-tree caller passes nonzero element-granularity pointer offsets into these mainloop A/B iterators (kernels call `add_pointer_offset` on the epilogue D iterator only). The defect surfaces for any external user advancing these public iterators manually.

items.title: Sparse split-K kernels offset the E operand without the kElementsPerElementE division
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`SparseGemmSplitKParallel`-style serial split-K in `include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sparse_gemm.h` offsets the E (metadata) operand by the wrong amount for slices beyond the first:

```cpp
// sparse_gemm.h:237
cutlass::MatrixCoord tb_offset_E{
  threadblock_tile_offset.m() * Mma::Shape::kM,
  threadblock_tile_offset.k() * params.gemm_k_size / kSparse,   // missing / kElementsPerElementE
};
```

The E iterator's extent is expressed in packed element-E columns and divides twice (`sparse_gemm.h:269`, `problem_size_k / kSparse / kElementsPerElementE`), and the sibling kernel `gemm_sparse_universal.h:622` divides twice as well when offsetting:

```cpp
cutlass::MatrixCoord tb_offset_E{
  threadblock_tile_offset.m() * Mma::Shape::kM,
  offset_k / kSparse / kElementsPerElementE,
};
```

With the missing division, every K-slice `>= 1` of a split-K sparse GEMM starts its metadata reads far past the end of the packed E tensor; all accesses are predicated off and the slice runs on zero-filled (invalid) metadata.

Concrete numbers: fp16 (`kElementsPerElementE == 2`), K=128, `split_k_slices = 2`: slice 1 has an E extent of 4 columns while its offset column is 32. Zero valid accesses.

The same formula is duplicated in two more copies of this kernel body:
- `sparse_gemm_with_absmax.h:322`
- `sparse_gemm_with_visitor.h:153`

Reachability note: nothing in-tree exercises it (`device::SparseGemm` with `split_k_slices > 1`; example 15 uses one slice), so this is latent, but the wrapper accepts split-K (`device/sparse_gemm.h` passes `args.batch_count` through).

### Suggested fix

Divide by `kElementsPerElementE` in the offset at all three sites, matching `gemm_sparse_universal.h`:

```cpp
threadblock_tile_offset.k() * params.gemm_k_size / kSparse / kElementsPerElementE,
```

items.title: [Store] Does Mooncake store plan to support awareness of layers, chunk ordering, and TP?
items.author: Hadigan
items.body_excerpt:
It looks like the current Mooncake store does not have awareness of layer granularity, chunk order (earlier vs. later chunks), or TP ranks. This can cause problems during cache eviction:

1. The store might evict KVs for only some layers, forcing prefill to recompute all layer KVs for those tokens.
2. The store might evict the KVs corresponding to the earliest chunk(s) of a token sequence, forcing prefill to recompute KVs for all chunks/tokens.
3. The store might evict KVs produced by some TP ranks, forcing all TP ranks to recompute KVs.

I think the Mooncake store should be aware of layers, chunk ordering, and TP. On eviction, it should evict a token’s KV caches for all layers and for all TP ranks together (i.e., keep KV state complete per token). 
From the chunk-order perspective, eviction policies should prefer removing KVs for later chunks first rather than evicting early-chunk KVs that make prefill expensive.

items.title: SM120 (RTX PRO 6000) MoE backend gaps: MoeConfig.backend schema missing MegaMoE entries, and no EP-capable path for this hardware
items.author: ItamarTerem
items.body_excerpt:
Hi TensorRT-LLM team,
Deploying a large MoE model (Kimi-K2.7-Code-NVFP4, 384 experts) on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120) via the pytorch backend, trtllm-serve, version 1.3.0rc20. Two related findings we wanted to raise:

1. MoeConfig.backend's pydantic Literal doesn't include MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL/MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM, even though create_moe.py's dispatch logic already handles both as real branches. Setting moe_config.backend: MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL in extra_llm_api_options.yaml fails pydantic validation before create_moe.py is ever reached, even though the underlying backend selection logic supports it. This looks like the config schema hasn't caught up to the dispatch logic yet.
2. More fundamentally: none of the EP-capable MoE backends currently work on SM120 in this build.
 - MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL / MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM: both explicitly require SM100/SM103 ("MegaMoECuteDsl requires SM100 family (SM100 or SM103); got SM120"), and fall back to CutlassFusedMoE.
 - WIDEEP: not SM-gated, but its GEMM compute still routes through the same CUTLASS kernel that produces silently incorrect output on SM120 in our testing, and additionally hit a binding mismatch in this build (run_moe() is missing value for argument '_37') before we could evaluate EP itself.
 - CUTEDSL (b12x): the only backend we've confirmed produces correct output on SM120, but has no EP support at the flashinfer level (num_local_experts != num_experts raises NotImplementedError in b12x_fused_moe).

Net result: there is currently no correct + EP-capable MoE path for SM120 in this stack, which limits per-GPU memory headroom for large-expert-count models on this hardware class.
Questions:

1. Is SM120 support planned for any of the MegaMoE/WideEP paths, or is SM100/SM103-first prioritization intentional for the near term?
2. Should we file the MoeConfig.backend schema gap as a separate, smaller issue, since that looks like a straightforward fix independent of the larger EP question?
3. Is there a recommended path for SM120 users running large MoE models today, or is CUTEDSL/no-EP the expected configuration for this hardware class in the current release?

Happy to share full repro steps/configs if helpful. Thanks for your work on this — appreciate the pointers.

items.title: [Feature]: Wire SM107 into nvfp4_gemm CuTe DSL dispatcher (cute_dsl_nvfp4_gemm_rubin has no caller)
items.author: farazkh80
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`trtllm::cute_dsl_nvfp4_gemm_rubin` (added in #19272) has no caller. The generic `nvfp4_gemm` dispatcher's CuTe DSL backend is still SM100/SM103-only, so SM107 (Rubin) can never select the Rubin NVFP4 CuTe DSL kernel through `nvfp4_gemm`.

## Details

- In `tensorrt_llm/_torch/custom_ops/torch_custom_ops.py` (`NVFP4GemmUnifiedRunner`), the `cutedsl` tactics are only collected when `get_sm_version()` is 100 or 103. On any other SM, an explicit `cutedsl`-only request raises "CuteDSL NVFP4 backend requires SM 100 (B200) or SM 103 (B300)". The `cutedsl` forward branch always builds `CuteDSLNVFP4BlackwellRunner`.
- On SM107 the only NVFP4 CuTe DSL path in use is the locality-domain inplace op (`cute_dsl_nvfp4_gemm_locality_domain_inplace_rubin`), reached from `Linear` when `enable_locality_domains` is set.
- `cute_dsl_nvfp4_gemm_rubin` is registered but unreachable.

## Proposed work

- Add SM107 support to the `nvfp4_gemm` CuTe DSL dispatcher: SM gate, tactic collection, and a forward branch that uses the Rubin runner.
- Make sure the SM100/SM103 path is unchanged.
- Add a test covering SM107 selection through `nvfp4_gemm`.

## References

- Review thread: https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/19272 (comment on `cute_dsl_nvfp4_gemm_rubin`, where the author agreed to a follow-up PR)

## llm-vram-calc

A zero-dependency Python CLI that answers the #1 question in local inference: **"will this quantization fit in my VRAM?"** — before the 40GB download.

```bash
pip install https://github.com/DangerousANEN/llm-vram-calculator/releases/download/v1.1.0/llm_vram_calculator-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl
llm-vram-calc

- 10+ model presets (Qwen 2.5/3, Llama 3.x, DeepSeek R1/V3, Phi-3, Gemma 2, Mistral)
- Quantizations from q2_k to f16 with per-model bit-precision maps
- Q8_0 auto-detection with llama.cpp fallback defaults
- Batch comparison across multiple configs
- **Offload layers calculator**: how many GPU layers fit when VRAM is short and system RAM picks up the rest
- **KV-cache estimator**: max context length for a given VRAM budget
- Verdict output: `fits` / `OOM` with exact MB breakdown (weights / KV-cache / overhead)

shortlist.title: [good-first-issue] tests: make flaky vllm_bench throughput comparisons reproducible
shortlist.author: maobaolong
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Parent tracker: #5313 · Onboarding: #3372

## Confirmed flaky behavior

`k3-multiprocess-test / vllm / vllm_bench / zmq` changes its throughput verdict without a source update:

| Build #5340, September 29, 2026 (UTC) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| [Original job](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eab1-a517-4a38-8163-b0ec7cfaff63) | LMCache throughput **7.34% slower** than baseline; fails the 5% limit |
| [Retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eaba-4671-4f79-a910-4a02cfa0cadf) | LMCache throughput **0.62% faster** than baseline; passes |

Both are `dev` builds of **`9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125`**, with no PR-base merge, vLLM **`0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676`**, and torch **`2.13.0+cu130`**. Both baseline and LMCache completed all 50 requests with 500400 input tokens. This is an intermittent benchmark verdict, not an installation failure.

The inputs are not reproducible across those attempts: the original uses seed `1790644335`, the retry `1790645482`. Each attempt uses the same seed for its own baseline/LMCache pair, but the default `RANDOM_SEED` comes from `date +%s`. The seed change is a confirmed confounder; it is **not proven to be the sole cause** of the throughput fluctuation.

## Bounded good-first task

Make this benchmark's inputs reproducible across retries, and make the comparison auditable. This is the first test-harness improvement for the confirmed flake, not a production performance optimization.

1. Replace the clock-derived default seed with a documented stable default; continue honoring an explicit `RANDOM_SEED` override.
2. Save a small comparison manifest next to `baseline.json` and `lmcache.json`: effective seed, model, request count and lengths, actual checkout SHA, installed vLLM/torch versions, and the two throughput values/verdict. Keep any new diagnostics local to this workload.
3. Preserve separate attempt results when used in CI. Follow the existing result-directory/cleanup conventions, and ensure the manifest is accessible in the job log or a public Buildkite artifact rather than merely naming a container-local file.
4. Add focused CPU-only regression coverage using stub benchmark commands: default seed is repeatable, both sides receive it, an override is honored, and success/failure summaries retain the actual numbers.

Keep the 5% throughput limit, request/token checks, and cache-retrieval validation. Do not add blanket retries, remove assertions, or present a fixed seed as proof of a resolved performance issue. #5227 already added retry mitigation; this task addresses reproducibility within the workload.

Starting points, checked at `42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052`:

- [Workload seed and result comparison](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/workloads/vllm/vllm-bench.sh).
- [Result cleanup/copying](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/cleanup.sh).
- [Buildkite step and existing retry policy](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/pipeline.yml).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Default inputs are identical across attempts; explicit overrides still work.
- [ ] A reviewer can recover both results, the effective inputs, versions, and verdict from public job output/artifacts.
- [ ] Stubbed CPU coverage exercises default/override and passing/failing results.
- [ ] GPU validation reports first-attempt results with a fixed seed; remaining fluctuation is reported as unresolved rather than hidden.
- [ ] Existing behavioral assertions and thresholds remain effective.

## Reproduce the CI workload

The evidence below comes from CI; this issue does not claim a local GPU reproduction. Use a dedicated Linux x86_64 GPU test host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit, two available CUDA GPUs capable of running separate `Qwen/Qwen3-14B` servers, sufficient host RAM for the default 80 GiB LMCache buffer (plus the mock L2 storage for the L2 case), and disk/network access for the image, wheels, and model. CI uses CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12, and a 1 GiB `/dev/shm`. A maintainer can run the GPU validation for a contributor who only has a CPU machine.

These commands build the public CI image recipe, explicitly start Bash, and pin the historical LMCache and vLLM revisions. They are a reproduction recipe, not a fully locked copy of every historical dependency or GPU scheduling condition. Run from a fresh directory; make the actual PR against current `dev`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache.git
cd LMCache
git checkout 9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125
docker build -t lmcache-flake-ci \
  -f .buildkite/k3_harness/ci-base.Dockerfile .
docker run --rm --gpus '"device=0,1"' --shm-size=1g \
  --entrypoint bash \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace/LMCache" -w /workspace/LMCache \
  -e MAX_JOBS=1 \
  -e INFERENCE_ENGINE=vllm \
  -e LMCACHE_REQUEST_TRANSPORT=zmq \
  -e LMCACHE_PR_BASE_MERGE=never \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_VERSION=0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676 \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_ARCHIVE_INDEX_URL=https://wheels.vllm.ai/0da126676e38f5dc1b02b2c4f48dc85f90f5a79f/cu130 \
  lmcache-flake-ci -c '
    set -e
    source /opt/venv/bin/activate
    command -v git uv python3 nvcc gcc g++
    nvidia-smi
    git config --global --add safe.directory /workspace/LMCache
    .buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/run.sh vllm_bench
  '
```

Use the linked failed and passed jobs as the initial reproduction pair. For subsequent GPU runs, record the actual checkout SHA, installed package versions, GPU model, input settings, and first-attempt result. A green retry alone does not show that the underlying fluctuation was fixed.

## Claim and contribution rules

This is primarily for a new contributor. Claim **one active sub-issue at a time** by commenting `/claim` here; check existing comments and ass

shortlist.title: [Bug] Disconnected streaming client leaves a zombie request that decodes to max_tokens and floods "state was deleted in TokenizerManager" (regression from #34160 revert)
shortlist.author: wkgcass
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

> Submitted by GLM-5.3

When a streaming client disconnects mid-generation, the scheduler-side request
is never aborted and keeps decoding until `max_tokens`. Every output batch for
that request logs:

```
Received output for rid='...' but the state was deleted in TokenizerManager.
```

at a high rate (observed ~15 lines/s per request, sustained for the entire
remaining generation — in production two zombie requests burned GPU for 15+
minutes and occupied both `--max-running-requests` slots, blocking all new
requests from being scheduled).

Root cause (verified on current `main`):

1. `TokenizerManager.generate_request` has an `except BaseException` cleanup
   that calls `_discard_pending_req_states(obj)`. It was added for failures
   *before* the request reaches the scheduler (e.g. input-length validation),
   but a client disconnect raises `asyncio.CancelledError` — also a
   `BaseException` — so the state of a request that **is running on the
   scheduler** gets popped immediately at disconnect time.

2. The delayed safety net then doesn't fire: `create_abort_task` (attached to
   the `StreamingResponse` as a background task, runs ~2s after teardown)
   calls `abort_request(rid)`, which early-returns on
   `tokenizer_worker_num == 1 and rid not in self.rid_to_state`. The
   `AbortReq` is never dispatched, so the scheduler never learns the client
   is gone and decodes to `max_tokens`; each `BatchStrOutput` for that rid
   hits the deleted-state error path.

This is a regression of 71043b9dbb ("Revert parallel request lifecycle
tracking from #32588", #34160). Before the revert, #32588 handled this
correctly: `_discard_pending_req_states(obj, request_lifecycles)` dispatched
`AbortReq` for every rid whose state had `dispatched == True` **before**
removing the state. The revert deleted the `dispatched` markers and the
abort-then-remove ordering, leaving the orphan window. Presumably not covered
by CI because it requires killing a streaming client mid-generation.

(The `HEALTH_CHECK`-prefixed rid skip next to the error log is a different,
known race — unrelated, see #11925.)

Suggested minimal fix (verified in production, restores the pre-revert
invariant without reintroducing full lifecycle tracking):

1. In `generate_request`, treat cancellation separately and only discard
   state if the request was never dispatched:

```python
        dispatched = False
        try:
            ...
            self._send_one_request(tokenized_obj)
            dispatched = True
            async for response in self._wait_one_response(obj, request):
                yield response
        except (asyncio.CancelledError, GeneratorExit):
            # Client disconnect mid-request: keep the state of a dispatched
            # request so the delayed background abort still finds it; the
            # scheduler's abort echo deletes it cleanly. Discarding here
            # orphans the scheduler-side request, which then decodes to
            # max_tokens.
            if not dispatched:
                self._discard_pending_req_states(obj)
            raise
        except BaseException:
            self._discard_pending_req_states(obj)
            raise
```

2. Add a `force` flag to `abort_request` that bypasses the
   `rid not in self.rid_to_state` early-return, and pass `force=True` from
   `create_abort_task` (the scheduler's `abort_request` handler scans by rid
   prefix and no-ops unknown rids, so force-dispatching is safe — it just
   closes the window where the state was already deleted elsewhere):

```python
    def abort_request(self, rid: str = "", abort_all: bool = False, force: bool = False):
        if not abort_all and not rid:
            ...
            return
        if (
            not abort_all
            and not force
            and get_serving().tokenizer_worker_num == 1
            and rid not in self.rid_to_state
        ):
            return
```

With this patch: disconnect → decode stops within the 2s abort window, zero
error lines; normal streaming completions (`[DONE]`) unaffected.

### Reproduction

Any model; the bug is in the tokenizer-manager layer and is
hardware/model-independent.

1. Launch a server:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server --model <any-model> --port 30000
```

2. Start a long streaming generation, then kill the client mid-stream:

```bash
curl -sN http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"<any-model>","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Count from 1 to 5000, one number per line."}],"max_tokens":16000,"stream":true}' &
sleep 10 && kill -9 %1
```

**Actual**: `sglang:num_running_reqs` stays 1 and the request decodes until
`max_tokens`; the log floods with the message above (same rid, repeated many
times per second).

**Expected**: the request is aborted shortly after the disconnect (within the
2s background-abort window) and decode stops.

### Environment

- sglang `main` (regression introduced by 71043b9dbb / #34160, still present
  as of a1f9508dd4; no commit has touched `tokenizer_manager.py` since —
  `except BaseException` cleanup and the guard are at current lines ~825
  and ~1952)
- single GPU, TP=1, `--max-running-requests 2`; speculative decoding enabled
  (DSPARK) on our instance, but nothing here is spec-specific
- reproduced and root-caused on a fork whose `tokenizer_manager.py` is
  unmodified upstream code

comments.author: eug3
comments.body:
### Additional production evidence + a working workaround (2x DGX Spark, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4)

We hit this exact bug in production today on **SGLang TP=2 across 2 DGX Spark nodes** (`Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`, speculative NEXTN, `--tokenizer-worker-num 1`). Sharing our numbers and a working mitigation in case it helps:

**Observed symptoms (identical to #36333 and #36876):**
- 3 zombie requests accumulated over hours (first at 11:58, then 13:02, then 14:41), each from a client that disconnected mid-stream.
- GPU pinned at ~95% for 2+ hours with **zero completed requests**; `sglang:num_running_reqs` stuck at 3.0.
- Log flooded with `Received output for rid=... but the state was deleted in TokenizerManager` — **~148,000 lines** sustained across hours.
- `POST /abort_request` returned 200 but had **no effect** (confirmed the `abort_request()` early-return: with `tokenizer_worker_num == 1` and `rid not in self.rid_to_state`, the `AbortReq` never reaches the scheduler — exactly as #36333 describes).
- New requests queued behind the zombies; spend/completion never logged for the zombies.

**Our workaround (patched `tokenizer_manager.py` in the running image, verified):**
1. `abort_request()`: removed the early-return when `rid not in self.rid_to_state` — always dispatch `AbortReq` to the scheduler (scheduler-side abort is safe for unknown rids; it scans queues and no-ops when absent).
2. `_handle_batch_output()`: when output arrives for an already-deleted state (orphan), proactively re-send `AbortReq(rid, abort_all=False)` to reap the scheduler-side task.

**Verification:** simulated client disconnect (kill curl 2s into a streaming responses call): `num_running_reqs` → 0 within 10s, GPU → 0%, subsequent requests unaffected. Concurrent test (3 streaming, 2 killed mid-stream, 1 completed): all slots reclaimed, the completed one finished normally. 60s observation window: zero growth of "state was deleted" after the initial reap.

**Note on #36876:** even with the AbortReq reaching the scheduler, `Scheduler.abort_request()` only sets `to_finish = FINISH_ABORT()` for requests found in `[running_batch, last_batch]` — during batch transitions (overlap scheduling / speculative decoding) a request can be in neither, leaving the same zombie. Our orphan-output reap (fix 2) happens to cover that window too, but the two fixes should ideally both land upstream. Happy to provide the full patch or a minimal repro script if useful.

comments.body:
**Validation datapoint for the suggested minimal fix: GB10 unified-memory ARM + 27B-NVFP4 + speculative decoding**

Applied the two-part minimal fix from the issue body (the `dispatched` flag + `force` flag on `abort_request`) as a read-only whole-file overlay on a dev build inside the broken window — `0.0.0.dev1+gf825d7293` (after `71043b9`, before `f478b2b`), confirmed broken pre-patch on this build. Nothing new to propose here; this is a datapoint from a topology I didn't see covered in this thread: **single NVIDIA GB10 (124608 MiB unified memory, ARM), TP=1, Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 with DFLASH speculative draft (incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2)**, `--max-running-requests 8`.

**A/B method (reproducible):**

1. Baseline: unpatched, count occurrences of the exact signature line `Received output for rid='...' but the state was deleted in TokenizerManager.` across the full server log — **2692** (4B first, same signature on 27B).
2. Kill-burst: fire 3 in-flight streaming requests, confirm `num_reqs = 3` via `/get_load` at t0, `kill -9` all clients mid-stream (~114 SSE chunks each at kill), watch drain:
   - unpatched: `num_running_reqs` held at 3 until `max_tokens`
   - patched: **3 → 0 in ~5 s**
3. Functional: short `stop|length`-terminated generations complete normally with `[DONE]`; 3/3 soaks clean, **0 Traceback / 0 ERROR** in full-log scans.

**Result: 2692 → 0 error lines, zero zombie decode time, MRR slots released within the 2 s abort window.**

Two notes for triage:

- Our overlay is a strict subset of [#35255](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/35255) (merged to main at `f478b2b`) — we don't have the chunked-prefill deferred-abort retry or the abort dedup, which is exactly why we plan to **drop the overlay entirely and rebuild from main ≥ `f478b2b`** rather than keep the local patch.
- The only thing this environment adds is confirmation that the fix holds **with the speculative-decoding draft path active on unified memory** — the disconnect/abort window behaves identically to the non-spec case above.

Happy to share the raw log excerpts and the overlay diff if useful for #35255 or the backport discussion.
